shard.title: Australasia and the Pacific
shard.author: Australasia & Pacific historian agent
shard.note: Australia and its colonies, New Zealand and the New Zealand realm, Papua New Guinea, and Britain's island empire across Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia. Territories in the Pacific island groups carry region 'pacific'; the shard region is 'australasia'. Antarctic units (aq-australian-antarctic, aq-ross-dependency) are deliberately left to the south-atlantic/polar shard. British Hawai'i (the 1843 Paulet affair) is covered by the atlantic-antarctic-outposts shard as 'british-hawaii-1843' and is deliberately not duplicated here.

territories.name: Commonwealth of Australia
territories.formalName: Commonwealth of Australia

namesOverTime.name: Commonwealth of Australia
namesOverTime.note: The word 'Commonwealth' was chosen over 'Dominion' or 'Kingdom' by the 1891 convention, borrowing from Cromwell's republic to please the colonies' democrats.

geoCoverage.label: Six colonies become six states, plus the Territory
geoCoverage.change: The six self-governing colonies federated under one Crown. Australia's external territories - Papua, New Guinea, Nauru, Norfolk Island, the Antarctic sector - are recorded separately in this atlas.

acquisitions.how: Six self-governing British colonies voted in referendums to merge into one federation, wrote their own constitution, took it to London, and had Westminster enact it as a British statute on 9 July 1900.

counterparties.name: The six colonies of New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania
counterparties.lost: Their separate existence as British colonies, and their customs revenue, defence forces and immigration powers, which went to Melbourne.

counterparties.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
counterparties.lost: Whatever standing they had held under colonial law. Section 127 ordered that they not be counted in the population, section 51(xxvi) let the new parliament make laws for every race except them, and the Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 struck them off the federal roll.
counterparties.note: The exclusions were deliberate and debated. They were not undone until 1962 (the federal vote) and 1967 (the referendum).

instrument.name: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900
instrument.note: Royal assent 9 July 1900; proclaimed to take effect on 1 January 1901. Britain amended only one clause of the Australians' draft, on appeals to the Privy Council.

people.name: Edmund Barton
people.role: first prime minister; led the federation campaign and then the Immigration Restriction Act

people.name: Henry Parkes
people.role: New South Wales premier whose 1889 Tenterfield speech started the campaign

people.name: Samuel Griffith
people.role: Queensland premier who drafted the 1891 constitution bill

acquisitions.resistance: None was armed. Aboriginal people were not consulted at any stage; the conventions that wrote the constitution had no Aboriginal delegates and the referendums were held on rolls they were kept off.

evidence.author: Helen Irving
evidence.work: To Constitute a Nation: A Cultural History of Australia's Constitution
evidence.supports: The making of the constitution and what the framers intended.

statusPeriods.label: A dominion: its own parliament, Britain's foreign policy
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Australians elected their own government and it did as it liked at home; Britain still declared war on Australia's behalf in 1914 and 1939, and the highest court of appeal was the Privy Council in London.
statusPeriods.franchise: All adult men and women from 1902, except that the Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 barred 'aboriginal natives of Australia, Asia, Africa, and the Islands of the Pacific' from the federal roll. Aboriginal Australians did not all get the federal vote until 1962.
statusPeriods.note: In 1914 Andrew Fisher promised Britain 'the last man and the last shilling'. Of about 416,000 Australians who enlisted, some 62,000 died - from a population of fewer than five million.

statusPeriods.label: Independent in fact; a few threads left to cut
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Australia adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1942 and backdated it to 1939, so Britain could no longer legislate for it. What remained were appeals to the Privy Council and Britain's residual power over the states, both ended in 1986.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default for 'dominion' is 1. After 1942 Britain had no legislative power over the Commonwealth at all and John Curtin had already told Churchill that Australia looked to America 'free of any pangs'; leaving this at 1 would overstate British authority by four decades.
statusPeriods.franchise: Aboriginal Australians won the federal vote in 1962; voting became compulsory for them, as for everyone, in 1984. The 1967 referendum passed with 90.77 per cent, the largest yes vote in Australian history.

date.display: between 1901 and 1986 - historians and lawyers disagree
date.note: There are four defensible answers. 1901: a self-governing federation. 1931/1942: the Statute of Westminster, adopted by Australia in 1942 and backdated to 3 September 1939, ended Britain's power to legislate for the Commonwealth. 1986: the Australia Acts ended Privy Council appeals and Britain's residual power over the states. Australian courts have variously used all three.

departures.how: Nobody fought and there was no independence day: Britain's authority over Australia was removed piece by piece, at Australia's request, by Australian and British statutes passed between 1901 and 1986.

becomes.name: Australia

led.name: John Curtin
led.role: prime minister who in 1941 turned to the United States 'free of any pangs' and in 1942 adopted the Statute of Westminster

led.name: Robert Menzies
led.role: prime minister who resisted cutting the last links and kept appeals to London alive into the 1960s

led.name: Bob Hawke
led.role: prime minister who negotiated the Australia Acts of 1986 with the states and with Britain

departures.movement: No independence movement. Australia's separation from Britain was driven by war, trade and law, not by nationalist agitation.

cost.note: Nobody died in Australia's separation from Britain. Australians did die in enormous numbers in Britain's wars: about 62,000 in 1914-18 and 39,000 in 1939-45, from a small population, which is part of why the connection loosened.

departures.borders: Nothing moved. Australia kept the state boundaries the surveyors had drawn, and kept the external territories it had been given - Papua, Norfolk Island, the Antarctic sector - which is why an ex-colony is still administering territories today.

instrument.name: Australia Act 1986 (Cth) and Australia Act 1986 (UK)
instrument.note: Two identical statutes, one passed at Westminster and one in Canberra, because nobody could agree which parliament had the power to end the other's power.

contested.note: The date of Australian independence is a live legal question, not a settled fact. Courts have treated 1901, 1942 and 1986 as the moment of separation depending on the issue in front of them.

positions.claim: Australia became independent in 1901: from that day it had its own parliament, its own laws and no British minister in its cabinet.
Independence dates from the Statute of Westminster Adoption Act 1942, backdated to 1939, which ended Britain's power to legislate for Australia.
Independence was completed only by the Australia Acts of 1986, which ended Privy Council appeals and British power over the states.
positions.heldBy: The High Court's reasoning in several modern cases

evidence.author: Anne Twomey
evidence.work: The Australia Acts 1986: Australia's Statutes of Independence
evidence.supports: The legal steps by which Britain's authority over Australia ended.

violence.note: The frontier did not stop at federation: the last officially sanctioned killings of Aboriginal people were at Coniston in the Northern Territory in 1928, twenty-seven years after Australia became a nation.

populationTransfer.note: Between about 1910 and 1970 governments removed somewhere between one in ten and one in three Aboriginal children from their families under laws that made officials their legal guardians. No government kept a national register of removals, so there is no agreed total and none can now be made; the 1997 Bringing Them Home inquiry gave a proportion instead, and found no purge of the archive.

commonwealth.note: Australia is one of fifteen Commonwealth realms that still share the British monarch as head of state. A referendum to become a republic was defeated in November 1999, 54.87 per cent to 45.13.

retainedTerritory.note: Australia still administers seven external territories it was handed by Britain or took under a mandate, including Norfolk Island, the Ashmore and Cartier Islands and 42 per cent of Antarctica.

consequences.borderLegacy: Australia is the only country that is also a continent, so it inherited no disputed land borders - only maritime ones, and the Torres Strait line that separates Islander families from their neighbours in Papua New Guinea.
consequences.economicLegacy: Wool, gold and wheat gave way to iron ore, coal and gas; Britain was Australia's main market until it joined the European Economic Community in 1973, after which Japan and then China replaced it.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, a Westminster parliament, an American-style federation and a constitution that mentioned Aboriginal people only to exclude them until 1967.

peak.populationNote: The first Commonwealth census, 31 March 1901. Section 127 of the constitution required that Aboriginal people be left out, so the figure is deliberately incomplete; estimates of the Aboriginal population that year are around 93,000 counted and probably more.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1901 census of Commonwealth of Australia
populationWarrant.supports: Commonwealth of Australia’s largest recorded population: 3,773,801 people, counted in 1901.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Stuart Macintyre
evidence.work: A Concise History of Australia
evidence.supports: Federation, the White Australia policy and the twentieth century.

evidence.author: Marilyn Lake
evidence.work: Drawing the Global Colour Line: White Men's Countries and the International Challenge of Racial Equality
evidence.supports: White Australia in its imperial and international context. Written with Henry Reynolds.

evidence.author: Anne Twomey
evidence.work: The Australia Acts 1986: Australia's Statutes of Independence
evidence.supports: How and when British legal authority over Australia ended.

pedagogy.hook: Australia's constitution came into force as an Act of the British Parliament, and the first law the new parliament passed was one to keep non-white people out.

misconception.belief: Australia became independent in 1901.
misconception.correction: In 1901 Australia got its own parliament, but Britain still made its foreign policy, still declared war on its behalf in 1914 and 1939, and still housed its highest court. Australia adopted the Statute of Westminster only in 1942, and the last British legal power over Australia ended on 3 March 1986. There is no independence day, which is why Australia Day is still an invasion date from 1788.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Australia is the model of the slow exit: no war, no independence day, no single document - just six decades of statutes. It is the opposite of India in 1947 and Kenya in 1963, and it shows that how a place left the empire depended mostly on who was allowed to vote in it.

territories.name: New South Wales
territories.formalName: Colony of New South Wales

namesOverTime.name: New South Wales
namesOverTime.note: Named by James Cook on Possession Island. He never explained the name; the coast looks nothing like South Wales.

namesOverTime.name: Country of the Eora, Dharug, Dharawal, Gundungurra, Wiradjuri and dozens of other nations

from.display: for tens of thousands of years before 1788
from.note: Archaeological dates for continuous Aboriginal occupation keep getting older; Madjedbebe in the Northern Territory is dated to about 65,000 years ago. No single start date can be given, so none is claimed here.

namesOverTime.note: There was no single name because there was no single polity: the land Phillip was given covered hundreds of nations with their own laws, languages and boundaries.

modernSuccessors.name: Australia (State of New South Wales, and the Australian Capital Territory)

geoCoverage.label: Claimed to the 135th meridian; occupied for about 30 km around Sydney
geoCoverage.change: Phillip's commission of 1787 gave him everything from Cape York to the southern tip of Tasmania and west to 135 degrees east, plus 'all islands adjacent in the Pacific Ocean'. On the ground the British held a few hundred hectares.

geoCoverage.label: Without Van Diemen's Land
geoCoverage.change: Sydney planted a garrison at Risdon Cove in Van Diemen's Land. This atlas shows the island separately from that day, though in law it stayed a dependency of New South Wales until 3 December 1825.

geoCoverage.label: Without the northern outposts
geoCoverage.change: Convict stations went north in the same month: Moreton Bay on 24 September 1824, and Melville Island off the Top End two days later. Both are shown here under Queensland and the Northern Territory.

geoCoverage.label: Without the Port Phillip District
geoCoverage.change: John Batman's syndicate crossed from Van Diemen's Land and signed a 'treaty' with Wurundjeri elders for 600,000 acres. Governor Bourke voided it and the district was taken by the Crown instead.

geoCoverage.label: The colony students would recognise
geoCoverage.change: South Australia was proclaimed at Glenelg. Victoria followed in 1851 and Queensland in 1859, leaving New South Wales roughly its modern shape.

acquisitions.how: On a small island off Cape York, James Cook raised a flag, fired three volleys and claimed the whole east coast of the continent for George III, having spoken to almost nobody who lived on it.

counterparties.name: The Aboriginal nations of eastern Australia
counterparties.lost: Sovereignty over roughly two million square kilometres, taken by a ceremony they were not present at and were never told about.
counterparties.note: Cook's secret instructions told him to take possession 'with the consent of the Natives' or, failing that, to claim land 'uninhabited'. He did neither: he recorded meeting people repeatedly, then claimed the coast anyway.

instrument.name: Secret Additional Instructions to Lieutenant James Cook, 30 June 1768
instrument.note: The instructions are a real Admiralty document; the claim of 1770 was made under them and had no treaty behind it.

people.name: James Cook
people.role: commander of HMS Endeavour; made the claim on Possession Island

people.name: Joseph Banks
people.role: naturalist on the voyage; later told a Commons committee the country was thinly peopled and would take convicts

acquisitions.resistance: At Kamay (Botany Bay) on 29 April 1770 two Gweagal men, one of them later named as Cooman, stood on the beach and threw spears at the landing party; Cook's men shot at them and took about fifty spears away.

evidence.author: Nicholas Thomas
evidence.work: Discoveries: The Voyages of Captain Cook
evidence.supports: The 1770 voyage, the Botany Bay encounter and the terms of the claim.

acquisitions.how: Eleven ships under Arthur Phillip landed about 1,370 people, roughly 750 of them convicts, at Sydney Cove, and began clearing land that belonged to the Eora without asking or paying for it.

counterparties.name: The Eora peoples of Sydney Harbour, including the Gadigal, Wangal, Cammeraygal and Bidjigal
counterparties.lost: Their fishing grounds, camps and freshwater within months, and about half their people to smallpox in April 1789.
counterparties.note: The 1789 epidemic's origin is disputed: it may have come from Macassan contact in the north, or from variolous matter carried by the fleet's surgeons. Nobody has proved either case.

instrument.name: Commission and Instructions to Governor Arthur Phillip
instrument.note: The instructions ordered Phillip to 'conciliate their affections' and punish anyone who harmed Aboriginal people. They also granted him every acre to dispose of as he saw fit.

people.name: Arthur Phillip
people.role: first governor; ordered both conciliation and the taking of the land

people.name: Bennelong
people.role: Wangal man seized on Phillip's orders in 1789 to act as intermediary; later sailed to England and returned

people.name: Pemulwuy
people.role: Bidjigal leader who fought a twelve-year guerrilla campaign against the settlement from 1790

acquisitions.resistance: Pemulwuy raided farms from 1790 until he was shot in 1802; his preserved head was sent to Joseph Banks in London. His son Tedbury fought on until 1810.

cost.note: No usable count exists of Aboriginal deaths around Sydney in the first decade. The smallpox of April 1789 alone is thought to have killed about half the people of the harbour.

evidence.author: Grace Karskens
evidence.work: The Colony: A History of Early Sydney
evidence.supports: The first decades of the settlement and its relations with the Eora.

statusPeriods.label: Rule by governor: a gaol run as a colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: For 35 years the governor was the entire government - he made the law, granted the land, controlled the only currency and commanded the troops - and his orders came by ship from London six months late.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Sydney, under the Home Office and from 1801 the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The New South Wales Act 1823 gave the governor a nominated Legislative Council of five to seven men and a Supreme Court, which was the first check on him.
statusPeriods.note: In 1808 the New South Wales Corps deposed Governor William Bligh in the only successful armed takeover of government in Australian history.

statusPeriods.label: A part-elected Council of landowners
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Two thirds of the Legislative Council were elected by men with property, one third were nominated by the governor, and the governor still held the veto and the Crown lands.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Sydney, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Men with freehold worth 200 pounds or a house worth 20 pounds a year. That excluded most former convicts, all women and, in practice, every Aboriginal person.
statusPeriods.note: Convict transportation to New South Wales ended in 1840 after about 80,000 people had been shipped there. The campaign against it was led by colonists who wanted cheap land, not by humanitarians.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government: local ministers, local parliament
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Ministers sat in and answered to an elected Legislative Assembly in Sydney and ran everything except defence and foreign policy; the governor became a signature.
statusPeriods.franchise: All adult men from 1858, one of the earliest manhood suffrages anywhere. Women got the vote in 1902. Aboriginal people were not barred by the words of the Act but were kept off the rolls in practice, and the 1902 Commonwealth franchise then barred them by name.
statusPeriods.note: New South Wales won responsible government and struck gold within five years of each other; the money paid for the parliament.

departures.how: After two referendums, New South Wales voted itself into a federation with the other five colonies and stopped being a separate British colony; it became a state inside the new Commonwealth of Australia, which was still under the Crown.

becomes.name: State of New South Wales, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: Henry Parkes
led.role: premier who called for federation in the Tenterfield speech of 1889 and did not live to see it

led.name: Edmund Barton
led.role: led the New South Wales federation campaign and became Australia's first prime minister

departures.movement: The federation movement and the Australasian Federal Conventions of 1891 and 1897-98

cost.note: Nobody died. New South Wales voters approved federation twice, narrowly in 1898 and comfortably in 1899, after the required majority was lowered.

departures.borders: The colonial borders became state borders and none of them moved. The straight lines that surveyors had drawn across Wiradjuri, Barkindji and Gamilaraay country in the 1830s and 1860s are still on the map today.

instrument.name: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900
instrument.note: An Act of the Westminster Parliament. Australians wrote the constitution; the British Parliament enacted it and amended one clause on appeals to the Privy Council.

evidence.author: Stuart Macintyre
evidence.work: A Concise History of Australia
evidence.supports: The federation campaign and the referendums.

violence.note: From Pemulwuy's raids of the 1790s to the Native Police campaigns on the Darling in the 1860s, New South Wales was taken by shooting parties, poisoned flour and punitive expeditions that colonial newspapers reported openly.

toll.note: There is no colony-level count. Historians working from newspaper and police records - Reynolds, and the Newcastle University massacre-mapping project led by Lyndall Ryan - put frontier deaths in New South Wales in the thousands, with Aboriginal deaths outnumbering settler deaths by roughly ten to one. Treat these as orders of magnitude, not measurements.

populationTransfer.note: About 80,000 convicts were transported to New South Wales between 1788 and 1840, roughly one in seven of them women, and a quarter to a third of them Irish.

consequences.borderLegacy: New South Wales began as half a continent and ended as one state, shedding Tasmania, Queensland, Victoria, South Australia and the Northern Territory in turn.
consequences.economicLegacy: Wool from the 1820s, gold from 1851 and coal from the Hunter Valley made Sydney the financial capital of the southern hemisphere by 1890.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law arrived with the First Fleet and was held to apply because the land was treated as legally empty - a fiction the High Court of Australia finally rejected in Mabo in 1992.

peak.populationNote: 1901 census. Section 127 of the new constitution required that 'aboriginal natives' be left out of the reckoning, so the number is knowingly incomplete.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1901 census of New South Wales
populationWarrant.supports: New South Wales’s largest recorded population: 1,354,846 people, counted in 1901.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Grace Karskens
evidence.work: The Colony: A History of Early Sydney
evidence.supports: Settlement, the Eora, and the first fifty years.

evidence.author: John Connor
evidence.work: The Australian Frontier Wars 1788-1838
evidence.publisher: University of New South Wales Press
evidence.supports: Aboriginal resistance and colonial military practice.

evidence.author: Robert Hughes
evidence.work: The Fatal Shore: A History of the Transportation of Convicts to Australia, 1787-1868
evidence.supports: The convict system and its scale.

pedagogy.hook: Arthur Phillip's orders told him to win the affection of the people already living at Sydney Cove. The same document handed him every acre of their land to give away.

misconception.belief: Australia was settled, not conquered - the British arrived on empty land and Aboriginal people simply died out from disease.
misconception.correction: Disease killed enormous numbers, but the land was taken by force over 140 years. Pemulwuy fought around Sydney until 1802; martial law was declared at Bathurst in 1824; the Native Police shot people on the Darling into the 1880s. Britain used the label 'settlement' because settlement, unlike conquest, meant no treaty and no compensation were owed.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: New South Wales is where the legal fiction of empty land was invented for Australia. Everything that followed - no treaty, no land purchase, no compensation - flows from the choice made in 1788 to call a continent of hundreds of nations 'settled' rather than 'conquered'.

territories.name: Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania)
territories.formalName: Colony of Van Diemen's Land, renamed Tasmania in 1856

namesOverTime.name: lutruwita

from.display: from before rising seas cut the island off
from.note: People walked to the island while it was joined to the mainland; Bass Strait flooded about 12,000 years ago, after which the palawa were isolated for some 400 generations. No precise start date is recoverable.

namesOverTime.note: palawa kani is the reconstructed language of the Tasmanian Aboriginal community; lutruwita is its name for the island.

namesOverTime.name: Van Diemen's Land
namesOverTime.note: Abel Tasman named it for Anthony van Diemen, the Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies who sent him.

namesOverTime.name: Tasmania
namesOverTime.note: The colony changed its name to shed the reputation of the convict system, which had ended three years earlier.

geoCoverage.label: The island and the Bass Strait islands
geoCoverage.change: A garrison of 49 people landed at Risdon Cove on the Derwent to keep the French out; the island was a dependency of New South Wales until 3 December 1825.

acquisitions.how: Lieutenant John Bowen landed 49 people, 24 of them convicts, at Risdon Cove on Muwinina country, sent from Sydney to stop the French claiming the island; David Collins moved the settlement to Hobart five months later.

counterparties.name: The nine nations of the Tasmanian Aboriginal peoples (palawa)
counterparties.lost: The whole island. Within thirty years almost every survivor had been removed to Flinders Island, and their hunting grounds had become sheep runs.
counterparties.note: Estimates of the Aboriginal population in 1803 range from about 3,000 to 7,000 across nine nations. By 1835 fewer than 300 were left alive.

people.name: John Bowen
people.role: lieutenant who founded the Risdon Cove camp

people.name: David Collins
people.role: moved the settlement to Sullivans Cove and founded Hobart in February 1804

people.name: Tongerlongeter
people.role: leader of the Oyster Bay nation who led the eastern resistance in the Black War and surrendered on terms in 1832

acquisitions.resistance: At Risdon Cove in May 1804 soldiers fired grapeshot into a hunting party; the death toll is disputed. From 1824 the Oyster Bay and Big River nations fought a co-ordinated eight-year campaign against the settlers.

evidence.author: Lyndall Ryan
evidence.work: Tasmanian Aborigines: A History Since 1803
evidence.supports: The settlement, the Black War and the removals.

statusPeriods.label: Penal dependency of New South Wales
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A lieutenant-governor at Hobart took orders from the governor in Sydney, who took them from London. The island's job was to hold convicts too dangerous or too repeatedly convicted for the mainland.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

to.note: The first partly elected Legislative Council was chosen in October 1851; the exact polling days differed between districts.

statusPeriods.label: A separate colony, and the empire's hardest prison
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor George Arthur ran the island with a nominated council, a convict record system that tracked every prisoner, and secondary punishment stations at Macquarie Harbour, Maria Island and Port Arthur.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Hobart, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.
statusPeriods.note: About 73,000 convicts were transported to Van Diemen's Land between 1803 and 1853 - nearly half of all convicts sent to Australia, on an island with a fraction of the mainland's space.

from.note: Elections under the Australian Colonies Government Act 1850 were held in October 1851.

to.note: The first parliament under responsible government met in November 1856; the constitution had been assented to in 1855.

statusPeriods.label: Part-elected Council; transportation ends
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Two thirds of the Legislative Council were elected by propertied men, and their first great campaign was to stop Britain sending any more convicts, which it did in 1853.
statusPeriods.franchise: Men with property. The Anti-Transportation League that dominated the elections was a movement of free settlers who wanted land and respectability.

from.note: The first responsible ministry took office in November 1856.

statusPeriods.label: Tasmania: responsible government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A local parliament and cabinet in Hobart governed the island; Britain kept defence and foreign affairs and the name Van Diemen's Land was dropped to bury the memory of the convict system.
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-qualified men until 1900, when manhood suffrage came in for the Assembly. Women voted from 1903.

departures.how: Tasmania voted for federation by the largest majority of any colony - it needed the mainland's markets - and became a state of the Commonwealth of Australia, still under the Crown.

becomes.name: State of Tasmania, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: Andrew Inglis Clark
led.role: Tasmanian attorney-general who drafted much of the constitution and imported the American federal design

led.name: Edward Braddon
led.role: premier who negotiated the financial clause protecting small states

departures.movement: The federation movement

cost.note: Nobody died. Tasmania's 1898 referendum returned about 81 per cent in favour, the highest of any colony.

departures.borders: Nothing moved. The island's coastline was its border and always had been.

violence.note: The Black War of 1824-31 was the most concentrated frontier conflict in Australian history: roughly 200 colonists and at least 600 Aboriginal Tasmanians were killed on an island the size of Ireland.

toll.note: Nicholas Clements and Lyndall Ryan, working from settler depositions and newspaper reports, count about 220 colonists and 600 to 900 Aboriginal people killed between 1824 and 1831. Both stress that killings of Aboriginal people were systematically under-reported.

warrant.author: Nicholas Clements
warrant.work: The Black War: Fear, Sex and Resistance in Tasmania
warrant.supports: Nicholas Clements and Lyndall Ryan, working from settler depositions and newspaper reports, count about 220 colonists and 600 to 900 Aboriginal people killed between 1824 and 1831.
warrant.check: University of Queensland Press, 2014. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

populationTransfer.note: Two removals define the island: about 73,000 convicts shipped in, and the surviving Aboriginal Tasmanians shipped out to Wybalenna on Flinders Island between 1832 and 1835, where most of them died.

consequences.economicLegacy: Whaling, wool and convict labour built Hobart; when transportation stopped in 1853 the island's economy stalled for forty years and its people left for the Victorian goldfields.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Port Arthur is now a World Heritage site and the largest tourist attraction in Tasmania, which is one way a society metabolises a prison.

peak.populationNote: 1901 census, which did not count Aboriginal Tasmanians. About 73,000 convicts had been landed on the island between 1803 and 1853.

populationWarrant.work: The 1901 census of Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania)
populationWarrant.supports: Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania)’s largest recorded population: 172,475 people, counted in 1901.

evidence.author: Lyndall Ryan
evidence.work: Tasmanian Aborigines: A History Since 1803
evidence.supports: The Black War, the removals and the survival of the community.

evidence.author: Nicholas Clements
evidence.work: The Black War: Fear, Sex and Resistance in Tasmania
evidence.supports: Casualty counts, and what the 1820s were like for the palawa and for the settlers.

evidence.author: Henry Reynolds
evidence.work: Fate of a Free People
evidence.supports: The negotiated surrenders of 1831-32 and the legal status of the conflict.

contested.note: Tasmania is the sharpest front in Australia's 'history wars'. Keith Windschuttle's The Fabrication of Aboriginal History (2002) argued that the killings were far fewer than historians claimed and were mostly criminal rather than military. Historians including Lyndall Ryan, Henry Reynolds and the contributors to Robert Manne's Whitewash (2003) replied with the settler records themselves. The disputed quantity is the count; that a war was fought and a people were removed is not in dispute.

positions.claim: Colonists killed at least 600 Aboriginal Tasmanians in an eight-year war that the government itself called a war and answered with martial law.
positions.heldBy: Lyndall Ryan, Nicholas Clements, Henry Reynolds

positions.claim: The recorded killings number in the low hundreds and were the work of individuals, not a war of conquest.

pedagogy.hook: In 1830 the government of Van Diemen's Land put 2,200 armed men in a line across the island and swept it for a month to catch every Aboriginal person left. The Black Line cost 30,000 pounds and captured two people.

misconception.belief: The Aboriginal Tasmanians were wiped out completely, and Truganini in 1876 was the last of them.
misconception.correction: Truganini was the last of the people who had lived through the Black War on the main island. Tasmanian Aboriginal families descended from women taken to the Bass Strait islands by sealers survived, kept their identity, and won recognition; tens of thousands of Tasmanians identify as Aboriginal today, and the palawa kani language is being rebuilt from records.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Van Diemen's Land shows the machinery of empire at its most concentrated: a penal colony, a frontier war, a forced removal and a rebranding, all on one island in fifty years. It also shows how a state destroys a record - and how descendants recover one.

keyDates.what: Risdon Cove settled to keep the French out
Martial law declared against Aboriginal Tasmanians
The Black Line begins
Transportation to the island ends after 73,000 convicts

territories.name: Western Australia
territories.formalName: Colony of Western Australia (the Swan River Colony)

namesOverTime.name: New Holland
namesOverTime.note: Dutch ships had charted the western coast since 1616 and wanted nothing to do with it.

to.note: Both names were used at once for several years; 'Western Australia' won out in official use.

geoCoverage.label: A third of a continent, held from two ports
geoCoverage.change: Major Edmund Lockyer landed soldiers and convicts at King George Sound on Christmas Day 1826 to forestall a French claim; the Swan River settlement followed in 1829. Most of the 2.5 million square kilometres was Aboriginal country in fact for another century.

acquisitions.how: Major Edmund Lockyer landed 20 soldiers and 23 convicts on Menang Noongar country at King George Sound, on orders from Sydney to occupy the south-west before a French expedition could, and formally claimed the western third of the continent on 21 January 1827.

counterparties.name: The Menang Noongar people
counterparties.lost: The harbour and hunting grounds around what became Albany; relations there stayed unusually peaceful for a decade, and the dispossession happened anyway.

people.name: Edmund Lockyer
people.role: commanded the party that occupied King George Sound

people.name: Mokare
people.role: Menang Noongar man who guided and interpreted for the garrison, and made the early peace possible

acquisitions.resistance: There was little at Albany. Mokare and the commandant Collet Barker built a working relationship that later colonists did not repeat elsewhere in the colony.

acquisitions.how: Captain Charles Fremantle took possession of the whole west coast on 2 May 1829 and Captain James Stirling proclaimed a free colony on 18 June, selling Whadjuk Noongar land to investors in London by the acre before anyone had surveyed it.

counterparties.name: The Whadjuk, Binjareb and other Noongar peoples
counterparties.lost: The Swan and Canning river country, taken as land grants at the rate of 40 acres for every three pounds of capital a settler brought.
counterparties.note: No purchase, no treaty and no reserve of any kind was made for Noongar people, though the Colonial Office had discussed the question.

people.name: James Stirling
people.role: founder and first governor; personally led the attack at Pinjarra in 1834

people.name: Yagan
people.role: Whadjuk Noongar leader who fought the settlers and was shot for a bounty in 1833; his head was taken to England and not returned until 1997

people.name: Jandamarra
people.role: Bunuba leader who turned on the police he had worked for and fought a three-year campaign in the Kimberley, 1894-97

acquisitions.resistance: Yagan led resistance on the Swan until he was killed in 1833. On 28 October 1834 Stirling led 25 men against a Binjareb camp at Pinjarra and killed between 15 and 80 people, including women and children; one soldier died.

cost.note: The Pinjarra death toll depends on who is counted and who is believed: Stirling reported 15 killed, later settler and Noongar accounts put it far higher. Noongar people call it a massacre, and the state government now uses that word too.

warrant.author: Governor James Stirling, in his own despatch, against later settler and Noongar accounts
warrant.work: Stirling’s despatch on the killings at Pinjarra
warrant.supports: The Pinjarra death toll depends on who is counted and who is believed: Stirling reported 15 killed, later settler and Noongar accounts put it far higher. Noongar people call it a massacre, and the state government now uses that word too.
warrant.check: Colonial administration returns are printed in the territory’s annual Blue Book and administration report; the British copies are in the CO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: Stirling led the party and wrote the return. The state government now calls it a massacre; the number in the despatch has not changed.

evidence.author: Neville Green
evidence.work: Broken Spears: Aborigines and Europeans in the Southwest of Australia
evidence.supports: Noongar resistance, Yagan and the Pinjarra killings.

to.note: The first partly elected Legislative Council met in December 1870.

statusPeriods.label: Governor and nominated council; convicts from 1850
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor appointed in London ruled with a handful of nominated officials. When the free colony failed for lack of labour, its own settlers petitioned for convicts, and Britain sent 9,721 men between 1850 and 1868.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Perth, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted until 1870.
statusPeriods.note: The last convict ship to Australia, the Hougoumont, reached Fremantle on 10 January 1868 carrying 62 Fenian prisoners among its 279 convicts.

from.note: The first partly elected Legislative Council met in December 1870.

statusPeriods.label: Part-elected Council
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Two thirds of the Legislative Council were elected by propertied men; the governor kept the Crown lands, which in a colony of this size was most of the power.
statusPeriods.franchise: Men with property worth 100 pounds. Aboriginal people were excluded by law from 1893 unless they held freehold.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government, then a gold rush
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Premier John Forrest's ministry answered to a local parliament; Britain kept a veto over Aboriginal affairs spending for seven years, then gave that up too.
statusPeriods.franchise: Adult men from 1893, women from 1899 - but the Constitution Acts Amendment Act 1893 explicitly barred 'aboriginal natives' from voting unless they owned freehold, and that bar lasted until 1962.
statusPeriods.note: Gold at Coolgardie in 1892 and Kalgoorlie in 1893 tripled the colony's population in a decade and produced the goldfields voters who dragged a reluctant Perth into federation.

departures.how: Western Australia joined the federation at the last minute, after goldfields miners from the eastern colonies petitioned to secede and join without Perth; it became a state of the Commonwealth of Australia.

becomes.name: State of Western Australia, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: John Forrest
led.role: premier who held out for concessions and then took the colony in

led.name: Frederick Vosper
led.role: goldfields editor and politician who led the 'Separation for Federation' campaign that forced Perth's hand

departures.movement: The goldfields federation movement

cost.note: Nobody died. In 1933 Western Australians voted two to one to leave the federation; Westminster declined to act on the petition and nothing happened.

departures.borders: The 129th meridian, drawn on a map in London in 1825 and shifted west in 1831, is still the border between Western Australia and the Northern Territory. It runs straight through Ngaanyatjarra and Yolngu country.

violence.note: The killing moved north with the pastoral frontier: Pinjarra in 1834, the Gascoyne and Pilbara from the 1860s, the Kimberley from the 1880s, and the Forrest River killings in 1926.

toll.note: There is no reliable colony-wide figure. Historians of the Kimberley and Pilbara frontiers give ranges in the thousands; Western Australia's frontier was the last to close, with killings recorded into the 1920s.

populationTransfer.note: Between 1838 and 1931 about 3,700 Aboriginal men and boys were imprisoned on Wadjemup (Rottnest Island), many for offences like spearing sheep; at least 370 died there and are buried in unmarked ground.

consequences.economicLegacy: The colony that could not feed itself in 1830 now ships more iron ore than any other place on earth, from Pilbara country whose traditional owners were shot off it within living memory of their grandparents.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The Noongar Settlement of 2018, worth about 1.3 billion Australian dollars, is the largest native title agreement in Australian history and covers the whole south-west corner.

peak.populationNote: 1901 census, which excluded Aboriginal people. The colony had only 46,290 counted residents in 1891 before the gold rush.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Western Australia’s largest recorded population: 184,124 people, counted in 1901.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Neville Green
evidence.work: Broken Spears: Aborigines and Europeans in the Southwest of Australia
evidence.supports: Noongar dispossession and resistance in the south-west.

evidence.author: Stuart Macintyre
evidence.work: A Concise History of Australia
evidence.supports: Colonial politics, convicts and federation.

evidence.author: Chris Owen
evidence.work: Every Mother's Son is Guilty: Policing the Kimberley Frontier of Western Australia 1882-1905
evidence.supports: Police violence and neck-chaining on the northern frontier.

pedagogy.hook: Western Australia was founded in 1829 as a free colony that refused convicts on principle. Twenty-one years later its settlers begged London to send them, because nobody else would work for what they paid.

misconception.belief: The Australian frontier closed in the nineteenth century, long ago and far away.
misconception.correction: In Western Australia it did not. Jandamarra fought the police in the Kimberley until 1897; Aboriginal men were still being marched in neck chains in the 1930s; the Forrest River killings happened in 1926; and Aboriginal Western Australians were barred from voting in state elections until 1962. That is within the lifetime of people alive now.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Western Australia is a third of the continent and shows how thin colonial control could be: two ports, a few thousand settlers, and a claim over 2.5 million square kilometres that took a hundred years and a great deal of shooting to make real.

The Swan River Colony proclaimed

territories.name: South Australia
territories.formalName: Province of South Australia

namesOverTime.name: South Australia
namesOverTime.note: Called a 'province', never a colony, because its founders wanted to advertise that no convict had ever been sent there.

geoCoverage.label: Between the 132nd and 141st meridians, later widened
geoCoverage.change: Governor John Hindmarsh read the proclamation under a gum tree at Glenelg. The province's boundaries were two lines of longitude fixed in London in 1834; the western one was moved to 129 degrees in 1861.

acquisitions.how: A private colonisation company sold Kaurna, Ngarrindjeri and Peramangk land to British buyers before a single ship sailed, and Governor Hindmarsh proclaimed the province at Glenelg with 546 settlers ashore.

counterparties.name: The Kaurna, Ngarrindjeri, Peramangk, Narungga and Adnyamathanha peoples
counterparties.lost: The Adelaide plains and the Murray mouth, sold in London as 'waste and unoccupied lands' while people were living on them.
counterparties.note: The Letters Patent of 19 February 1836 that created the province expressly reserved the rights of 'any Aboriginal Natives' to lands they occupied. The clause was never enforced, and South Australian courts have wrestled with it ever since.

instrument.name: South Australia Act 1834 and the Letters Patent of 19 February 1836
instrument.note: The Act described the land as 'waste and unoccupied'. The Letters Patent two years later contradicted it by protecting Aboriginal occupation. Both documents were in force at once.

people.name: Edward Gibbon Wakefield
people.role: designed 'systematic colonisation' - selling land dear so labourers could not escape wage work - while imprisoned for abducting an heiress

people.name: John Hindmarsh
people.role: first governor; proclaimed the province at Glenelg

people.name: Kadlitpina (Captain Jack)
people.role: Kaurna elder who negotiated with the newcomers over the Adelaide plains

acquisitions.resistance: Ngarrindjeri people fought settlers along the lower Murray; after the wreck of the Maria in 1840 a police party hanged two Ngarrindjeri men at the scene without trial on the governor's authority.

evidence.author: Robert Foster
evidence.work: Fatal Collisions: The South Australian Frontier and the Violence of Memory
evidence.supports: Frontier violence in South Australia and how it was remembered.

to.note: The first partly elected Legislative Council was elected in August 1851.

statusPeriods.label: Governor and land commissioners, then bankruptcy
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Power was split between a governor answering to London and colonisation commissioners answering to investors; they fought, the province went bankrupt in 1841, and Britain took it over as an ordinary Crown colony in 1842.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Adelaide, under the Colonial Office and the South Australian Colonization Commission
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Copper at Kapunda in 1842 and Burra in 1845 rescued the finances.

from.note: The first partly elected Legislative Council was elected in August 1851.

statusPeriods.label: Part-elected Council
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Sixteen of the 24 councillors were elected on a wide male franchise; the governor kept the rest and the Crown lands.
statusPeriods.franchise: Men with a small property or income qualification - deliberately wider than in the eastern colonies.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government and the secret ballot
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A bicameral parliament in Adelaide with responsible ministers, elected by secret ballot - an Australian invention that England copied in 1872 and that the world still calls the Australian ballot.
statusPeriods.franchise: All adult men from 1856. Women won the vote in 1894 and, uniquely in the world at that date, the right to stand for parliament with it. Aboriginal people were not excluded by the words of the Act, and a small number of Aboriginal men and women did vote.

departures.how: South Australia voted for federation in 1898 and 1899 and became a state of the Commonwealth, taking the Northern Territory in with it until it handed that to the federal government in 1911.

becomes.name: State of South Australia, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: Charles Cameron Kingston
led.role: premier, drafter of the constitution and one of the delegates who took it to London

led.name: Catherine Helen Spence
led.role: campaigner elected in 1897 as Australia's first female political candidate, standing for the Federal Convention

departures.movement: The federation movement

cost.note: Nobody died. South Australian women voted in the federation referendums, the only women in the world at the time voting on the constitution of a new nation.

departures.borders: The 141st meridian, surveyed badly in 1847, still runs about 3.6 kilometres too far west, so a strip of South Australia has been administered by Victoria for 175 years and both parliaments have agreed to leave it alone.

violence.note: The province advertised itself as the humane alternative to convict Australia and killed people anyway: the Maria hangings of 1840, the Rufus River killings of 1841, and the Coorong and far north frontier into the 1860s.

toll.note: Robert Foster and Amanda Nettelbeck count more than 100 recorded frontier killings in the settled districts and estimate far more went unrecorded in the north. Precise totals do not exist.

warrant.author: Robert Foster
warrant.work: Fatal Collisions: The South Australian Frontier and the Violence of Memory
warrant.supports: Robert Foster and Amanda Nettelbeck count more than 100 recorded frontier killings in the settled districts and estimate far more went unrecorded in the north.
warrant.check: Wakefield Press, 2001. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

populationTransfer.note: Assisted passages brought British labourers and, from 1838, about 500 Lutherans fleeing Prussia, who founded the Barossa Valley and made South Australia the most German place in the empire.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copper, then wheat, then wine. The Wakefield land price also produced Australia's first serious urban plan: Colonel William Light's grid for Adelaide, ringed by parkland that was never sold.
consequences.languageAndLaw: South Australia gave the world the secret ballot in 1856, votes for women in 1894 and the Torrens system of land title in 1858 - which is now used from Canada to Malaysia, and which was designed to make it simpler to sell land taken from Aboriginal owners.

peak.populationNote: 1901 census, excluding Aboriginal people, and excluding the Northern Territory's separately counted population.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: South Australia’s largest recorded population: 358,346 people, counted in 1901.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Robert Foster
evidence.work: Fatal Collisions: The South Australian Frontier and the Violence of Memory
evidence.supports: Frontier violence and its erasure from public memory.

evidence.author: Douglas Pike
evidence.work: Paradise of Dissent: South Australia 1829-1857
evidence.supports: The Wakefield scheme, the religious dissenters and the early constitution.

evidence.author: Henry Reynolds
evidence.work: The Law of the Land
evidence.supports: The 1836 Letters Patent clause protecting Aboriginal occupation and its fate.

pedagogy.hook: The document that created South Australia in 1836 promised to protect the land 'now actually occupied or enjoyed' by Aboriginal people. The same government was selling that land in London before the ships left.

misconception.belief: South Australia was the good colony: free settlers, no convicts, no violence.
misconception.correction: No convicts is true. No violence is not. Police hanged two Ngarrindjeri men without trial in 1840, a punitive expedition killed about 30 Maraura people at Rufus River in 1841, and the Kaurna language had almost no fluent speakers left by 1860. A colony can be founded on principle and still be founded on someone else's country.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: South Australia is the control experiment. It had no convicts, an unusually democratic constitution, a written promise to Aboriginal landholders and progressive politics - and the dispossession happened anyway, which tells you the cause was the land system, not the character of the settlers.

keyDates.what: Letters Patent promise to protect Aboriginal-occupied land
The province proclaimed at Glenelg
Responsible government, with the world's first secret ballot
The Northern Territory annexed to South Australia
Women win the vote and the right to stand for parliament

territories.name: Victoria
territories.formalName: Colony of Victoria (until 1851 the Port Phillip District of New South Wales)

namesOverTime.name: Victoria
namesOverTime.note: Named for the queen, two weeks before gold was found at Clunes.

geoCoverage.label: The Port Phillip District, then the colony
geoCoverage.change: Squatters crossed Bass Strait from Van Diemen's Land looking for grass. Victoria was administered from Sydney until it separated on 1 July 1851.

acquisitions.how: John Batman got eight Wurundjeri elders to mark a document exchanging 600,000 acres for blankets, knives and an annual tribute; Governor Bourke declared the deal void on 26 August 1835 and took the land for the Crown instead.

counterparties.name: The Wurundjeri, Boonwurrung and other peoples of the Kulin nation
counterparties.lost: The grasslands around Port Phillip Bay, and then the whole of what became Victoria within twenty years - the fastest dispossession on the continent.
counterparties.note: Whether the elders thought they were selling land at all is doubtful: tanderrum, the ceremony they performed, granted temporary safe passage, not ownership.

instrument.name: Batman's Treaty, voided by Governor Bourke's Proclamation of 26 August 1835
instrument.note: The only document in Australian history in which British settlers tried to buy land from its Aboriginal owners. The Crown destroyed it precisely because recognising the purchase would have recognised the owners.

people.name: John Batman
people.role: Van Diemen's Land grazier who staged the purchase; he had earlier led parties hunting Aboriginal Tasmanians

people.name: Richard Bourke
people.role: Governor of New South Wales; his proclamation restated that only the Crown could grant land in Australia

people.name: Billibellary
people.role: Wurundjeri ngurungaeta (headman) who was one of the marks on Batman's document and later worked to protect his people through the Protectorate

people.name: William Barak
people.role: Wurundjeri leader who as a boy witnessed Batman's meeting and spent his life defending Coranderrk station

acquisitions.resistance: The Eumeralla wars in the Western District ran through the 1840s. The Kulin population around Port Phillip fell from perhaps 15,000 in 1835 to about 2,000 by 1850, from killings, disease and starvation.

evidence.author: Bain Attwood
evidence.work: Possession: Batman's Treaty and the Matter of History
evidence.supports: Batman's document, the Bourke proclamation and their afterlife in Australian argument.

statusPeriods.label: The Port Phillip District, governed from Sydney
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A superintendent at Melbourne, Charles La Trobe, answered to the governor in Sydney 900 kilometres away, while squatters occupied the country faster than any official could survey it.
statusPeriods.franchise: From 1843 the district elected six members to the New South Wales Legislative Council, who mostly resigned in protest to force separation.
statusPeriods.note: The Port Phillip Protectorate of 1839-1849 appointed four Protectors of Aborigines; it was starved of funds, achieved little, and was abolished as a failure.

statusPeriods.label: A new colony, then a gold rush
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A part-elected Legislative Council under Lieutenant-Governor La Trobe tried to govern a population that tripled in three years and a goldfield policed by monthly licence hunts.
statusPeriods.franchise: Propertied men. Diggers on the goldfields paid 30 shillings a month for a licence and had no vote at all, which is what produced Eureka.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government; the richest colony in the empire
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Ministers responsible to an elected Assembly governed from Melbourne, a city that gold had made the wealthiest per head in the world by the 1880s.
statusPeriods.franchise: Manhood suffrage for the Assembly from 1857, and payment of members from 1870, so working men could sit. Women voted from 1908, the last Australian colony or state to allow it. The Aboriginal Protection Act 1869 gave the Board power over where Aboriginal Victorians lived, worked and married.

departures.how: Victoria voted for federation by four to one, hosted the opening of the first federal parliament in the Melbourne Exhibition Building, and kept the federal capital for 26 years until Canberra was built.

becomes.name: State of Victoria, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: Alfred Deakin
led.role: Victorian leader of the federation movement and Australia's second prime minister

led.name: Vida Goldstein
led.role: suffragist who organised women's support for federation and in 1903 became one of the first women in the British Empire to stand for a national parliament

departures.movement: The federation movement and the Australian Natives' Association

cost.note: Nobody died. Victoria's 1899 referendum returned about 94 per cent in favour.

departures.borders: The Murray River became the border with New South Wales - and because the 1850 Act gave New South Wales the whole river, the boundary is the southern bank, so Victoria owns no part of its greatest river.

violence.note: Victoria was taken in fifteen years. Massacres at Convincing Ground (about 1833-34), Faithfull Creek (1838), Campaspe Plains (1839) and through the Western District killed hundreds; survivors were pushed onto mission stations.

toll.note: Ian Clark's district-by-district survey of the Western District and the Newcastle massacre-mapping project put Aboriginal deaths in Victoria in the low thousands between 1836 and 1853; settler deaths were in the low hundreds. Records are settler records.

warrant.author: Ian D. Clark
warrant.work: Scars in the Landscape: A Register of Massacre Sites in Western Victoria 1803-1859
warrant.supports: Ian Clark's district-by-district survey of the Western District and the Newcastle massacre-mapping project put Aboriginal deaths in Victoria in the low thousands between 1836 and 1853; settler deaths were in the low hundreds.
warrant.check: Aboriginal Studies Press, 1995. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

populationTransfer.note: Gold brought about 500,000 people to Victoria in a decade, including some 40,000 Chinese miners who were then taxed, segregated and attacked at Buckland River in 1857 and Lambing Flat across the border in 1861.

consequences.economicLegacy: Victorian gold - about 20 million ounces between 1851 and 1860, roughly a third of the world's output - paid for Melbourne's boulevards, its parliament and Australia's first industrial working class.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Victoria in 2023-25 ran Australia's first formal truth-telling inquiry into colonisation, the Yoorrook Justice Commission, and is negotiating the country's first statewide treaty with Aboriginal Victorians.

peak.populationNote: 1901 census, excluding Aboriginal people. The colony had 77,345 counted residents in 1851 and 540,322 ten years later.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Victoria’s largest recorded population: 1,201,341 people, counted in 1901.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Bain Attwood
evidence.work: Possession: Batman's Treaty and the Matter of History
evidence.supports: The 1835 'treaty' and the doctrine that replaced it.

evidence.author: Geoffrey Blainey
evidence.work: The Rush That Never Ended: A History of Australian Mining
evidence.supports: The gold rushes and their effect on colonial society.

evidence.author: Ian D. Clark
evidence.work: Scars in the Landscape: A Register of Massacre Sites in Western Victoria 1803-1859
evidence.supports: Documented massacre sites in western Victoria.

pedagogy.hook: In 1835 John Batman signed the only land treaty British settlers ever made with Aboriginal Australians. The Governor tore it up in eleven weeks - because admitting they could sell the land meant admitting they owned it.

misconception.belief: Eureka in 1854 was a rebellion against British rule, Australia's version of the American Revolution.
misconception.correction: The diggers at Ballarat wanted the vote and an end to the licence fee, not a republic. About 22 miners and six soldiers died in fifteen minutes. Thirteen men were tried for treason and every jury acquitted them, and within two years Victoria had manhood suffrage and the secret ballot. It was a taxation revolt that won.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Victoria compresses the whole colonial story into one lifetime: a fake treaty in 1835, the fastest dispossession in Australia, a gold rush that made it the richest place on earth, an armed revolt in 1854, and manhood suffrage by 1857.
