territories.name: Queensland
territories.formalName: Colony of Queensland (until 1859 the Moreton Bay District of New South Wales)

namesOverTime.name: Queensland
namesOverTime.note: Queen Victoria chose the name herself, rejecting 'Cooksland'.

geoCoverage.label: Moreton Bay, then a colony reaching to the Torres Strait
geoCoverage.change: A penal station was planted at Redcliffe on Yuggera country in September 1824. Queensland separated from New South Wales in 1859, annexed the Torres Strait islands in 1872 and 1879, and did not control its far north and west until the 1890s.

acquisitions.how: John Oxley landed convicts and soldiers at Redcliffe to build a punishment station for men who had reoffended in New South Wales; it moved to the Brisbane River in 1825 and closed to free settlers until 1842.

counterparties.name: The Yuggera, Turrbal and Quandamooka peoples
counterparties.lost: The Brisbane River mouth and Moreton Bay, first to a prison and then to a port.

people.name: John Oxley
people.role: surveyor-general who chose the site

people.name: Dundalli
people.role: Dalla man who led resistance around Brisbane for a decade and was publicly hanged in 1855

acquisitions.resistance: Dundalli's campaign kept settlers off parts of the Pine and Caboolture rivers into the 1850s; his public execution in Brisbane in January 1855 was staged as a warning.

date.note: The Queensland Coast Islands Act took effect in 1879; the earlier 1872 annexation had covered only islands within 60 miles of the coast.

acquisitions.how: Queensland annexed the rest of the Torres Strait islands, up to within a few kilometres of New Guinea, to control the pearl-shell and beche-de-mer fisheries the islanders were already working for European boats.

counterparties.name: The Torres Strait Islander peoples, including the Meriam of Mer
counterparties.lost: Sovereignty over their islands and seas; Islanders were then governed under the same protection laws as Aboriginal Queenslanders, needing permits to travel or marry.
counterparties.note: It was a Meriam claim to Mer that produced the Mabo judgment in 1992, which destroyed the doctrine of terra nullius for the whole country.

instrument.name: Queensland Coast Islands Act 1879

people.name: Eddie Koiki Mabo
people.role: Meriam man from Mer who brought the case that overturned terra nullius; he died five months before the judgment

acquisitions.resistance: The Islanders did not resist militarily in 1879. They organised instead: the maritime strike of 1936 shut down the pearling fleet and won Islander control of the boats and councils.

statusPeriods.label: Moreton Bay: a penal station, then a district of New South Wales
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A commandant ran the prison until 1839, then Sydney ran the district; squatters pushed north up the Darling Downs from 1840 with no administration ahead of them at all.
statusPeriods.franchise: The district voted in New South Wales elections from 1843 on a property franchise; the goal of the men elected was separation.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government from the day it separated
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Queensland got a parliament and responsible ministers immediately on separation, and used them to fund a Native Police force of Aboriginal troopers under white officers to clear country ahead of the pastoralists.
statusPeriods.franchise: Manhood suffrage from 1872 for the Assembly; women from 1905. The Aboriginals Protection and Restriction of the Sale of Opium Act 1897 removed almost all rights from Aboriginal Queenslanders and was copied by other states.
statusPeriods.note: The Native Police operated from 1848 to about 1905 and is the single largest killer on the Australian frontier.

departures.how: Queensland joined the federation in a single referendum won by 7,492 votes, with the sugar districts voting against because federation meant the end of Pacific Islander labour.

becomes.name: State of Queensland, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: Samuel Griffith
led.role: premier and constitutional drafter; his 1891 draft is the skeleton of the Australian constitution and he became the first Chief Justice

led.name: Charles Lilley
led.role: premier and later chief justice who opposed the Islander labour trade from the bench and the platform

departures.movement: The federation movement

cost.note: Nobody died in the federation process. Its immediate consequence for Queensland was the deportation of about 7,500 Pacific Islanders under the Pacific Island Labourers Act 1901.

departures.borders: Queensland's northern boundary runs within a few kilometres of the Papua New Guinea coast, cutting through a strait that Torres Strait Islanders had crossed and traded across for thousands of years. A 1978 treaty finally allowed free movement across it again.

violence.note: Queensland had the longest and deadliest frontier in Australia. The Native Police, a state force of Aboriginal troopers commanded by white officers, 'dispersed' camps for over fifty years, and 'dispersal' was a euphemism everyone in Brisbane understood.

toll.note: Raymond Evans and Robert Orsted-Jensen, working from Native Police returns and settler records, estimate at least 24,000 and possibly over 60,000 Aboriginal deaths in Queensland between 1824 and 1900, against roughly 1,500 settlers killed. The figures are reconstructions from the killers' own paperwork and are contested at the upper end.

warrant.author: Raymond Evans
warrant.supports: Raymond Evans and Robert Orsted-Jensen, working from Native Police returns and settler records, estimate at least 24,000 and possibly over 60,000 Aboriginal deaths in Queensland between 1824 and 1900, against roughly 1,500 settlers killed.
warrant.check: Cambridge University Press, 2007. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

populationTransfer.note: Between 1863 and 1904 about 62,000 Pacific Islanders were brought to Queensland's cane fields, some by contract and some by kidnapping; after federation about 7,500 of them were deported.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar, cattle, gold and later coal. The sugar industry was built on Islander labour, then rebuilt on a tariff designed to make white labour affordable - a founding piece of the White Australia bargain.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The Meriam people of Mer won the Mabo judgment in 1992, so Australian native title law was made by Torres Strait Islanders from the last islands Queensland annexed.

peak.populationNote: 1901 census, excluding Aboriginal people. About 9,300 Pacific Islanders were in the colony that year.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Queensland’s largest recorded population: 498,129 people, counted in 1901.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Raymond Evans
evidence.work: A History of Queensland
evidence.supports: The colony's foundation, the Native Police and the labour trade.

evidence.author: Timothy Bottoms
evidence.work: Conspiracy of Silence: Queensland's Frontier Killing Times
evidence.supports: Documented frontier killings and the Native Police.

evidence.author: Noel Loos
evidence.work: Invasion and Resistance: Aboriginal-European Relations on the North Queensland Frontier 1861-1897
evidence.supports: Aboriginal resistance in north Queensland.

contested.note: The Queensland frontier death toll is the most disputed number in Australian history. Evans and Orsted-Jensen's estimate of 24,000 to 65,000 Aboriginal deaths is derived from Native Police strength and reported 'dispersals'; critics argue the multipliers are too high. Nobody disputes that the Native Police existed, were paid by the parliament, or that their reports used 'dispersed' to mean 'shot'.

pedagogy.hook: Queensland's parliament paid for a police force of Aboriginal troopers whose job was to shoot Aboriginal people. It ran for over fifty years, and its own reports called the killing 'dispersal'.

misconception.belief: Frontier violence in Australia was the work of a few lawless settlers, not of governments.
misconception.correction: In Queensland it was a line item in the budget. The Native Police Force was established in 1848, funded by the colonial parliament, commanded by commissioned officers, and operated until about 1905. Its own returns are the main evidence historians use to count the dead.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Queensland links the two great violences of the Pacific in one economy: land taken from Aboriginal people by a state police force, worked by Pacific Islanders brought across the sea under contracts many of them never agreed to.

keyDates.what: Penal station founded at Moreton Bay
The Native Police Force established
Queensland separates from New South Wales
The Don Juan lands the first Pacific Islander labourers in Brisbane

date.note: The Queensland Coast Islands Act took effect during 1879.

keyDates.what: The outer Torres Strait islands annexed
Mabo: the High Court rejects terra nullius

territories.name: Northern Territory
territories.formalName: The Northern Territory of South Australia, from 1911 of the Commonwealth

namesOverTime.name: Northern Territory
namesOverTime.note: Before 1863 it had no name at all in British administration: it was the part of New South Wales nobody had reached.

geoCoverage.label: 1.35 million square kilometres claimed; three forts, all abandoned
geoCoverage.change: Captain Gordon Bremer claimed the north coast on 26 September 1824 and built Fort Dundas on Melville Island. It and its successors failed; the interior was governed by Warlpiri, Arrernte, Yolngu and Larrakia law for another century.

acquisitions.how: Captain Gordon Bremer claimed the coast from 129 to 135 degrees east for Britain and landed marines on Tiwi country at Melville Island to build a trading post meant to capture the Macassan and Chinese trade; it was abandoned in 1829.

counterparties.name: The Tiwi people of Melville and Bathurst Islands
counterparties.lost: Nothing permanent in 1824 - they drove the garrison into its stockade and outlasted it - but the claim of sovereignty made over their heads was never withdrawn.

counterparties.name: The Makassar trepang fleets of Sulawesi
counterparties.lost: A trade with Yolngu people that was centuries old; British and then Australian customs rules ended the Macassan voyages in 1906.
counterparties.note: The Yolngu and Makassar had a trading relationship with its own shared vocabulary, songs and law, and it long predates the British claim.

people.name: Gordon Bremer
people.role: naval captain who claimed the north coast and founded Fort Dundas

people.name: John Lort Stokes
people.role: surveyed and named Port Darwin from HMS Beagle in 1839

acquisitions.resistance: The Tiwi kept Fort Dundas under attack from the start. Fort Wellington (1827-29) and Victoria at Port Essington (1838-49) also failed; the British abandoned the north coast entirely for sixteen years.

acquisitions.how: Letters patent transferred everything between 129 and 138 degrees east from New South Wales to South Australia, which wanted a northern port and a telegraph line to Asia and got a debt instead.

counterparties.name: The Larrakia, Warlpiri, Arrernte, Yolngu, Warumungu and dozens of other nations
counterparties.lost: Legal title to their entire country, transferred between two colonial governments neither of which had asked them anything.

instrument.name: Letters Patent annexing the Northern Territory to South Australia

people.name: Charles Todd
people.role: South Australian superintendent of telegraphs who drove the Overland Telegraph through the centre in 1870-72

acquisitions.resistance: The Overland Telegraph and the cattle stations that followed it brought fifty years of killing: Barrow Creek in 1874, the Coniston killings in 1928, and many in between that were never recorded.

statusPeriods.label: Claimed from Sydney; three failed forts
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Sovereignty was asserted over 1.35 million square kilometres and exercised over a few hectares of stockade. Between 1849 and 1864 there was no British presence on the north coast at all.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default for a crown colony is 5, meaning full direct rule. Nothing of the kind existed here: Britain held three coastal forts, all abandoned, while Aboriginal nations governed the interior. Shading this 5 would make the map lie.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

statusPeriods.label: Run by South Australia, badly and at a loss
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Government Resident at Palmerston (Darwin) answered to Adelaide, 3,000 kilometres away, which spent 40 years losing money on the place and handed it to the Commonwealth in 1911.
statusPeriods.franchise: Territory residents had no vote of their own. About 3,000 Chinese labourers were brought in for the goldfields and railway in the 1870s and 1880s, and were then legislated against.
statusPeriods.note: South Australia's Northern Territory Aboriginals Act 1910 and the Commonwealth's Aboriginals Ordinance 1918 made the Chief Protector the legal guardian of every Aboriginal child, which is the legal machinery of the Stolen Generations.

departures.how: The Northern Territory entered the Commonwealth of Australia as part of South Australia, which then surrendered it to the federal government on 1 January 1911 because it could no longer afford it.

becomes.name: Northern Territory, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: Vincent Lingiari
led.role: Gurindji stockman who led the Wave Hill walk-off in 1966 and won the first return of land to its traditional owners in 1975

led.name: Charles Cameron Kingston
led.role: South Australian premier who took the Territory into federation as part of his state

departures.movement: The federation movement; later, the Gurindji and Yolngu land rights movements

cost.note: Nobody died at federation. Territory residents had no vote in the referendums that created the Commonwealth, and no federal representation of any kind until 1922, and then only a member who could not vote on most matters until 1968.

departures.borders: The 129th and 138th meridians and the 26th parallel are three straight lines drawn on paper in London and Adelaide. They cut Warlpiri, Pitjantjatjara and Ngaanyatjarra country into three jurisdictions with different laws.

violence.note: The Northern Territory frontier stayed open until 1928, when police killed at least 31 and probably many more Warlpiri, Anmatyerre and Kaytetye people around Coniston and a board of inquiry found the killings justified.

toll.note: The 1929 board of inquiry accepted 31 deaths at Coniston. Warlpiri oral history and later historians put it between 60 and 200. Territory-wide frontier deaths from the 1870s to the 1920s are unknown and certainly in the thousands.

warrant.author: The Commonwealth board of inquiry into the Coniston killings
warrant.work: Report of the Board of Inquiry concerning the killing of natives in Central Australia
warrant.supports: The 1929 board of inquiry accepted 31 deaths at Coniston. Warlpiri oral history and later historians put it between 60 and 200. Territory-wide frontier deaths from the 1870s to the 1920s are unknown and certainly in the thousands.
warrant.check: Commonwealth Parliamentary Papers, and the file series at the National Archives of Australia.
warrant.note: The board accepted 31; Warlpiri oral history and later historians put it between 60 and 200. The board was appointed to settle the question and did not.

populationTransfer.note: The Aboriginals Ordinance 1918 made the Chief Protector the guardian of every Aboriginal child in the Territory, and children of mixed descent were taken to institutions at Kahlin, the Bungalow and Croker Island for half a century.

retainedTerritory.note: Almost half the Northern Territory is now Aboriginal freehold under the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 - the strongest land rights law in Australia, passed because the Gurindji walked off Wave Hill station in 1966 and stayed off for nine years.

consequences.economicLegacy: Cattle, gold, then uranium, bauxite and gas. Aboriginal pastoral workers were paid in rations rather than wages until an equal pay ruling in 1966, which stations answered by evicting them.
consequences.languageAndLaw: More Aboriginal languages are still spoken in the Northern Territory than anywhere else in Australia, and its Aboriginal population share, about 30 per cent, is by far the highest of any Australian jurisdiction.

peak.populationNote: 1901 census of the Northern Territory of South Australia, which counted settlers and Chinese residents but not Aboriginal people, who were the overwhelming majority of the actual population.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Northern Territory’s largest recorded population: 4,811 people, counted in 1901.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Tony Roberts
evidence.work: Frontier Justice: A History of the Gulf Country to 1900
evidence.supports: Frontier violence in the Gulf country and its documentation.

evidence.author: Alan Powell
evidence.work: Far Country: A Short History of the Northern Territory
evidence.supports: The failed forts, South Australian administration and the Commonwealth takeover.

evidence.author: Peter Read
evidence.work: The Stolen Generations: The Removal of Aboriginal Children in New South Wales 1883 to 1969
evidence.publisher: New South Wales Ministry of Aboriginal Affairs
evidence.supports: The legal machinery and practice of child removal.

pedagogy.hook: Britain claimed the Top End in 1824 and then failed to hold it three times. Between 1849 and 1864 there was not a single British person living on a coastline the empire had already coloured pink.

misconception.belief: If a place is coloured British on an old map, Britain governed it.
misconception.correction: The Northern Territory was British on every map from 1824. In fact Britain abandoned the coast entirely for sixteen years, and Warlpiri and Arrernte people in the centre first met a European in the 1870s. The map showed a claim, not a government - which is true of a great deal of the empire in Africa and the Pacific too.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Territory is the clearest case in the empire of the gap between a claim and a government - and then, from 1966, the place where Aboriginal Australians won back more land than anywhere else, starting with 200 Gurindji stockmen who walked off a British-owned cattle station.

keyDates.what: Bremer claims the north coast; Fort Dundas built and later abandoned
Annexed to South Australia
The Overland Telegraph opens; the centre is invaded by cattle

date.note: The Coniston killings ran from 24 August into October 1928; the start date is the first recorded killing.

keyDates.what: The Coniston killings, the last officially sanctioned massacre
The Gurindji walk off Wave Hill station
Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act

territories.name: Norfolk Island
territories.formalName: Settlement, later Territory, of Norfolk Island

namesOverTime.name: Norfolk Island
namesOverTime.note: Cook named it for the Duchess of Norfolk, who had died the year before.

geoCoverage.label: First settlement
geoCoverage.change: Philip Gidley King landed 23 people six weeks after the First Fleet reached Sydney, to grow flax and pine for the navy. Neither worked.

geoCoverage.label: Second settlement: the penal station, then the Pitcairners
geoCoverage.change: The island was reoccupied as a place of secondary punishment for convicts who had reoffended in New South Wales. Between 1814 and 1825 it was deliberately left empty and its buildings burned.

acquisitions.how: Lieutenant Philip Gidley King landed 15 convicts and 8 free men from HMS Supply to secure the island's Norfolk pine and native flax for the Royal Navy, six weeks after the First Fleet reached Sydney Cove.

counterparties.name: No resident population in 1788
counterparties.note: Polynesian people from the Kermadecs or New Zealand lived on Norfolk between roughly the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries and left before Europeans arrived; their stone tools, banana plants and burials are in the archaeological record. The island was empty in 1788, but it had not always been.

people.name: Philip Gidley King
people.role: founded the settlement and later governed New South Wales

acquisitions.how: Britain reoccupied the empty island as a punishment station for twice-convicted convicts, on Governor Brisbane's instruction that the criminal there should be 'forever excluded from all hope of return'.

counterparties.name: No resident population in 1825
counterparties.note: The first settlement had been evacuated and burned in 1814 precisely so that nobody could use the island; it was empty when the convict ships came back.

people.name: Alexander Maconochie
people.role: commandant 1840-44 who replaced flogging with a marks system prisoners could earn their way out of; he was recalled for being too lenient and his ideas became the basis of modern parole

people.name: John Price
people.role: commandant 1846-53 whose regime was so brutal that men drew lots to commit murder in order to be hanged; he was later killed by convicts at Melbourne

acquisitions.resistance: Convicts mutinied in 1826, 1834 and 1846. After the 1834 rising thirteen men were hanged; the priest who attended them, William Ullathorne, reported that the men condemned to die thanked God and the men reprieved wept.

evidence.author: Robert Hughes
evidence.work: The Fatal Shore: A History of the Transportation of Convicts to Australia, 1787-1868
evidence.supports: The second penal settlement, Maconochie and Price.

statusPeriods.label: First settlement, under Sydney
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A lieutenant-governor answered to Sydney. At its height in 1792 the island held about 1,100 people, a sixth of the entire British population of Australia.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

statusPeriods.gapReason: Between 1814 and 1825 Britain deliberately held nobody on Norfolk Island. The settlement was evacuated and its buildings burned so that no other power - and no escaped convict - could use it, and the island stood empty for eleven years.
statusPeriods.label: The empire's harshest penal station
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A commandant with military power and no oversight ran a prison for men already transported once, on an island 1,400 kilometres from anywhere, where the mail came a few times a year.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingston, under Sydney and from 1844 under Hobart
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

statusPeriods.label: A distinct settlement of the Pitcairn descendants
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The whole population of Pitcairn - 194 people descended from the Bounty mutineers and Polynesian women - was moved here and given the island; it was run as a separate settlement, then from 1897 through the Governor of New South Wales.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingston, under the Governor of New South Wales from 1897
statusPeriods.franchise: The Pitcairners brought their own law with them, including a franchise that had included women since 1838.
statusPeriods.note: A third of the settlers went home to Pitcairn within eight years, saying Norfolk was too crowded and too full of ghosts.

departures.how: Britain handed Norfolk Island to the Commonwealth of Australia as an external territory; Norfolk Islanders were not asked, and have been arguing about it ever since.

becomes.name: Territory of Norfolk Island, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: David Buffett
led.role: Norfolk Islander who led the campaign for self-government, served as Chief Minister, and after Australia abolished the island's legislature in 2015 petitioned the United Nations for re-listing

led.name: Andrew Fisher
led.role: Australian prime minister whose government took the island under the Norfolk Island Act 1913

departures.movement: None at the time; a Norfolk Island self-determination movement grew from the 1970s and petitioned the United Nations in 2016

cost.note: Nobody died. The island's grievance is constitutional, not violent: islanders argue that the 1856 grant of the island to the Pitcairners was a promise Australia broke.

departures.borders: Nothing moved. The island is 1,400 kilometres from Sydney and 700 from New Caledonia, and Australia's claim to it comes entirely from a British transfer the islanders did not agree to.

instrument.name: Norfolk Island Act 1913 (Cth)
instrument.note: Accepted the island as an Australian territory with effect from 1 July 1914.

violence.note: The second settlement, 1825-55, was designed to be the worst place in the empire: floggings of 100 lashes, men chained in the pit at Kingston, and mutinies in 1826, 1834 and 1846 that ended in mass hangings.

toll.note: No total exists. Thirteen men were hanged after the 1834 mutiny and twelve after 1846; deaths from flogging, overwork and disease were not systematically recorded.

populationTransfer.note: Two whole populations were moved in and out: convicts twice, and in 1856 the entire population of Pitcairn Island, 194 people, sailed 6,000 kilometres to a place they had never seen.

consequences.economicLegacy: Whaling, then bananas, then tourism, then an offshore tax status Australia abolished in 2016 when it took over the island's services.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Norf'k, the creole of eighteenth-century English and Tahitian that the Pitcairners brought, is spoken on the island and is co-official with English.

peak.populationNote: In 1792 the island held about 1,100 people, roughly a sixth of all the Europeans in Australia. The 2021 Australian census counted 2,188 residents.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Norfolk Island’s largest recorded population: 1,100 people, counted in 1792.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Robert Hughes
evidence.work: The Fatal Shore: A History of the Transportation of Convicts to Australia, 1787-1868
evidence.supports: The penal settlements and their regimes.

evidence.author: Merval Hoare
evidence.work: Norfolk Island: A Revised and Enlarged History 1774-1998
evidence.supports: The island's settlements, the Pitcairn arrival and Australian administration.

pedagogy.hook: In 1856 the entire population of Pitcairn Island - 194 people descended from the Bounty mutineers - was shipped 6,000 kilometres to Norfolk Island and given a former prison to live in.

misconception.belief: Norfolk Island has always been Australian.
misconception.correction: It was a British settlement from 1788, run at various times from Sydney, Hobart and London, and handed to Australia only in 1914 without asking the islanders. Norfolk Islanders lost their own legislature in 2015-16 and asked the United Nations to relist the island as a non-self-governing territory. The argument is not settled.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Norfolk shows the empire's habit of moving whole populations like furniture - convicts in, convicts out, Pitcairners across the ocean - and of transferring islands between governments without asking the people who live on them.

The island abandoned and its buildings burned

Transferred to Australia

territories.name: Ashmore and Cartier Islands
territories.formalName: Territory of Ashmore and Cartier Islands

namesOverTime.name: Pulau Pasir

from.display: for centuries before the British claim
from.note: Rotinese and Bajo fishermen from what is now Indonesia used the reefs long before any European claim; no date can be fixed for when the use began.

namesOverTime.note: 'Sand island'. The graves of Indonesian fishermen are still on Ashmore Reef.

namesOverTime.name: Territory of Ashmore and Cartier Islands
namesOverTime.note: Cartier Island was added to the claim in 1909 and to the name when Australia took the territory over in 1934.

modernSuccessors.name: Australia (Territory of Ashmore and Cartier Islands)

geoCoverage.label: Three sand cays and a reef in the Timor Sea
geoCoverage.change: Britain annexed Ashmore Reef for its guano; Cartier Island followed in 1909.

acquisitions.how: Britain annexed Ashmore Reef by order in council so that a British company could dig its guano, and added Cartier Island on 7 August 1909 for the same reason.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: Nobody lived on the cays, but Rotinese and Bajo fishermen from Timor and Sulawesi had worked the reefs for generations and buried their dead there. Their access was cut when Australia declared a marine reserve, then partly restored by a 1974 memorandum of understanding that still governs the reef.

instrument.name: Order in Council annexing Ashmore Island, 1878

evidence.author: Stuart Kaye
evidence.work: Australia's Maritime Boundaries
evidence.publisher: Centre for Maritime Policy, University of Wollongong
evidence.supports: The legal history of Australia's offshore territories and their boundaries.

statusPeriods.label: Annexed for guano, then forgotten
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody governed it. The islands were annexed, mined briefly for guano and phosphate, and then left to the fishermen who had always used them.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default for a crown colony is 5. No administration of any kind existed here: there was no officer, no law court and usually nobody present, so 5 would be false.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody lived there.

departures.how: Britain transferred the islands to Australia by order in council, and Australia accepted them under the Ashmore and Cartier Islands Acceptance Act 1933; they were administered through the Northern Territory.

becomes.name: Territory of Ashmore and Cartier Islands, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: Joseph Lyons
led.role: Australian prime minister whose government legislated to accept the islands

cost.note: Nobody died and nobody was displaced in 1934. The consequences came later, for Indonesian fishermen excluded from reefs their families had used for centuries and for asylum seekers whose boats reached Ashmore from the 1990s.

departures.borders: Ashmore Reef sits 140 kilometres from Indonesia and 320 from Australia, which is why it became the front line of Australia's border policy and the reason it was excised from Australia's migration zone in 2001.

instrument.name: Ashmore and Cartier Islands Acceptance Act 1933 (Cth)

consequences.borderLegacy: The islands sit closer to Indonesia than to Australia and give Australia a claim to seabed and fisheries in the Timor Sea; they were excised from Australia's migration zone in 2001 so that people landing there could not apply for asylum.
consequences.economicLegacy: Guano and phosphate were dug out in the 1880s and 1890s and the islands have produced nothing since.

peak.populationNote: No permanent population, then or now. Indonesian fishermen visit under a 1974 memorandum of understanding, and Australian customs vessels are usually the only people present.

evidence.author: Stuart Kaye
evidence.work: Australia's Maritime Boundaries
evidence.publisher: Centre for Maritime Policy, University of Wollongong
evidence.supports: The annexations of 1878 and 1909 and the 1934 transfer.

evidence.author: Natasha Stacey
evidence.work: Boats to Burn: Bajo Fishing Activity in the Australian Fishing Zone
evidence.supports: Bajo and Rotinese use of Ashmore Reef and the 1974 memorandum of understanding.

contested.note: The exact dates and instruments of the 1878 and 1909 annexations are poorly documented in accessible sources, because nobody at the time thought a guano reef mattered. What is certain is that Britain claimed them in the late nineteenth century and transferred them to Australia in 1934.

pedagogy.hook: Britain annexed Ashmore Reef in 1878 for bird droppings. A century later the same three sand cays became the front line of Australia's border policy.

misconception.belief: Empires only bothered with places that were valuable or populated.
misconception.correction: Britain claimed hundreds of uninhabited rocks, reefs and cays - for guano, for cable stations, for coaling, or simply to stop another power having them. Those claims are why Australia, Britain and France still have territory and seabed rights scattered across two oceans today.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The smallest imperial claims have the longest afterlives: a reef annexed for fertiliser in 1878 now decides where a boat can seek asylum and where a gas field belongs.

territories.name: Coral Sea Islands
territories.formalName: Coral Sea Islands Territory

from.note: The Queensland Coast Islands Act took effect during 1879; contemporary practice treated the Coral Sea cays as within the British sphere from about then, but no single proclamation names them.

geoCoverage.label: Scattered reefs and sand cays east of the Great Barrier Reef
geoCoverage.change: The cays were worked for guano by British and colonial companies from the 1860s and treated as British without ever being separately annexed.

date.note: No proclamation names these cays individually. This date follows the Queensland Coast Islands Act, after which British and colonial authorities treated the Coral Sea cays as British.

acquisitions.how: British and colonial guano companies occupied and dug out cays such as Willis, Cato and Lihou from the 1860s, and the British and Queensland authorities treated the whole scatter of reefs as British without ever passing a law that named them.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: The cays have no fresh water and have never had a permanent population. Torres Strait Islander and Pacific voyagers knew the reefs; nobody lived on them.

contested.note: There is no single instrument by which Britain took the Coral Sea cays, which is why this record is dated loosely and marked low confidence. Australia's Coral Sea Islands Act 1969 declared them Australian territory on the assumption that they were already British.

evidence.author: Stuart Kaye
evidence.work: Australia's Maritime Boundaries
evidence.publisher: Centre for Maritime Policy, University of Wollongong
evidence.supports: The uncertain legal basis of Australia's Coral Sea claim.

from.note: See how it was taken: no instrument names these cays, so the date is a convention, not a proclamation.

statusPeriods.label: British by assumption rather than by proclamation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody governed them. Guano diggers came and went, a weather station was put on Willis Island in 1921, and no court, officer or law ever sat there.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default for a crown colony is 5. There was no administration at all - the status is a legal shadow, not a government - so anything above 1 would misrepresent it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere in particular; Brisbane took a practical interest from 1921
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody lived there.

departures.how: Australia passed the Coral Sea Islands Act 1969 declaring the reefs an Australian territory, tidying up a claim that Britain had never properly made and nobody had ever contested.

becomes.name: Coral Sea Islands Territory, Commonwealth of Australia

led.name: John Gorton
led.role: Australian prime minister whose government legislated the territory into existence

cost.note: Nobody died and nobody was displaced: nobody lived there. The only permanent residents have been the three or four staff of the Willis Island weather station.

departures.borders: The territory's boundary was drawn by Australian statute in 1969 and extended in 1997; it gives Australia jurisdiction over 780,000 square kilometres of sea and about three square kilometres of land.

instrument.name: Coral Sea Islands Act 1969 (Cth)

consequences.borderLegacy: Three square kilometres of sand generate jurisdiction over three quarters of a million square kilometres of ocean, now the world's third-largest marine park.
consequences.economicLegacy: Guano in the nineteenth century; nothing since but weather observations and turtles.

peak.populationNote: The only inhabitants have been the small staff of the Willis Island weather station, established in 1921 to give Queensland warning of cyclones.

evidence.author: Stuart Kaye
evidence.work: Australia's Maritime Boundaries
evidence.publisher: Centre for Maritime Policy, University of Wollongong

contested.note: This is the thinnest record in the region and is marked low confidence deliberately. No British instrument names these cays; Australia legislated in 1969 on the assumption that they were already British, and nobody has ever disputed it. Where the evidence is thin, this atlas says so rather than inventing a date.

pedagogy.hook: Australia's Coral Sea Islands Territory has three square kilometres of land, four residents on a good day, and jurisdiction over an area of ocean bigger than France and Germany combined.

misconception.belief: Every part of the empire was formally taken by a treaty, a war or a proclamation you can look up.
misconception.correction: Plenty of it was not. The Coral Sea cays were dug for guano, assumed to be British, and then legislated into Australian territory in 1969 without anyone ever finding the document that made them British in the first place. Empires accumulated by habit as well as by conquest.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is an honest example of the limits of the record: this atlas can tell you exactly when Hong Kong was leased and cannot tell you when Britain took these reefs, because nobody wrote it down.

date.note: A conventional date; no proclamation names the cays.

keyDates.what: The cays treated as British after the Queensland annexations

territories.name: New Zealand
territories.formalName: Colony, then Dominion, of New Zealand

from.note: Māori arrived from East Polynesia in the late thirteenth century; Aotearoa is now the standard Māori name for the whole country, though in the nineteenth century it usually meant the North Island.

namesOverTime.name: Nieuw Zeeland
namesOverTime.note: Dutch cartographers named it after the province of Zeeland following Abel Tasman's 1642 voyage. Tasman never landed: four of his men were killed at Golden Bay and he sailed away.

namesOverTime.name: New Zealand
namesOverTime.note: Cook anglicised the Dutch name during his 1769-70 circumnavigation of the islands.

modernSuccessors.name: New Zealand / Aotearoa
modernSuccessors.note: A Commonwealth realm; the Treaty of Waitangi is treated by its courts and parliament as a founding document with continuing legal force.

geoCoverage.label: The North, South and Stewart Islands, with the Chathams and Kermadecs
geoCoverage.change: Hobson proclaimed sovereignty over the North Island by cession and the South Island by discovery on 21 May 1840. The Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau and Western Samoa, which New Zealand later administered, are recorded separately here.

acquisitions.how: At Waitangi, and then at more than fifty gatherings around the country, about 540 rangatira signed a treaty with Britain - but the Māori text they signed and the English text London kept did not say the same thing.

counterparties.name: The rangatira and hapū of the Māori nations, including Ngāpuhi, Waikato-Tainui, Ngāti Toa, Ngāi Tahu and Te Āti Awa
counterparties.lost: Under the English text, sovereignty. Under the Māori text they signed, only kāwanatanga - governorship - while keeping tino rangatiratanga, full chieftainship, over their lands, villages and treasures.
counterparties.note: Britain had already recognised Māori independence: in 1835 the Crown formally acknowledged He Whakaputanga, the Declaration of Independence of the United Tribes. That makes 1840 a treaty between recognised parties, not a claim over empty land.

instrument.name: Te Tiriti o Waitangi / The Treaty of Waitangi
instrument.note: Henry Williams and his son translated the English draft overnight on 4-5 February. About 540 rangatira signed nine sheets during 1840; only 39 signed an English-language sheet. Where two texts of a treaty differ, international law prefers the one the indigenous party signed - the principle of contra proferentem - which is the Māori text.

people.name: William Hobson
people.role: naval captain and first governor; presented and signed the treaty

people.name: Hōne Heke Pōkai
people.role: Ngāpuhi rangatira, first to sign at Waitangi, and within five years the first to fight the Crown over what it meant

people.name: Tāmati Wāka Nene
people.role: Ngāpuhi rangatira whose speech at Waitangi persuaded the meeting to sign, and who later fought on the Crown's side

people.name: Henry Williams
people.role: missionary who translated the treaty into Māori overnight, choosing the word kāwanatanga for sovereignty

people.name: Te Wherowhero
people.role: Waikato paramount chief who refused to sign and was later crowned the first Māori King

acquisitions.resistance: Signing was not surrender. Hōne Heke cut down the flagstaff at Kororāreka four times between July 1844 and March 1845 and then fought the Northern War, arguing that the Crown had taken more than the treaty gave it.

contested.note: What the treaty transferred is the central question of New Zealand history. In 2014 the Waitangi Tribunal found that the northern rangatira who signed in February 1840 did not cede sovereignty; the Crown's position is that it acquired sovereignty in 1840, however that was understood at the time.

positions.claim: The rangatira ceded governorship and kept sovereignty; the Crown gained the right to control its own settlers, not to rule Māori.
positions.heldBy: Waitangi Tribunal report Wai 1040 (2014); Ranginui Walker; most Māori scholarship

positions.claim: The Crown acquired sovereignty over New Zealand in 1840, and the treaty's guarantees operate within that sovereignty.
positions.heldBy: The New Zealand Crown's long-standing legal position

evidence.author: Claudia Orange
evidence.work: The Treaty of Waitangi
evidence.supports: The negotiation, the two texts, the signings and their immediate consequences.

acquisitions.how: Hobson proclaimed British sovereignty over the North Island by cession under the treaty and over the South Island by right of discovery, without waiting for southern signatures, because a French colonising expedition was on its way to Akaroa.

counterparties.name: Ngāi Tahu and the other iwi of Te Waipounamu (the South Island)
counterparties.lost: Any argument that their land came under the Crown by their own consent; the proclamation claimed the island on the ground that Cook had seen it in 1770.
counterparties.note: Ngāi Tahu rangatira did sign the treaty later in 1840, which makes the 'discovery' claim both unnecessary and revealing about what Britain thought it needed.

instrument.name: Hobson's proclamations of sovereignty, 21 May 1840
instrument.note: Published in the London Gazette on 2 October 1840.

people.name: Charles Lavaud
people.role: French naval officer who arrived at Akaroa in August 1840 to find the Union Jack already flying

acquisitions.resistance: None at the moment of proclamation. The South Island's grievance was worked out in land purchases instead: Ngāi Tahu sold 34.5 million acres between 1844 and 1864 for about 14,750 pounds, with reserves promised and never properly made.

to.note: The first elections under the 1852 Constitution Act were held between July and October 1853; there was no single polling day.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony: a governor, and a treaty already in dispute
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor ruled with a nominated council, held the sole right to buy Māori land, and spent the 1840s discovering that he could not enforce a decision anywhere a chief did not agree with it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Auckland from 1841, under Sydney until 3 May 1841 and then the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Māori outnumbered settlers roughly ten to one in 1840 and still outnumbered them in 1855.
statusPeriods.note: New Zealand was a dependency of New South Wales from January 1840 until it was made a separate colony on 3 May 1841.

from.note: Elections to the first General Assembly ran from July to October 1853; it met in May 1854.

statusPeriods.label: A settler parliament, elected by settlers
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Constitution Act 1852 created a General Assembly and six provinces, elected on a property franchise defined in a way that excluded almost every Māori man, because Māori land was held communally and not by individual title.
statusPeriods.franchise: Men holding individual freehold worth 50 pounds or paying rent above a threshold. Communal Māori title did not qualify, so about 100 Māori men could vote out of a population of some 60,000.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government - and war over land
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Settler ministers ran everything except Māori affairs, which the governor kept until 1863 and then handed over too. The colonial parliament then voted to confiscate Māori land and to invade the Waikato.
statusPeriods.franchise: Four Māori seats were created in 1867 for a population entitled by numbers to about sixteen. All men could vote from 1879; New Zealand gave women the vote on 19 September 1893, the first self-governing country in the world to do so.
statusPeriods.note: British imperial troops - up to 12,000 of them at the peak in 1864 - fought the New Zealand Wars alongside colonial forces and Māori allies until they were withdrawn in 1870.

statusPeriods.label: Dominion of New Zealand
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: New Zealand changed its title from colony to dominion, mostly for prestige. Britain still ran foreign policy, the Privy Council was still the final court, and New Zealand declined to adopt the Statute of Westminster for sixteen years.
statusPeriods.franchise: All adult men and women, Māori included, though Māori voted in separate seats until 1975 and could not choose which roll to be on until 1967.
statusPeriods.note: New Zealand sent about 100,000 people overseas in the First World War from a population of just over a million; some 18,000 died. It was the most heavily committed country in the empire per head.

statusPeriods.label: Legally independent, still tidying up
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: New Zealand finally adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1947, so Britain could no longer legislate for it. Appeals to the Privy Council in London continued until 2004, longer than in any other former dominion.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default for 'dominion' is 1. After 1947 Britain had no power to legislate for New Zealand and no role in its government; leaving this at 1 would imply a British authority that had ended.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage; the voting age fell to 18 in 1974. Māori won the right to choose between the Māori and general rolls in 1967 and proportional representation from 1996 raised Māori representation sharply.

date.display: between 1907 and 1987 - there is no independence day
date.note: Candidate dates: 26 September 1907 (dominion status), 25 November 1947 (Statute of Westminster Adoption Act), 1 January 1987 (Constitution Act 1986 came into force) and even 2004 (the Supreme Court replaced the Privy Council). New Zealand has never held an independence ceremony.

departures.how: New Zealand's separation from Britain happened by statute, slowly and without enthusiasm: it turned down the Statute of Westminster for sixteen years, kept appeals to London until 2004, and still has the British monarch as head of state.

becomes.name: New Zealand / Aotearoa

led.name: Joseph Ward
led.role: premier who asked for the title of Dominion in 1907

led.name: Peter Fraser
led.role: prime minister whose government adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1947 and helped write the United Nations Charter

led.name: Whina Cooper
led.role: led the 1975 land march from Te Hāpua to Parliament that forced the Treaty back into New Zealand law

departures.movement: No independence movement against Britain. The movement that changed New Zealand was Māori: Kīngitanga, Kotahitanga, Rātana, Ngā Tamatoa and the 1975 land march.

cost.note: Nobody died in New Zealand's separation from Britain. The wars that shaped the country were fought inside it, between the Crown and Māori, between 1845 and 1872.

departures.borders: Nothing moved. New Zealand's borders are coastlines - and it kept the Pacific territories Britain had given it: the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau are still in free association or under New Zealand administration today.

instrument.name: Statute of Westminster Adoption Act 1947, and the Constitution Act 1986
instrument.note: The 1947 Act adopted the 1931 Statute; the Constitution Act 1986 repealed the last of the imperial constitutional statutes and came into force on 1 January 1987.

contested.note: As in Australia, there is no agreed date. The choice matters because 1907 makes New Zealand independent before the New Zealand Wars generation had died, while 1987 makes it younger than most of its people.

evidence.work: Dominion of New Zealand: Statesmen and Status 1907-1945
evidence.publisher: New Zealand Institute of International Affairs
evidence.supports: Dominion status and the long delay in adopting the Statute of Westminster.

violence.note: The New Zealand Wars of 1845-72 killed roughly 2,900 people. The Crown then confiscated about 3.2 million acres from iwi it declared to be in rebellion - including from iwi that had fought on its own side.

toll.note: James Belich counts about 2,150 Māori dead (including Māori fighting for the Crown) and about 745 British, colonial and allied dead. Vincent O'Malley's work on the Waikato invasion suggests Māori civilian deaths were undercounted. Nobody kept a register.

populationTransfer.note: Assisted immigration brought some 100,000 Britons in the 1870s alone under Julius Vogel's scheme, deliberately overwhelming the Māori population that the wars had already halved.

toll.note: The Māori population fell from perhaps 100,000 in 1769 to 42,113 at the 1896 census - the nadir - through introduced disease, war, confiscation and displacement. It is now about 900,000, roughly 17 per cent of New Zealanders.

commonwealth.note: New Zealand is a Commonwealth realm sharing the British monarch as head of state, and its own realm includes the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau and the Ross Dependency.

consequences.borderLegacy: New Zealand's land borders are internal: the raupatu confiscation lines of 1864-65, which are still visible in who owns what in Taranaki and the Waikato today.
consequences.economicLegacy: Refrigerated shipping from 1882 turned New Zealand into Britain's farm - lamb, butter and cheese - until Britain joined the European Economic Community in 1973 and the market vanished within a decade.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Te reo Māori was beaten out of children in schools for generations and became an official language in 1987. The Treaty is now enforced through the Waitangi Tribunal and settlements worth more than 2.5 billion New Zealand dollars.

peak.populationNote: 1911 census: 1,008,468 including Māori, of whom 49,844 were counted as Māori. The Māori population had bottomed out at 42,113 in 1896.

evidence.work: The Great War for New Zealand: Waikato 1800-2000

contested.note: Whether Māori ceded sovereignty in 1840 is disputed between the Crown's legal position and the Waitangi Tribunal's 2014 finding, and it is a live political argument in New Zealand right now. The atlas gives both positions rather than choosing.

pedagogy.hook: The Treaty of Waitangi exists in two versions. The 540 rangatira who signed it signed the Māori one, and the Māori one never uses the word for sovereignty.

misconception.belief: New Zealand was colonised peacefully by treaty, unlike Australia.
misconception.correction: There was a treaty, and then there was a war. Between 1845 and 1872 the Crown fought Māori across the North Island, deployed up to 12,000 imperial troops - more than it sent to any other settler colony - and confiscated 3.2 million acres. A treaty made the colonisation legal in British eyes; it did not make it peaceful.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: New Zealand is the empire's only settler colony founded on a signed treaty with the people already there, which is why it is the only one where those people can still take the Crown to a tribunal and win. The treaty is not history in New Zealand; it is current law.

territories.name: Cook Islands
territories.formalName: The Cook Islands (a British protectorate, then part of New Zealand)

from.display: the Māori name, used alongside the English one
from.note: The islands were settled from Tahiti and the Marquesas around the sixth to twelfth centuries; each island has its own name and there was no single name for the group before Europeans grouped them.

to.note: The Russian cartographer Adam von Krusenstern renamed the group for Cook in the 1820s; the change spread slowly.

from.note: Named by a Russian admiralty cartographer for a British captain who never saw most of them.

modernSuccessors.name: Cook Islands
modernSuccessors.note: Self-governing in free association with New Zealand. Cook Islanders are New Zealand citizens; the Cook Islands runs its own foreign policy and has diplomatic relations with more than 50 states, but has no seat at the United Nations.

geoCoverage.label: Fifteen islands across two million square kilometres of sea
geoCoverage.change: A British protectorate was declared over Rarotonga at the ariki's own request; the northern atolls were added in 1888-89 and New Zealand annexed the lot in 1901.

acquisitions.how: Captain Bourke of HMS Hyacinth raised the flag over Rarotonga at the request of Queen Makea Takau Ariki, who had petitioned Britain three times because France had just annexed the Society Islands 1,100 kilometres away.

counterparties.name: The ariki of Rarotonga, Aitutaki, Mangaia and the northern atolls
counterparties.lost: Their foreign relations, and eventually their government - though in 1888 they gained the protection they had asked for and kept their titles, which the ariki still hold.
counterparties.note: This is one of the small number of British takings that began as a request from the people who ended up under British rule. It did not stay on those terms: New Zealand annexed the islands outright thirteen years later.

people.name: Makea Takau Ariki
people.role: paramount chief of Rarotonga who petitioned Queen Victoria for protection against France and got it

people.name: Frederick Moss
people.role: first British Resident, who set up a federal parliament of the ariki in 1891 and was removed for taking it seriously

acquisitions.resistance: There was none in 1888. Resistance came later and was constitutional: the Cook Islands Progressive Association of the 1940s and Albert Henry's campaign for self-government.

acquisitions.how: New Zealand's boundaries were redrawn by order in council to swallow the whole group, after the ariki had signed a deed of cession in 1900 believing they were dealing with Britain rather than Wellington.

counterparties.name: The ariki and people of the Cook Islands
counterparties.lost: Their protectorate status and their federal parliament; from 1901 they were governed by a New Zealand Resident Commissioner under New Zealand law.

instrument.name: Order in Council extending the boundaries of the Colony of New Zealand
instrument.note: Made on 13 May 1901, effective 11 June 1901. The same instrument brought in Niue, which then demanded and got a separate administration.

people.name: Richard Seddon
people.role: New Zealand premier who wanted a Pacific empire of his own and got the Cook Islands and Niue

evidence.author: Dick Scott
evidence.work: Years of the Pooh-Bah: A Cook Islands History
evidence.publisher: Cook Islands Trading Corporation and Hodder & Stoughton
evidence.supports: The protectorate, the New Zealand annexation and the Resident Commissioners.

statusPeriods.label: British protectorate at the ariki's request
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Resident advised a federal parliament of ariki and elected members; Britain handled foreign affairs, and the islands' own chiefs handled almost everything else.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Rarotonga, under the Western Pacific High Commission in Fiji
statusPeriods.franchise: The 1891 federal parliament had elected members chosen by island councils - one of the earliest representative bodies in the Pacific.

statusPeriods.label: Governed by New Zealand as part of New Zealand
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Resident Commissioner appointed in Wellington ran the islands under New Zealand law; islanders were New Zealand subjects with no vote in the parliament that governed them.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Rarotonga, under the Department of Island Territories, Wellington
statusPeriods.franchise: Island councils had limited elected members. A Legislative Council with an elected majority came only in 1957 and a Legislative Assembly in 1958.
statusPeriods.note: New Zealand's administration was slow and often incompetent: the 1918 influenza reached Rarotonga on a New Zealand government ship, and copra prices were controlled from Wellington for the benefit of New Zealand traders.

departures.how: Cook Islanders voted in a United Nations-observed election and chose full self-government in free association with New Zealand, keeping New Zealand citizenship and the right to move there - an arrangement neither colony nor independence.

becomes.name: Cook Islands

led.name: Albert Henry
led.role: founded the Cook Islands Party and became the first Premier in 1965; deposed in 1978 for electoral fraud

led.name: Sir Thomas Davis (Pa Tuterangi Ariki)
led.role: physician and writer who founded the opposition Democratic Party in 1971 and became prime minister in 1978, the second leader of the self-governing Cook Islands

departures.movement: Cook Islands Party

cost.note: Nobody died. The cost has been demographic: more than three times as many Cook Islanders now live in New Zealand and Australia as in the islands, because free association gave every one of them the right to leave.

departures.borders: No land border exists. Free association gave the Cook Islands one of the largest exclusive economic zones in the world - nearly two million square kilometres - around 236 square kilometres of land.

instrument.name: Cook Islands Constitution Act 1964 (NZ)
instrument.note: Passed by the New Zealand parliament in 1964 and brought into force on 4 August 1965 after the election.

populationTransfer.note: Peruvian slave ships raided the northern atolls in 1862-63, carrying off hundreds of people from Penrhyn and Rakahanga; almost none came back. A century later free association emptied the islands again, voluntarily.

toll.note: Estimates of the Peruvian raids across Polynesia run to about 3,600 people taken in 1862-63, of whom perhaps a tenth ever returned. Island-by-island figures are unreliable.

commonwealth.note: The Cook Islands is not a Commonwealth member in its own right, because it is in free association with New Zealand rather than fully independent. It belongs to the Pacific Islands Forum and to many United Nations agencies.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copra, then citrus, then pearls and tourism. The largest single source of income for many families is money sent home from New Zealand and Australia.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Cook Islands Māori and English are both official; the law is New Zealand-derived but land is held under customary title and cannot be sold to outsiders.

peak.populationNote: 1966 census, the peak resident population. The 2021 count was about 15,000 resident, with more than 80,000 Cook Islanders in New Zealand and Australia.

populationWarrant.supports: Cook Islands’s largest recorded population: 19,247 people, counted in 1966.

evidence.author: Dick Scott
evidence.work: Years of the Pooh-Bah: A Cook Islands History
evidence.publisher: Cook Islands Trading Corporation and Hodder & Stoughton
evidence.supports: Protectorate, annexation, New Zealand administration and self-government.

evidence.author: W. David McIntyre
evidence.work: Winding Up the British Empire in the Pacific Islands
evidence.supports: Free association as a constitutional route out of empire.

pedagogy.hook: The Cook Islands asked to become British. Queen Makea Takau petitioned London three times, and got a protectorate in 1888 - then found herself annexed by New Zealand thirteen years later.

misconception.belief: Every colony was taken against the will of its people.
misconception.correction: Some small Pacific states asked for British protection, because the realistic alternative was annexation by France, Germany or the United States - or being emptied by slave ships and labour recruiters. Choosing the least bad option under duress is not the same as consent, and it is not the same as conquest either.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Free association, invented here in 1965, is a third way out of empire that neither India nor Ghana had: full self-government plus the citizenship of the former ruler. Three Pacific states use it, and it explains why more Cook Islanders live in Auckland than in Rarotonga.

territories.name: Niue
territories.formalName: Niue (Savage Island)

from.note: Settled from Samoa and Tonga about 1,000 years ago. The name is usually explained as 'behold the coconut'.

namesOverTime.name: Savage Island

to.note: The insulting English name faded from official use around the time of the protectorate, though it lingered on charts for decades.

namesOverTime.note: Cook tried to land three times, was driven off each time, and named the island for the people who refused him.

modernSuccessors.name: Niue
modernSuccessors.note: Self-governing in free association with New Zealand; Niueans are New Zealand citizens.

geoCoverage.label: One raised coral island, 260 square kilometres
geoCoverage.change: A British protectorate was declared after two decades of Niuean petitions to Queen Victoria asking for it.

acquisitions.how: Britain finally accepted a protectorate over Niue after ignoring petitions from its kings for twenty-one years; the islanders wanted protection from labour recruiters and from annexation by anyone else.

counterparties.name: The patu-iki (kings) and village councils of Niue
counterparties.lost: Very little at first: they had asked for this. What they lost came in 1901, when New Zealand annexed the island and appointed a Resident Commissioner over their heads.
counterparties.note: King Fataaiki wrote to Queen Victoria in 1879 and again in 1887: 'Do not cast us away'. The letters are in the archives; the reply took thirteen years.

people.name: Fataaiki
people.role: patu-iki of Niue who petitioned Queen Victoria twice for British protection

people.name: Nukai Peniamina
people.role: Niuean who trained as a missionary in Samoa and was the first allowed to land back home in 1846, ending the island's isolation

acquisitions.resistance: Niue had spent a century keeping outsiders off: Cook was repelled three times in 1774, and missionaries were refused landing until a Niuean brought Christianity himself in 1846.

acquisitions.how: The same order in council that took the Cook Islands attached Niue to New Zealand, 2,400 kilometres from Rarotonga and 480 from its nearest neighbour; Niueans objected and were given their own administration in 1903.

counterparties.name: The people of Niue
counterparties.lost: Their separate protectorate status, and control of their own government to a New Zealand Resident Commissioner.

instrument.name: Order in Council extending the boundaries of the Colony of New Zealand
instrument.note: Effective 11 June 1901. Niue was administered with the Cook Islands until Niueans successfully demanded a separate administration in 1903.

statusPeriods.label: British protectorate, for fourteen months
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain declared the protectorate and did essentially nothing with it; the island's village councils continued to govern.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nominally the Western Pacific High Commission in Fiji
statusPeriods.franchise: Village councils and the patu-iki governed by consensus.

statusPeriods.label: Part of New Zealand, run by a Resident Commissioner
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A New Zealand Resident Commissioner governed with a Niuean island council; Niueans were New Zealand subjects and then citizens, with no vote for the parliament in Wellington that made their laws.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Alofi, under the Department of Island Territories, Wellington
statusPeriods.franchise: An elected Island Council existed from 1901 with advisory powers; a Legislative Assembly with real powers came in 1960.
statusPeriods.note: In 1953 the Resident Commissioner, Cecil Larsen, was murdered by five Niuean prisoners - the only killing of a colonial administrator in New Zealand's Pacific territories.

departures.how: Niueans voted in a United Nations-observed referendum for self-government in free association with New Zealand rather than independence or integration, and kept New Zealand citizenship.

becomes.name: Niue

led.name: Robert Rex
led.role: led the self-government negotiations and served as Premier from 1974 until his death in 1992

led.name: Young Vivian
led.role: cabinet minister at self-government and later Premier; one of the drafters of the constitution

departures.movement: The Niue constitutional talks of 1965-74

cost.note: Nobody died. The referendum was won on a turnout of about 60 per cent, with 887 votes for self-government and 469 against.

departures.borders: None. Niue is a single island 480 kilometres from its nearest neighbour, which is why it is the most isolated self-governing state in the Pacific.

instrument.name: Niue Constitution Act 1974 (NZ)

populationTransfer.note: Niue's population has fallen by two thirds since self-government, from about 5,200 in 1966 to under 1,700 today, because free association gave every Niuean the right to live in New Zealand and most of them took it.

toll.note: About 30,000 people of Niuean descent live in New Zealand, roughly twenty times the population of the island itself. The figures come from New Zealand census self-identification and are approximate.

commonwealth.note: Niue is not a Commonwealth member in its own right; it takes part in Pacific regional bodies and is a party to United Nations treaties in its own name.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copra, passionfruit and taro all failed as exports. Niue now runs on New Zealand budget support, its internet domain name and a small tourism industry built on whales and caves.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Niuean and English are official. Land is held under customary title by families, and cannot be sold.

peak.populationNote: 1966 census, the highest ever recorded. The 2022 census counted about 1,681 residents.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Niue’s largest recorded population: 5,194 people, counted in 1966.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Terry Chapman
evidence.work: Niue: A History of the Island
evidence.publisher: Institute of Pacific Studies, University of the South Pacific
evidence.supports: Niuean petitions, the protectorate, New Zealand administration and self-government.

evidence.author: W. David McIntyre
evidence.work: Winding Up the British Empire in the Pacific Islands
evidence.supports: The constitutional route to free association.

pedagogy.hook: Niue's king wrote to Queen Victoria in 1879 asking to be made a British protectorate. Britain took twenty-one years to answer, and then handed the island to New Zealand within fourteen months.

misconception.belief: Independence always increases a country's population and strength.
misconception.correction: Niue chose self-government with New Zealand citizenship in 1974, and two thirds of its people used that citizenship to leave. Its population went from 5,194 in 1966 to under 1,700 today. Free association gave Niueans real choices; it did not give Niue a future its own people would stay for.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Niue is the smallest self-governing state in the world and shows what the end of empire looks like when a territory is too small to stand alone: not flags and armies, but a negotiated relationship, a passport and an emptying island.

territories.name: Tokelau
territories.formalName: Tokelau (the Union Islands)

from.note: Settled about a thousand years ago from Samoa, Tonga and Tuvalu. The name means 'north' or 'north wind'.

namesOverTime.name: Union Islands
namesOverTime.note: The colonial name, dropped after the Second World War.

modernSuccessors.name: Tokelau (New Zealand)
modernSuccessors.note: Legally part of New Zealand, and still on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories because Tokelauans have twice voted not to leave it.

from.note: Captain Oldham of HMS Egeria declared the protectorate over the three atolls during June 1889; the atolls were visited on different days.

geoCoverage.label: Three atolls: Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo
geoCoverage.change: Britain declared a protectorate over the atolls, mainly to keep them out of German and American hands.

geoCoverage.label: Handed to New Zealand to administer
geoCoverage.change: Britain transferred the administration to New Zealand, which ran the atolls from Apia in Western Samoa - a mandate it did not own governing a colony it did not own.

date.note: The three atolls were proclaimed on different days in June 1889 by Captain Oldham of HMS Egeria.

acquisitions.how: A British warship raised the flag over Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo to stop Germany or the United States claiming them, and then almost nobody from Britain visited for twenty-five years.

counterparties.name: The people of Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo
counterparties.lost: Their independence in law, though in practice the village councils of elders, the taupulega, went on governing and still do.
counterparties.note: The islands had already lost far more to Peruvian slave ships in 1863, which took away most of the able-bodied men of Fakaofo and Nukunonu.

people.name: Charles Oldham
people.role: commander of HMS Egeria, who proclaimed the protectorate

acquisitions.resistance: None recorded. Tokelau's population had been halved a generation earlier by slave raiders and disease and was in no condition to resist anything.

from.note: Proclaimed over three atolls on separate days in June 1889.

statusPeriods.label: British protectorate, barely administered
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody governed Tokelau. The Western Pacific High Commission in Fiji had jurisdiction on paper and sent a ship every few years; the taupulega, the village councils of elders, governed in fact.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default for a protectorate is 3. Here even that overstates it: there was no resident official of any kind, and British authority amounted to an occasional visiting warship.
statusPeriods.franchise: The taupulega of each atoll governed by consensus of family heads, as they still do.

statusPeriods.label: Annexed into the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Tokelau was attached to a colony 2,000 kilometres away, run from Ocean Island, whose administrators spoke a different language and rarely came.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Ocean Island (Banaba), Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony
statusPeriods.franchise: The taupulega continued to govern in practice.

statusPeriods.label: Administered by New Zealand from Apia
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: New Zealand's administrator of Western Samoa - a League of Nations mandate - also administered Tokelau, so a mandated territory's officials governed a British protectorate.
statusPeriods.franchise: The taupulega continued to govern the atolls.

departures.how: Britain handed sovereignty over the three atolls to New Zealand under the Tokelau Islands Act 1948; the 1,500 Tokelauans were not asked, and it was the third administration they had been passed to without consultation.

becomes.name: Tokelau, a territory of New Zealand

led.name: Peter Fraser
led.role: New Zealand prime minister whose government legislated Tokelau into New Zealand

departures.movement: None in 1949. Tokelau's own self-government movement came in the 2000s and its people twice voted it down.

cost.note: Nobody died. Tokelau has since voted twice on leaving New Zealand's administration - in 2006 and 2007 - and fallen short of its own two-thirds threshold both times, the second by sixteen votes: 446 for and 232 against.

departures.borders: Three atolls with about 12 square kilometres of land spread over 170 kilometres of ocean. Swains Island, 200 kilometres away and culturally Tokelauan, was taken by the United States in 1925 and is American still.

instrument.name: Tokelau Islands Act 1948 (NZ)
instrument.note: Effective 1 January 1949. The name was changed from the Union Islands to Tokelau in 1946.

populationTransfer.note: In 1863 Peruvian slave ships took away most of the able-bodied men of Fakaofo and Nukunonu; the atolls lost roughly half their people, and the survivors rebuilt the villages around the families that were left.

toll.note: Contemporary accounts describe about 250 Tokelauan men taken in 1863. Almost none returned. Precise figures do not exist because the raiders kept no honest records.

consequences.economicLegacy: There is almost no economy: copra failed, the atolls have no airstrip, and Tokelau lives on New Zealand budget support and fishing licence revenue from its exclusive economic zone.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Tokelauan and English are official, and the taupulega - councils of family elders - still make the decisions on each atoll, which is why the referendums were run atoll by atoll.

peak.populationNote: The population peaked around 1,900 in the mid-1960s before a New Zealand resettlement scheme moved families to Wellington. The 2019 census counted 1,647.

evidence.author: Antony Hooper
evidence.work: Tokelau: A Historical Ethnography
evidence.supports: Tokelauan society, the slave raids and colonial administration. Written with Judith Huntsman.

evidence.author: W. David McIntyre
evidence.work: Winding Up the British Empire in the Pacific Islands
evidence.supports: Tokelau's transfers between administrations and its referendums.

contested.note: Tokelau's early colonial record is thin: the 1889 proclamations were made from a warship over three atolls on different days, and the exact dates are reported inconsistently. The atolls' population history before 1900 rests on missionary estimates.

pedagogy.hook: Tokelau has voted twice to stop being a colony and twice said no - the second time, in 2007, by sixteen votes.

misconception.belief: Colonised people always want independence, and any territory still governed from outside must be held against its will.
misconception.correction: Tokelau's 1,500 people set their own threshold of two thirds and did not reach it, twice. Three atolls with 12 square kilometres of land, no airport and a rising sea have to weigh sovereignty against New Zealand citizenship, budget support and evacuation. They chose the second, for now.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Tokelau is the empire's endgame in miniature: passed from Fiji to the Gilberts to New Zealand without ever being asked, and now asked repeatedly and choosing to stay. It also shows the UN decolonisation list for what it is - a live list, not a historical one.

keyDates.what: Peruvian slave ships take most of the men of Fakaofo and Nukunonu

date.note: Proclaimed on three atolls on separate days.
