territories.name: Western Samoa
territories.formalName: Territory of Western Samoa, under New Zealand mandate and trusteeship

from.display: the islands' own name, in continuous use
from.note: Samoa has been settled for about 3,000 years; the name has never changed, only the adjectives Europeans put in front of it.

namesOverTime.name: Western Samoa
namesOverTime.note: The country dropped 'Western' in 1997; American Samoa, still American, kept its adjective.

geoCoverage.label: Upolu, Savai'i and the smaller islands
geoCoverage.change: A New Zealand expeditionary force took the German colony without firing a shot, three weeks into the First World War.

acquisitions.how: 1,400 New Zealand troops landed at Apia and took the German colony without a shot being fired - the second German territory anywhere to fall in the First World War - and then governed it under martial law for six years.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Its richest Pacific colony, its copra plantations and its cable station, all seized in a single morning.

counterparties.name: The matai and fa'amatai of Samoa
counterparties.lost: One coloniser for another. Samoan leaders had fought a civil war and three foreign navies in the 1890s to keep control of their own government; in 1914 they were not consulted about the change.

people.name: Robert Logan
people.role: New Zealand colonel and first administrator, whose refusal to quarantine a ship in 1918 killed a fifth of the population

people.name: Erich Schultz
people.role: the German governor, who surrendered without resistance

acquisitions.resistance: None in 1914. Samoan resistance to New Zealand rule came later and was overwhelmingly non-violent: the Mau movement of the 1920s and 1930s.

acquisitions.how: The League of Nations gave New Zealand a Class C mandate over Western Samoa - the category for territories judged least ready for self-rule, to be administered as if they were part of the mandatory power's own territory.

counterparties.name: The people of Western Samoa
counterparties.lost: Any prospect of returning to the self-government they had before 1900. A Class C mandate meant government by New Zealand law, with an obligation only to report annually to Geneva.
counterparties.note: Samoans petitioned the League directly in 1927 and 1928. The League forwarded the petitions to New Zealand, the government they were complaining about.

instrument.name: League of Nations Class C Mandate for Western Samoa

people.name: Olaf Frederick Nelson
people.role: Samoan-Swedish merchant who led the Mau movement, funded its newspaper and was exiled from Samoa for ten years

acquisitions.resistance: The Mau - 'firmly held opinion' - organised a boycott, its own police and its own tax system from 1926, and at its peak had the support of most Samoans on Upolu.

evidence.author: Michael Field
evidence.work: Mau: Samoa's Struggle Against New Zealand Oppression
evidence.supports: The Mau movement, the influenza epidemic and Black Saturday.

acquisitions.how: The United Nations converted the mandate into a trusteeship with an explicit duty to prepare Samoa for independence, and sent visiting missions that Samoan leaders used to force the pace.

counterparties.name: The people of Western Samoa
counterparties.lost: Nothing further. This was the first step out: within a year the 1947 Samoa Amendment Act created a Council of State and a Legislative Assembly with a Samoan majority.

instrument.name: United Nations Trusteeship Agreement for Western Samoa

statusPeriods.label: New Zealand military occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A New Zealand colonel governed by military order with no legal title beyond conquest, no Samoan participation and no oversight from anyone.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Apia, under New Zealand military command
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The fono of matai continued to meet and were ignored.
statusPeriods.note: On 7 November 1918 the administrator let the SS Talune dock from Auckland with influenza aboard, and refused an American offer of medical help. About 8,500 Samoans died - more than a fifth of the population - while American Samoa, 100 kilometres away and under quarantine, lost nobody.

statusPeriods.label: New Zealand mandate; the Mau resists
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An administrator appointed in Wellington governed under New Zealand law and reported once a year to Geneva. When most Samoans withdrew their cooperation through the Mau, the administration answered by exiling leaders and, on 28 December 1929, by shooting into a crowd.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Apia, under the Department of Island Territories, Wellington
statusPeriods.franchise: Samoans had no vote. A Legislative Council of officials and European residents advised the administrator.

statusPeriods.label: United Nations trusteeship, on a road to independence
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: New Zealand still administered Samoa, but under a UN agreement that required it to prepare the country for self-government, with visiting missions Samoans could petition directly.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Apia, under Wellington and the UN Trusteeship Council
statusPeriods.franchise: The Legislative Assembly from 1948 had a Samoan majority chosen by the fono of matai. Universal adult suffrage came only in 1990, by referendum, in independent Samoa.

departures.how: After a United Nations-supervised plebiscite in May 1961 in which Samoans voted for independence, New Zealand's trusteeship ended and Samoa became the first Pacific island country to govern itself again in the twentieth century.

becomes.name: Independent State of Western Samoa

led.name: Malietoa Tanumafili II
led.role: joint head of state at independence and then sole head of state for 45 years

led.name: Tupua Tamasese Mea'ole
led.role: joint head of state at independence; brother of the Mau leader shot in 1929

led.name: Fiame Mata'afa Faumuina Mulinu'u II
led.role: first prime minister; led the constitutional convention

departures.movement: The Mau, and the constitutional conventions of 1954 and 1960

cost.note: Nobody died in 1962. The cost had been paid earlier: about 8,500 dead in the 1918 influenza and eleven Samoans shot on Black Saturday in 1929, including the Mau's leader Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III.

departures.borders: The line through the Samoan archipelago was drawn by Germany, Britain and the United States in 1899, splitting one people and one language between two states. It is still there: Samoa is independent, American Samoa is a United States territory, and families cross it with visas.

instrument.name: Western Samoa Act 1961 (NZ) and the Constitution of the Independent State of Western Samoa
instrument.note: The constitution was adopted by a constitutional convention on 28 October 1960 and approved in the plebiscite of 9 May 1961; independence took effect on 1 January 1962.

evidence.author: Malama Meleisea
evidence.work: The Making of Modern Samoa: Traditional Authority and Colonial Administration in the History of Western Samoa
evidence.publisher: Institute of Pacific Studies, University of the South Pacific
evidence.supports: The path from mandate to independence and the role of the matai system.

violence.note: On 28 December 1929 New Zealand police fired on an unarmed Mau procession in Apia. Eleven Samoans were killed, including the movement's leader Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III, who told his people as he died: 'My blood has been spilt for Samoa... do not dream of avenging it.'

toll.note: Accounts give between nine and eleven Samoan dead and one New Zealand policeman killed. In 2002 New Zealand's prime minister Helen Clark formally apologised in Apia for Black Saturday and for the influenza deaths.

populationTransfer.note: Germany imported thousands of Chinese and Melanesian indentured labourers for the copra plantations, and New Zealand inherited and continued the system until the 1930s.

commonwealth.note: Samoa joined the Commonwealth in 1970, eight years after independence, and is a republic with an elected head of state.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copra, cocoa and bananas gave way to remittances: more Samoans live in New Zealand, Australia and the United States than in Samoa, and money sent home is a fifth of the economy.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The fa'amatai - government through chiefly title-holders - was written into the 1960 constitution and still elects most of parliament. Samoa is the only Pacific country whose independence constitution built its own institutions in rather than copying Westminster whole.

peak.populationNote: 1961 census, just before independence. The 1918 influenza had killed about 8,500 people out of roughly 38,000, so the population took a generation to recover.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Western Samoa’s largest recorded population: 114,400 people, counted in 1961.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Malama Meleisea
evidence.work: The Making of Modern Samoa: Traditional Authority and Colonial Administration in the History of Western Samoa
evidence.publisher: Institute of Pacific Studies, University of the South Pacific
evidence.supports: Samoan political authority under German and New Zealand rule.

evidence.author: Michael Field
evidence.work: Mau: Samoa's Struggle Against New Zealand Oppression
evidence.supports: The influenza epidemic, the Mau and Black Saturday.

evidence.author: Damon Salesa
evidence.work: Racial Crossings: Race, Intermarriage, and the Victorian British Empire
evidence.supports: British and settler racial policy in the nineteenth-century Pacific, including Samoa.

pedagogy.hook: In November 1918 New Zealand's administrator let an infected ship dock at Apia. A fifth of Samoa died. In American Samoa, 100 kilometres away, the governor quarantined the port and not one person died of influenza.

misconception.belief: Mandates and trusteeships were a gentler kind of colony, supervised by the League of Nations and then the UN.
misconception.correction: A Class C mandate meant government as if the territory were the ruler's own soil, with a yearly report to Geneva. When Samoans petitioned the League in 1927 and 1928, the League passed the petitions to New Zealand to answer. Supervision only started to bite under the UN after 1946 - and then it worked, and Samoa was independent within sixteen years.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Samoa was the first Pacific colony to become independent, and it did it through a movement that was overwhelmingly non-violent, using the paperwork of the international system against the country administering it.

territories.name: Fiji
territories.formalName: Colony of Fiji

from.note: Settled about 3,000 years ago. 'Fiji' comes from the Tongan pronunciation, Fisi, which Cook heard and wrote down.

geoCoverage.label: About 330 islands, ceded by their chiefs
geoCoverage.change: Cakobau and twelve other chiefs signed a Deed of Cession at Levuka after Britain had twice refused to take the islands.

geoCoverage.label: With Rotuma
geoCoverage.change: The chiefs of Rotuma, 460 kilometres to the north and culturally Polynesian rather than Fijian, ceded their island to Britain and it was attached to Fiji. Rotumans have argued about that ever since.

acquisitions.how: Cakobau and twelve other high chiefs signed the islands over to Queen Victoria at Levuka - their third attempt to be annexed - because settler debt, an American damages claim and the labour trade had made their kingdom ungovernable.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Fiji and its high chiefs, led by Ratu Seru Epenisa Cakobau
counterparties.lost: Sovereignty, formally and by signature. What they kept was unusual: Fijian land was declared inalienable, and about 83 per cent of Fiji is still held under customary iTaukei title today.
counterparties.note: Cakobau had offered Fiji to Britain in 1858 and been refused. Britain accepted in 1874 partly to bring the Pacific labour trade under control and partly because the alternative was an American or Australian settler takeover.

instrument.name: Deed of Cession of Fiji
instrument.note: Signed at Levuka by Cakobau and twelve chiefs and by Sir Hercules Robinson for the Crown. Fijian nationalists and the courts have argued about its terms ever since; it is invoked in Fijian politics to this day.

people.name: Ratu Seru Epenisa Cakobau
people.role: Vunivalu of Bau and self-styled King of Fiji, who ceded the islands

people.name: Arthur Hamilton Gordon
people.role: first substantive governor, who banned the sale of Fijian land and the use of Fijian labour on plantations - and therefore imported Indian labour instead

people.name: Hercules Robinson
people.role: Governor of New South Wales, who accepted the cession for the Crown

acquisitions.resistance: The interior of Viti Levu did not accept the cession. The Kai Colo people fought the colonial government in 1876; hundreds were killed and many survivors were deported to other islands.

cost.note: Four months after cession, Cakobau's party returned from Sydney with measles and the colonial government did not quarantine them. Between a quarter and a third of all Fijians died in 1875 - commonly given as about 40,000 out of roughly 140,000. The lower bound reflects historians who put the pre-epidemic population lower.

warrant.author: The colonial government of Fiji, in its reports on the epidemic
warrant.work: Colonial reports on the measles epidemic of 1875
warrant.supports: Four months after cession, Cakobau's party returned from Sydney with measles and the colonial government did not quarantine them. Between a quarter and a third of all Fijians died in 1875 - commonly given as about 40,000 out of roughly 140,000. The lower bound reflects historians who put the pre-…
warrant.check: Colonial administration returns are printed in the territory’s annual Blue Book and administration report; the British copies are in the CO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The colonial government counted the deaths its own failure to quarantine had caused.

evidence.author: Deryck Scarr
evidence.work: Fiji: A Short History
evidence.supports: The cession, Gordon's administration and the colony's structure.

acquisitions.how: The chiefs of Rotuma, exhausted by wars between Catholic and Wesleyan converts, ceded their island to Britain, which attached it to Fiji 460 kilometres away.

counterparties.name: The seven district chiefs of Rotuma
counterparties.lost: Their independence, and their separate identity in colonial administration; Rotumans are Polynesian and speak an unrelated language, but were governed as part of a Melanesian colony.
counterparties.note: Rotuma voted against joining independent Fiji in 1970 and has periodically sought separate status since.

instrument.name: Deed of Cession of Rotuma

to.note: The member system became a full ministerial system during September 1967; no single day marks it.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony governed through the chiefs
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor ruled with a nominated council, but Gordon's system governed Fijians through their own chiefs and a Great Council of Chiefs, kept Fijian land unsaleable, and brought in Indian indentured workers to cut the cane instead.
statusPeriods.franchise: Europeans elected members from 1904; Indo-Fijians won elected seats in 1929 after a campaign; Fijians were represented by nominees of the Great Council of Chiefs until 1963, when Fijians and women of all communities finally got the vote.
statusPeriods.note: The governor of Fiji was also the High Commissioner for the Western Pacific from 1877 to 1952, which made Suva the administrative capital of Britain's whole island empire.

from.note: Internal self-government under a ministerial system began in September 1967.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government under Ratu Mara
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Fijian chief minister and cabinet ran internal affairs from Suva while Britain kept defence and foreign policy for three more years.
statusPeriods.franchise: A communal roll system: voters registered as Fijian, Indian or General and elected members of their own community, a design that made ethnicity the organising fact of Fijian politics and outlived the colony.

departures.how: Fiji became independent on the ninety-sixth anniversary of the cession, after London conferences at which Fijian chiefs, who feared being outnumbered, and Indo-Fijian leaders, who wanted one person one vote, agreed a compromise neither of them liked.

becomes.name: Dominion of Fiji, a republic from 1987

led.name: Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara
led.role: first prime minister; led the Alliance Party and governed for the next seventeen years

led.name: A.D. Patel
led.role: leader of the Federation Party who fought for a common roll and one person one vote, and died in 1969 before independence

led.name: Sidiq Koya
led.role: succeeded Patel and negotiated the independence compromise on behalf of Indo-Fijians

departures.movement: The Alliance Party and the National Federation Party

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. The cost came later: military coups in 1987, 2000 and 2006, and the emigration of tens of thousands of Indo-Fijians, whose share of the population fell from 51 per cent in 1966 to under 35 per cent today.

departures.borders: No border moved. The division that mattered was inside it - a communal electoral roll inherited from the colony, which made every election a census.

instrument.name: Fiji Independence Act 1970

evidence.author: Brij V. Lal
evidence.work: Broken Waves: A History of the Fiji Islands in the Twentieth Century
evidence.supports: The politics of decolonisation and the communal franchise.

populationTransfer.note: Between 1879 and 1916 the colonial government brought 60,965 people from India to Fiji under five-year indentures - girmit, from the English word 'agreement' - and by 1946 their descendants outnumbered indigenous Fijians in their own country.

toll.note: 60,965 indentured migrants arrived on 87 voyages between 1879 and 1916. About 60 per cent stayed at the end of their contracts. Mortality on the estates in the early years ran above 40 per thousand a year, and the 1916 Andrews and Pearson report on conditions helped end the system.

violence.note: The colonial government put down the Kai Colo of the Viti Levu highlands in 1876 with a campaign of village burning and deportation, and hanged the leaders of the 1873 Burns killings without much of a trial.

commonwealth.note: Fiji became a republic in 1987 and left the Commonwealth; it rejoined in 1997, was suspended after the 2006 coup, and was fully readmitted in 2014.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar built the colony and still shapes it: the mills were British-owned, the cane was cut by Indo-Fijian tenants on land leased from Fijian owners, and when the leases began expiring in the 1990s it caused a political crisis.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Three languages - Fijian, Fiji Hindi and English - and a land system in which 83 per cent of the country is inalienable customary title, which Gordon created in 1875 to protect Fijians and which now defines who can farm what.

peak.populationNote: 1966 census: 240,960 Indo-Fijians (50.5 per cent) and 202,176 indigenous Fijians (42.4 per cent). The 1875 measles epidemic had killed roughly a third of the Fijian population in a single year.

populationWarrant.supports: Fiji’s largest recorded population: 476,727 people, counted in 1966.

pedagogy.hook: Four months after Fiji became British, the governor let a ship land without quarantine. Measles killed about a third of all Fijians in 1875 - roughly 40,000 people in a few months.

misconception.belief: Britain conquered Fiji, as it conquered most of its colonies.
misconception.correction: Fiji's chiefs offered the islands to Britain in 1858 and were turned down; Britain accepted a signed Deed of Cession in 1874. That was not free choice - settler debt, a 45,000-dollar American damages claim and an out-of-control labour trade had wrecked Cakobau's kingdom - but it was a treaty, and Fijians still cite its wording in court and in parliament.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Fiji shows how one colonial decision can shape a country for a century: protecting Fijian land meant importing Indian workers, which produced two peoples of nearly equal size, a communal voting system, and four coups since independence.

territories.name: Tonga
territories.formalName: Kingdom of Tonga, a British protected state

from.display: the kingdom's own name, in continuous use
from.note: Settled about 3,000 years ago; the Tuʻi Tonga line of paramount chiefs goes back roughly a thousand years, which makes it one of the oldest continuous polities in the Pacific.

namesOverTime.name: Friendly Islands

to.note: The English name fell out of official use as the kingdom's own name was accepted.

namesOverTime.note: Cook's name for them. On his third visit Tongan chiefs debated killing him and his crew and could not agree on a method, which is why he sailed away thinking them friendly.

geoCoverage.label: An independent kingdom under British protection
geoCoverage.change: Tonga signed a Treaty of Friendship giving Britain control of its foreign relations, and kept its king, its constitution, its land law and its parliament.

acquisitions.how: King George Tupou II signed a Treaty of Friendship handing Tonga's foreign relations to Britain, six months after Germany had traded away its own claim to Tonga in exchange for a free hand in Samoa.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Tonga under King George Tupou II
counterparties.lost: Control of its foreign relations, and from 1905 a veto held by a British Agent and Consul over land dealings and senior appointments. It never lost its monarchy, its constitution or an acre of its land.
counterparties.note: Tonga had been recognised as an independent state by Germany in 1876, Britain in 1879 and the United States in 1888 - which is exactly why it had something to protect.

instrument.name: Treaty of Friendship between Great Britain and Tonga
instrument.note: Negotiated by Basil Thomson. A supplementary agreement of 1905 gave the British Agent a veto over the king's appointments and land grants; both were revised in 1958 and 1968 to hand the powers back.

people.name: Tāufaʻāhau (King George Tupou I)
people.role: unified Tonga, abolished serfdom and gave it a written constitution in 1875, which is why there was a state for Britain to protect rather than a coast to annex

people.name: George Tupou II
people.role: signed the Treaty of Friendship

people.name: Basil Thomson
people.role: British official who negotiated the treaty and had earlier been Tonga's prime minister

acquisitions.resistance: None was needed. Tonga's defence was its 1875 constitution, which made all land the property of the Crown and unsaleable to foreigners, so there was nothing for settlers to buy and no debt crisis to justify annexation.

evidence.author: I.C. Campbell
evidence.work: Island Kingdom: Tonga Ancient and Modern
evidence.supports: The 1875 constitution, the Treaty of Friendship and the protectorate years.

statusPeriods.label: Protected state: Britain handles foreign affairs
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The king governed Tonga; a British Consul handled its dealings with the outside world and nothing else.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nukuʻalofa; foreign relations from the Western Pacific High Commission in Suva
statusPeriods.franchise: Tonga's 1875 constitution gave every adult male taxpayer a vote for the people's representatives in the Legislative Assembly, alongside nobles' representatives and the king's ministers.

to.note: A revised agreement in 1968, following an earlier revision in 1958, returned the remaining powers to the Tongan government.

statusPeriods.label: A tighter grip after 1905
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A supplementary agreement gave the British Agent and Consul a veto over the appointment of ministers and over land dealings, after Britain decided the kingdom's finances were being mismanaged.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nukuʻalofa, with a British Agent and Consul
statusPeriods.franchise: Unchanged: adult male taxpayers elected the people's representatives. Women got the vote in 1960.
statusPeriods.note: Queen Sālote Tupou III reigned from 1918 to 1965 and became famous across the Commonwealth for riding through the rain in an open carriage at the 1953 coronation.

from.note: The 1968 revised Treaty of Friendship restored the Tongan government's control over appointments and finance.

statusPeriods.label: Powers handed back before the treaty ends
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Tonga ran its own internal affairs completely again; only foreign relations and defence remained with Britain, and both went in 1970.
statusPeriods.franchise: Adult men and, from 1960, women elected the people's representatives to the Legislative Assembly.

departures.how: Britain and Tonga ended the Treaty of Friendship by agreement, and Tonga took back its foreign relations - the only country in the Pacific that had never lost its government, its monarchy or its land.

becomes.name: Kingdom of Tonga

led.name: Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV
led.role: king who negotiated the end of the protectorate

led.name: Prince Tuʻipelehake
led.role: prime minister at independence and through the 1970s

departures.movement: None. There was no independence movement because there had been no colonisation to resist.

cost.note: Nobody died. Tonga is the only Pacific state whose exit from the British system cost nothing at all, because it had never surrendered anything but its foreign policy.

departures.borders: Not one line moved. Tonga's boundaries in 1970 were those of the kingdom Tāufaʻāhau had unified in the 1840s.

instrument.name: Treaty of Friendship between the United Kingdom and Tonga, 1970

commonwealth.note: Tonga is a Commonwealth member with its own monarch - one of only a few, alongside Malaysia, Lesotho and Eswatini.

retainedTerritory.note: Tonga kept everything: all land belongs to the Crown and cannot be sold to foreigners, a rule from the 1875 constitution that survived seventy years of protection unchanged.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copra, bananas, squash to Japan, and now remittances: about half of Tonga's income comes from Tongans living in New Zealand, Australia and the United States.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Tongan is the everyday language, the 1875 constitution is still in force in amended form, and the nobility still elects nine of the parliament's seats - though the 2010 reforms finally gave elected commoners a majority after the 2006 riots in Nukuʻalofa.

peak.populationNote: Estimate for 1970, the year the protectorate ended; the 1966 census counted 77,429. About 100,000 Tongans now live abroad.

evidence.author: I.C. Campbell
evidence.work: Island Kingdom: Tonga Ancient and Modern
evidence.supports: The unification, the 1875 constitution and the protectorate.

evidence.author: Sione Lātūkefu
evidence.work: Church and State in Tonga: The Wesleyan Methodist Missionaries and Political Development, 1822-1875
evidence.supports: How the constitution of 1875 was made and why it mattered.

pedagogy.hook: Tonga is the only Pacific country never colonised. Its defence was a constitution written in 1875 that made all land the property of the Crown, so there was nothing for a settler to buy.

misconception.belief: Small Pacific islands had no chance against European empires - they were annexed as a matter of course.
misconception.correction: Tonga was not. A king who unified the islands by 1845, converted to Methodism, abolished serfdom and issued a written constitution in 1875 created a state that European powers had to recognise. In 1900 Tonga signed away its foreign policy and kept everything else, and got it all back in 1970.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Tonga is the counter-example that makes the rest of the Pacific legible. Where a strong centralised state existed before Europeans arrived, empire had to negotiate; where it did not, empire annexed. The difference was mostly about whether land could be bought.

Treaty of Friendship: Tonga becomes a British protected state
Queen Sālote Tupou III begins a 47-year reign
The protectorate ends by agreement

territories.name: British Solomon Islands
territories.formalName: British Solomon Islands Protectorate

namesOverTime.name: Islas Salomón
namesOverTime.note: Álvaro de Mendaña named them for King Solomon's mines, which he did not find. He then lost the islands so completely that Europeans could not locate them again for two centuries.

namesOverTime.name: Solomon Islands
namesOverTime.note: The word 'British' was dropped from the name three years before independence.

geoCoverage.label: The southern Solomons, extended by treaty in 1900
geoCoverage.change: A warship declared a protectorate over the southern islands to control the labour trade. Santa Cruz was added in 1898-99 and Germany handed over Choiseul, Santa Isabel, the Shortlands and Ontong Java in 1900 - keeping Bougainville, which is why Bougainville is in Papua New Guinea today.

acquisitions.how: Captain Herbert Gibson of HMS Curacoa raised the flag over Guadalcanal, Malaita, New Georgia, San Cristobal and Savo, to bring the labour recruiters and the traders who armed them under some kind of British law.

counterparties.name: The peoples of the southern Solomon Islands, including the Kwaio, Kwara'ae, To'abaita and Are'are of Malaita and the Roviana of New Georgia
counterparties.lost: Their independence in law. In practice a protectorate with one Resident Commissioner and no troops did not govern Malaita's interior for another thirty years.
counterparties.note: The islands had already lost about 30,000 people to the Queensland and Fiji labour trade since the 1870s, which is the main reason Britain acted at all.

people.name: Charles Morris Woodford
people.role: first Resident Commissioner from 1896; governed a country of 100,000 people with a handful of officials and a punitive gunboat

people.name: Basiana
people.role: Kwaio leader who killed District Officer William Bell and his party at Gwee'abe in 1927 over a tax the Kwaio had never agreed to; hanged in 1928

acquisitions.resistance: Malaita was never really conquered. In October 1927 Kwaio men killed the district officer collecting head tax; the punitive expedition that followed killed about 60 Kwaio, detained 200, and desecrated their shrines - a grievance the Kwaio still raise today.

cost.note: The 1927 Kwaio punitive expedition: about 60 killed in the bush, roughly 200 detained at Tulagi where some 30 died of dysentery, and shrines destroyed. Figures come from the administration's own reports and from Kwaio oral history collected by Roger Keesing, and the two do not agree.

warrant.author: Roger M. Keesing
warrant.work: Lightning Meets the West Wind: The Malaita Massacre
warrant.supports: The 1927 Kwaio punitive expedition: about 60 killed in the bush, roughly 200 detained at Tulagi where some 30 died of dysentery, and shrines destroyed.
warrant.check: Oxford University Press, 1980. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

evidence.author: Judith A. Bennett
evidence.work: Wealth of the Solomons: A History of a Pacific Archipelago, 1800-1978
evidence.supports: The labour trade, the protectorate and the plantation economy.

acquisitions.how: Under the settlement that gave Germany a free hand in Samoa, Germany handed Britain the northern Solomons - Choiseul, Santa Isabel, the Shortlands and Ontong Java - while keeping Bougainville and Buka for its New Guinea colony.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Four island groups it had claimed since 1886, traded away for a clear run at Samoa.
counterparties.note: No Solomon Islander was consulted, and the line Germany kept - leaving Bougainville out - is the reason Bougainville has spent thirty years trying to get out of Papua New Guinea.

instrument.name: Anglo-German Convention of 14 November 1899 respecting Samoa and the Solomon Islands
instrument.note: Signed 14 November 1899; the transfer of the islands took effect in 1900. Part of the same bargain as the Tripartite Convention on Samoa of 2 December 1899.

statusPeriods.label: Protectorate run on a shoestring from Tulagi
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Resident Commissioner under the Western Pacific High Commission in Fiji governed through district officers, head taxes and the occasional punitive expedition; Lever Brothers and Burns Philp ran the coconut plantations that paid for it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Tulagi, under the Western Pacific High Commission in Suva
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Solomon Islanders were governed by ordinance and by their own chiefs where the administration could not reach, which was most places.
statusPeriods.note: The head tax of 1923 was the immediate cause of the Kwaio killing of District Officer Bell in 1927.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation and the Guadalcanal campaign
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan took Tulagi in May 1942; American forces landed on Guadalcanal in August and fought there for six months. British administration ceased. Solomon Islanders served as scouts, carriers and coastwatchers on the Allied side in large numbers.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The status 'occupied' defaults to 5 for British occupation of somewhere else. Here the protectorate was occupied by Japan and then fought over by the United States: British authority was nil, so the degree is 0.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.
statusPeriods.note: The Guadalcanal campaign killed roughly 7,100 Americans and 31,000 Japanese. Solomon Islanders saw the two richest countries on earth spend more on their islands in six months than Britain had in fifty years, and drew conclusions.

statusPeriods.label: Protectorate restored, and immediately challenged
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain came back to a country that had just watched the Americans and did not want it. From 1944 the Maasina Rule movement organised its own councils, courts and tax on Malaita; the administration jailed about 2,000 people and then negotiated.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Honiara, from 1952 the seat of the Western Pacific High Commission
statusPeriods.franchise: Local councils from the 1950s; the first common-roll general election was held in 1970 and full ministerial government came in 1974.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A chief minister and cabinet drawn from an elected legislative assembly ran the country; Britain kept defence and foreign affairs for eighteen months.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage on a common roll.

departures.how: Solomon Islands became independent after constitutional talks in London, with Britain leaving behind a parliament, a police force and a country of 87 languages held together by pidgin.

becomes.name: Solomon Islands

led.name: Peter Kenilorea
led.role: chief minister and then first prime minister

led.name: Solomon Mamaloni
led.role: chief minister 1974-76 who led the country to self-government and later served three terms as prime minister

led.name: Aliki Nono'oohimae
led.role: Are'are leader of Maasina Rule, jailed by the British and later a member of the legislature that took the country to independence

departures.movement: Maasina Rule, and the elected assemblies of the 1970s

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. Between 1998 and 2003 the country came apart in fighting between Malaitan and Guadalcanal militias; about 200 people were killed and 20,000 displaced, and an Australian-led regional mission restored order in 2003.

departures.borders: Bougainville, geographically and culturally part of the Solomons chain, stayed on the other side of a line Britain and Germany drew in 1899, and is now trying to leave Papua New Guinea. The Solomons kept the borders the two empires agreed.

instrument.name: Solomon Islands Act 1978

populationTransfer.note: Between about 1870 and 1911 roughly 30,000 Solomon Islanders were recruited or kidnapped for the plantations of Queensland and Fiji; the villages of Malaita and Guadalcanal lost most of a generation of young men.

toll.note: Estimates for Solomon Islanders taken to Queensland and Fiji range from about 25,000 to 30,000 engagements between 1870 and 1911. Some people went more than once and many never returned, so the number of individuals is lower and the number of deaths unknown.

violence.note: The protectorate's authority rested on gunboats and punitive expeditions - against New Georgia headhunters in the 1890s and against the Kwaio in 1927 - and on a head tax that people who had never seen a coin were expected to pay.

commonwealth.note: Solomon Islands is a Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state, represented by a Solomon Islander governor-general.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copra and then logging: Malaysian and other foreign companies have cut the forests at several times the sustainable rate since the 1990s, and timber royalties are the state's largest domestic income.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Around 87 languages are spoken; Solomon Islands Pijin, which grew out of the Queensland plantations, is the national lingua franca - the labour trade's most durable legacy.

peak.populationNote: 1976 census, two years before independence. The population is now over 700,000.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1976 census of British Solomon Islands
populationWarrant.supports: British Solomon Islands’s largest recorded population: 196,823 people, counted in 1976.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Judith A. Bennett
evidence.work: Wealth of the Solomons: A History of a Pacific Archipelago, 1800-1978
evidence.supports: The whole colonial period, the labour trade and the plantation economy.

evidence.author: Hugh Laracy
evidence.work: Pacific Protest: The Maasina Rule Movement, Solomon Islands, 1944-1952
evidence.publisher: Institute of Pacific Studies, University of the South Pacific
evidence.supports: Maasina Rule and its suppression.

evidence.author: Roger M. Keesing
evidence.work: Lightning Meets the West Wind: The Malaita Massacre
evidence.supports: The 1927 Kwaio killings and the punitive expedition. Written with Peter Corris.

pedagogy.hook: Britain declared the Solomon Islands a protectorate in 1893 mainly to police British ships that were kidnapping Solomon Islanders. It took 30,000 of them before anyone in London acted.

misconception.belief: Protectorates were a light form of empire that left local people alone.
misconception.correction: The Solomons protectorate had one Resident Commissioner, a few district officers and no army - and it still imposed a head tax that people paid in plantation labour, burned villages that resisted, and destroyed Kwaio shrines in 1927. Thin administration did not mean gentle administration; it meant occasional, concentrated violence instead of continuous control.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Solomons show the Pacific pattern in full: a labour trade that emptied villages, an empire that annexed to regulate its own traders, a wartime occupation that broke the spell, and a protest movement - Maasina Rule - that Britain jailed and then negotiated with.

territories.name: Gilbert and Ellice Islands
territories.formalName: Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony

from.display: the Gilbertese name for their own chain
from.note: The sixteen atolls of the Gilberts have been settled for around 3,000 years.

namesOverTime.name: Gilbert and Ellice Islands
namesOverTime.note: Named for two British sea captains, Thomas Gilbert and Edward Ellice, who sailed past.

namesOverTime.name: Kiribati and Tuvalu
namesOverTime.note: 'Kiribati' is the Gilbertese pronunciation of 'Gilberts'; 'Tuvalu' means 'eight standing together', for the eight inhabited islands.

geoCoverage.label: Sixteen Gilbertese atolls and nine Ellice islands
geoCoverage.change: Captain Davis of HMS Royalist declared a protectorate atoll by atoll in May 1892, and the Ellice Islands in October.

geoCoverage.label: A colony spread across 3.5 million square kilometres of ocean
geoCoverage.change: The protectorate became a colony and swallowed Ocean Island, Fanning and Washington in 1916, Christmas Island in 1919 and the Phoenix Islands in 1937. Tokelau was attached from 1916 to 1926 and is recorded separately here.

geoCoverage.label: The Gilberts alone, for nine months
geoCoverage.change: Tuvalu became independent on 1 October 1978, nine months before the Gilberts.

acquisitions.how: Captain Edward Davis of HMS Royalist sailed from atoll to atoll raising the flag and reading a proclamation, declaring a protectorate over sixteen Gilbertese atolls in May and the nine Ellice islands in October.

counterparties.name: The people of the Gilbert Islands (Tungaru) and the Ellice Islands
counterparties.lost: Independence in law, and later their own land: Banaba was dug away entirely and its people resettled 2,600 kilometres from home.
counterparties.note: Two peoples with different languages, religions and histories - Micronesian Gilbertese and Polynesian Tuvaluans - were joined in one colony for administrative convenience, and separated again by referendum 83 years later.

people.name: Edward Davis
people.role: commander of HMS Royalist, who proclaimed the protectorate

people.name: Albert Ellis
people.role: prospector who recognised phosphate in a lump of rock used as a doorstop in a Sydney office in 1900, and so doomed Banaba

acquisitions.resistance: Little at the moment of proclamation; Gilbertese communities had already been fought over by traders, and the atoll of Abaiang had lost people to Peruvian slavers in 1863.

evidence.author: Barrie Macdonald
evidence.work: Cinderellas of the Empire: Towards a History of Kiribati and Tuvalu
evidence.supports: The protectorate, the colony, Banaba and the separation of 1975.

acquisitions.how: Weeks after phosphate was identified on Banaba, a British company signed a document with Banaban elders granting mining rights over the whole island for 999 years at 50 pounds a year, and Britain annexed the island into the protectorate.

counterparties.name: The Banaban people of Ocean Island
counterparties.lost: Their island. Roughly 22 million tonnes of phosphate were dug out between 1900 and 1979, stripping about nine tenths of the surface and leaving bare limestone pinnacles.
counterparties.note: The 1900 agreement was written in English, signed by people who could not read it, and covered land the company had not yet surveyed. The Banabans challenged it in the English High Court in 1975-76 and largely lost.

instrument.name: Agreement between the Pacific Islands Company and the Banaban landowners, 3 May 1900
instrument.note: A 999-year mining right over the whole island for 50 pounds a year. From 1920 the mine was run by the British Phosphate Commissioners on behalf of the British, Australian and New Zealand governments.

people.name: Rotan Tito
people.role: Banaban leader who fought the phosphate companies and the British government for compensation from the 1940s to the 1970s

acquisitions.resistance: Banabans refused to sell more land from the 1920s; the administration passed an ordinance in 1928 letting it take the land compulsorily. In December 1945 the surviving Banabans were shipped to Rabi Island in Fiji, 2,600 kilometres away, and most of their descendants are still there.

evidence.author: Katerina Martina Teaiwa
evidence.work: Consuming Ocean Island: Stories of People and Phosphate from Banaba
evidence.supports: The mining of Banaba, the removal of its people and the fight for compensation.

statusPeriods.label: Protectorate under the Western Pacific High Commission
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Resident Commissioner with a handful of staff administered 33 atolls scattered over an area the size of India, mostly by visiting them once a year in a schooner.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Tarawa, then Ocean Island (Banaba) from 1908, under the High Commission in Suva
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Island councils of elders (the unimwane) ran village affairs under a colonial magistrate.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony, capital on a phosphate mine
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The colony was governed from Ocean Island, which existed to be dug up: the phosphate paid the colony's bills, and from 1920 the British Phosphate Commissioners sold it to Australian and New Zealand farmers at cost.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation; Tarawa and Banaba
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan occupied the Gilberts and Banaba three days after Pearl Harbor. The American assault on Betio in November 1943 killed about 6,000 people in 76 hours, and on Banaba the garrison massacred most of the remaining labourers in 1945.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: 'Occupied' defaults to 5 for a British occupation. Here Britain was the party removed: the colony was occupied by Japan and then fought over, and British authority was nil.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere; the administration withdrew to Funafuti
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.
statusPeriods.note: The Ellice Islands were not occupied and became an American base; Funafuti's airstrip is still the country's international airport.

statusPeriods.label: Restored colony, capital moved to Tarawa
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British administration returned, moved the capital to Tarawa, shipped the Banabans to Fiji, and slowly built representative institutions: an advisory council in 1963, a House of Representatives in 1967 and ministerial government in 1974.
statusPeriods.franchise: Elections to the House of Representatives from 1967 on a common roll; universal adult suffrage.
statusPeriods.note: In a referendum in August and September 1974 the Ellice Islanders voted 3,799 to 293 to separate from the Gilberts. Separation took effect on 1 October 1975.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government in the Gilberts
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A chief minister and an elected House of Assembly at Tarawa ran the Gilberts while Britain kept defence and foreign affairs; Tuvalu, separated since 1975, was on the same path to its own independence.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage on a common roll.
statusPeriods.note: Tuvalu became independent on 1 October 1978 and the Gilberts followed as Kiribati on 12 July 1979.

departures.how: Ellice Islanders voted 93 per cent to separate from the Gilberts, became the separate colony of Tuvalu in 1975, and took independence three years later as one of the smallest countries on earth.

becomes.name: Tuvalu

led.name: Toaripi Lauti
led.role: first prime minister of Tuvalu; led the separation campaign

led.name: Sir Fiatau Penitala Teo
led.role: first governor-general of Tuvalu

departures.movement: The Ellice separation campaign

cost.note: Nobody died. Tuvaluans voted for separation because Polynesian Ellice Islanders were a minority in a Micronesian-majority colony and expected to be outvoted; Britain accepted the result and paid for the split.

departures.borders: The line between Tuvalu and Kiribati was drawn by a referendum rather than by a colonial official - one of the few borders in this atlas that the people who live inside it chose.

instrument.name: Tuvalu Act 1978

departures.how: The Gilberts became the Republic of Kiribati, taking with them the Line and Phoenix Islands and, over Banaban objections, Banaba - the island that had paid for the colony and been destroyed doing it.

becomes.name: Republic of Kiribati

led.name: Ieremia Tabai
led.role: chief minister at 28 and first president of Kiribati at 29

led.name: Rotan Tito
led.role: Banaban leader whose campaign for compensation and for Banaban separation shaped the independence negotiations

departures.movement: The House of Assembly parties of the 1970s; the Banaban separatist campaign

cost.note: Nobody died. Britain paid an ex gratia sum of about 10 million Australian dollars into a Banaban trust fund in 1977, after the High Court in London found in Tito v Waddell that the Crown owed the Banabans no fiduciary duty.

departures.borders: Kiribati straddles the equator and the antimeridian and spans 3.5 million square kilometres of ocean - the legacy of a colony assembled from whatever atolls Britain picked up. Banaba stayed inside it against the wishes of most Banabans, who live in Fiji.

instrument.name: Kiribati Act 1979

populationTransfer.note: Two forced moves define this colony: about 1,000 Gilbertese resettled in the Phoenix Islands from 1938 and moved again to the Solomons when the scheme failed, and 703 Banabans shipped to Rabi Island in Fiji in December 1945.

toll.note: 703 Banabans and some 300 other residents were landed on Rabi in December 1945 with tents and four months' rations. About 6,000 people of Banaban descent now live in Fiji; roughly 300 live on Banaba.

violence.note: In 1942-45 Japan occupied the Gilberts and Banaba. The American assault on Betio killed about 1,000 Marines and 4,700 Japanese and Korean personnel in three days, and in 1945 the Banaba garrison machine-gunned about 150 surviving labourers; one man survived by hiding in a cave.

toll.note: Betio, 20-23 November 1943: roughly 1,000 American dead and about 4,700 Japanese and Korean dead, of whom only 17 Japanese and 129 Korean labourers were taken alive. The Banaba massacre of August 1945 killed about 150 more. Figures are US Marine Corps and post-war commission records.

consequences.economicLegacy: The colony ran on Banaban phosphate, which paid for its administration and, at cost price, for Australian and New Zealand farms. When the mine closed in 1979 Kiribati lost most of its export income overnight and has lived on fishing licences and a sovereign trust fund since.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Gilbertese and Tuvaluan are both alive and official in their countries; the colonial habit of governing through the unimwane, the councils of old men, survives in local government.

peak.populationNote: 1973 census: about 51,900 in the Gilberts and Line Islands and 5,900 in the Ellice Islands. The land area is about 837 square kilometres scattered over 3.5 million square kilometres of ocean.

misconception.belief: Colonies were exploited by private companies; the British government's role was to govern, not to profit.
misconception.correction: On Banaba the government was the company. From 1920 the British Phosphate Commissioners - owned jointly by the British, Australian and New Zealand governments - ran the mine and sold the phosphate to their own farmers below world price. The Banabans got royalties of a few pence a tonne and, in 1945, a boat to Fiji.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Kiribati and Tuvalu show two things at once: an empire that manufactured a country out of unrelated peoples for administrative convenience, and the only case in this region where the people themselves voted to redraw the border - and got it.

territories.name: Canton and Enderbury Islands
territories.formalName: Canton and Enderbury Islands, an Anglo-American condominium

from.display: the Gilbertese and English names now in use
from.note: The islands had no permanent population when Europeans found them, though Polynesian remains have been found on other Phoenix atolls.

geoCoverage.label: Two uninhabited atolls in the middle of the Pacific
geoCoverage.change: Britain annexed the Phoenix Islands into the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony; the United States claimed Canton and Enderbury under its own guano law, and the two governments split the difference.

acquisitions.how: Britain annexed the Phoenix Islands to the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony because the new trans-Pacific flying boat routes needed a fuelling stop, and Canton had the only usable lagoon.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: Canton and Enderbury were uninhabited when annexed. Britain then settled Gilbertese families on other Phoenix atolls between 1938 and 1940 under the Phoenix Islands Settlement Scheme, because the Gilberts were overcrowded.

counterparties.name: The United States
counterparties.lost: Nothing yet - it contested the claim within months, on the basis of nineteenth-century guano-era landings, and Britain refused to give way.
counterparties.note: Both powers landed parties in 1937-38 and both raised flags. It was as close as Britain and the United States came to a territorial standoff in the twentieth century.

acquisitions.how: Rather than fight over two coral atolls, Britain and the United States agreed to govern Canton and Enderbury jointly for fifty years, each keeping its own claim and neither pressing it.

counterparties.name: The United States
counterparties.lost: Nothing. Britain and the United States each kept their claim alive and shared the airfield; it was the least costly imperial dispute in the Pacific.

instrument.name: Anglo-American agreement on the joint administration of Canton and Enderbury Islands
instrument.note: A fifty-year joint administration announced by both governments in April 1939, without either abandoning its claim to sovereignty.

people.name: Harry Maude
people.role: British colonial officer who organised the Phoenix Islands Settlement Scheme and later wrote the standard histories of Pacific labour recruiting

evidence.author: Harry Maude
evidence.work: Of Islands and Men: Studies in Pacific History
evidence.supports: The Phoenix Islands Settlement Scheme and the Anglo-American arrangement.

statusPeriods.label: Annexed to the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British officer raised the flag and left a caretaker party; the Americans arrived and did the same on the other side of the lagoon.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default for a crown colony is 5, but Britain's control was openly contested by the United States from within weeks and never uncontested on the ground.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Ocean Island (Banaba), Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody lived there.

statusPeriods.label: Governed jointly with the United States
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain and the United States administered the two atolls together for fifty years: American airline and later air force staff on Canton, a British magistrate visiting, and Gilbertese labourers doing the work.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Jointly from London and Washington; day to day from Canton itself
statusPeriods.franchise: The population was a few hundred airline staff, servicemen and Gilbertese workers, none of whom voted for anything.
statusPeriods.note: Canton was a Pan American flying boat stop from 1938, a wartime airbase, a civil airliner refuelling stop into the 1960s, and a NASA and missile tracking station after that. Then jet aircraft got the range to overfly it and everyone left.

departures.how: The condominium ended when Kiribati became independent, and the United States renounced its claims to Canton, Enderbury and twelve other islands in the Treaty of Tarawa signed that September.

becomes.name: Republic of Kiribati

led.name: Ieremia Tabai
led.role: first president of Kiribati, who signed the Treaty of Tarawa with the United States

departures.movement: Kiribati's independence negotiations

cost.note: Nobody died. About 40 people were living on Canton when the condominium ended; the airfield and its ghost town are still there.

departures.borders: The treaty gave Kiribati fourteen islands the United States had claimed under an 1856 guano law, and with them an exclusive economic zone of over three million square kilometres for a country with 811 square kilometres of land.

instrument.name: Treaty of Tarawa (Treaty of Friendship between the United States and Kiribati)
instrument.note: Signed 20 September 1979, ratified in 1983. The United States relinquished claims to fourteen islands in the Phoenix and Line groups.

populationTransfer.note: The Phoenix Islands Settlement Scheme moved about 1,000 Gilbertese onto three waterless atolls between 1938 and 1940 to relieve overcrowding; drought defeated it and by 1963 the settlers had been moved again, to Gizo and Wagina in the Solomon Islands.

toll.note: Roughly 1,000 people were resettled from the Gilberts to Sydney, Hull and Gardner islands, and moved on again to the Solomons between 1955 and 1963. Their descendants in the Solomons number several thousand.

consequences.borderLegacy: Kiribati's enormous maritime zone comes from atolls two empires collected for guano, aircraft and prestige. The Phoenix Islands Protected Area, declared in 2008, is one of the largest marine reserves on earth.
consequences.economicLegacy: Guano, then aviation fuel, then nothing. Canton's airstrip is intact and unused.

peak.populationNote: Canton's population peaked at a few hundred airline and military staff with Gilbertese workers in the 1950s and 1960s. Fewer than 30 people live there now.

evidence.author: Harry Maude
evidence.work: Of Islands and Men: Studies in Pacific History
evidence.supports: The Phoenix Islands Settlement Scheme and British policy in the group.

evidence.author: Barrie Macdonald
evidence.work: Cinderellas of the Empire: Towards a History of Kiribati and Tuvalu
evidence.supports: The colony's expansion into the Phoenix and Line Islands.

contested.note: The 1937 annexation and the 1939 condominium were announced rather than legislated, and different sources give slightly different dates for the flag-raisings. Neither government ever conceded the other's claim to sovereignty, which is why the arrangement lasted forty years without a settlement.

pedagogy.hook: In 1939 Britain and the United States nearly fell out over two uninhabited coral atolls, and settled it by agreeing to govern them jointly for fifty years without either side admitting the other owned them.

misconception.belief: Condominiums were a nineteenth-century oddity, like the New Hebrides.
misconception.correction: The last British condominium was set up in 1939 and lasted until 1979, and it existed because aeroplanes had made a waterless atoll with a big lagoon strategically valuable. Empires kept taking territory for as long as the technology kept changing what was worth having.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Canton is the empire in miniature at its very end: a place claimed for a technology - the flying boat - that was obsolete within twenty years, settled with people moved from somewhere else, and handed to a new republic that mostly wanted the fishing rights.

territories.name: New Hebrides
territories.formalName: Anglo-French Condominium of the New Hebrides

namesOverTime.name: New Hebrides
namesOverTime.note: Cook's name, after the Scottish islands.

namesOverTime.name: Vanuatu
namesOverTime.note: From 'vanua', land, and 'tu', to stand: 'the land that stands'. The name was chosen by the independence movement to replace two European ones.

geoCoverage.label: Eighty islands governed by two empires at once
geoCoverage.change: Britain and France converted their 1887 joint naval commission into a condominium: one archipelago, two administrations, two police forces, two currencies and three legal systems.

acquisitions.how: Neither Britain nor France would let the other have the islands, and neither wanted the cost of them alone, so they agreed to rule jointly - creating a government so absurd that officials themselves called it the Pandemonium.

counterparties.name: The ni-Vanuatu peoples of the eighty islands
counterparties.lost: Their land to French and Australian planters, and any legal status at all: under the condominium ni-Vanuatu could be British subjects or French citizens or neither, and in practice they were neither - stateless in their own country until 1980.
counterparties.note: The population had already collapsed. Disease and the labour trade cut it by something like eighty to ninety per cent between the 1860s and the 1930s, when a census counted about 45,000 people.

instrument.name: Anglo-French Convention concerning the New Hebrides
instrument.note: Signed in London on 20 October 1906 and refined by the Protocol of 1914, which came into force in 1922 and remained the constitution of the islands until 1980.

people.name: John Higginson
people.role: Irish-born French citizen whose Compagnie Calédonienne bought up New Hebrides land in the 1880s to force a French annexation

people.name: Jimmy Stevens
people.role: founded the Nagriamel land movement in 1963 and led the Santo rebellion of 1980

people.name: Walter Lini
people.role: Anglican priest who founded the Vanua'aku Pati and became the first prime minister

acquisitions.resistance: Resistance took the form of movements the administrations could not understand: the John Frum movement on Tanna from 1940, which rejected missionaries, money and the British administration, and Nagriamel from 1963, which demanded the return of alienated land.

evidence.author: Howard Van Trease
evidence.work: The Politics of Land in Vanuatu: From Colony to Independence
evidence.publisher: Institute of Pacific Studies, University of the South Pacific
evidence.supports: Land alienation, the condominium's structure and the road to independence.

statusPeriods.label: Two empires, one archipelago, no citizens
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: There were two Resident Commissioners, two police forces in different uniforms, two currencies, two health and school systems, and three legal codes - British, French, and a joint 'native' code applied by a court whose president was appointed by the King of Spain.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Vila, jointly from London and Paris
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted until 1975, and ni-Vanuatu held no citizenship of any state until independence in 1980. A Representative Assembly was elected in 1975 and again in 1979.
statusPeriods.note: Because the two powers could not agree on anything, they built two of everything. Vanuatu still runs an English school system and a French school system side by side.

departures.how: The condominium ended after the Vanua'aku Pati won the 1979 elections; France, which had backed the French-speaking parties, dragged its feet, and a secessionist rebellion on Espiritu Santo had to be put down by Papua New Guinean troops after independence day.

becomes.name: Republic of Vanuatu

led.name: Walter Lini
led.role: Anglican priest, leader of the Vanua'aku Pati and first prime minister

led.name: Jimmy Stevens
led.role: led the Nagriamel movement and the Santo rebellion; jailed for fourteen years

led.name: Barak Sopé
led.role: Vanua'aku Pati organiser and later prime minister; a leading voice for immediate independence

departures.movement: Vanua'aku Pati (the New Hebrides National Party)

cost.note: The Santo rebellion of May to August 1980 was short and mostly bloodless: Alexis Yolou, a leader on Tanna, and Jimmy Stevens's son were among a small number killed. Papua New Guinean troops occupied Espiritu Santo and Stevens surrendered in August.

departures.borders: The condominium's borders became Vanuatu's, but the deeper legacy was inside them: land alienated to planters was returned to customary owners at independence, the only Pacific state to do it so completely.

instrument.name: New Hebrides Act 1980 and the Constitution of the Republic of Vanuatu
instrument.note: The constitution returned all land to its customary owners: 'all land in the Republic belongs to the indigenous custom owners and their descendants'.

populationTransfer.note: The labour trade took tens of thousands of ni-Vanuatu to Queensland, Fiji, Samoa and New Caledonia from the 1860s; Tanna and Erromango lost so many young men that some villages never recovered.

toll.note: Roughly 40,000 engagements of ni-Vanuatu are recorded in the Queensland and Fiji labour trades between 1863 and 1904. Pre-contact population estimates vary so widely - from about 200,000 to over 600,000 - that the scale of the collapse cannot be stated precisely, only that the 1935 census counted about 45,000 people.

violence.note: Both administrations used punitive naval bombardments against villages that killed traders or missionaries, and both jailed the leaders of the John Frum movement on Tanna in the 1940s and 1950s.

commonwealth.note: Vanuatu is a republic and a member of both the Commonwealth and the Francophonie - the only Pacific state in both, which is the condominium's tidiest legacy.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copra and cattle on plantations that were handed back to customary owners in 1980; today tourism, an offshore finance centre, and money sent home by seasonal workers in New Zealand and Australia.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Vanuatu has more languages per head than anywhere on earth - about 110 for 300,000 people - and three official languages: Bislama, English and French. Bislama grew out of the plantations where ni-Vanuatu were sent to work.

peak.populationNote: 1979 census, the year before independence. The 1935 census had counted about 45,000, the low point after seventy years of disease and labour recruiting.

populationWarrant.supports: New Hebrides’s largest recorded population: 111,251 people, counted in 1979.

pedagogy.hook: In the New Hebrides there were two police forces, two currencies, two school systems and three legal codes - and the people who lived there were citizens of nothing at all until 1980.

misconception.belief: Colonial rule was at least efficient - it built administrations that worked.
misconception.correction: The Anglo-French condominium built two of everything and agreed on nothing for 74 years. Ni-Vanuatu could not be citizens, could not vote until 1975, and watched most of the best land pass to planters. Officials called it the Pandemonium. Empire was often not competent; it was just powerful.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Vanuatu is the only place in this atlas where independence returned all the land to its customary owners, written into the constitution. It shows what decolonisation could do when the movement leading it decided land, not just flags, was the point.

territories.name: Nauru
territories.formalName: Nauru, under British Empire mandate and United Nations trusteeship

from.note: Settled about 3,000 years ago by Micronesian and Polynesian people organised in twelve tribes, whose emblems are the twelve points of the star on the modern flag.

namesOverTime.name: Pleasant Island
namesOverTime.note: Named by Captain John Fearn of the Hunter, who did not land.

geoCoverage.label: Twenty-one square kilometres of phosphate
geoCoverage.change: An Australian force took the German colony three months into the First World War. The mandate that followed was granted to the British Crown and exercised by Australia on behalf of Britain, Australia and New Zealand together.

acquisitions.how: An Australian expeditionary force landed and took the island from Germany without a fight, primarily to secure the phosphate mine that had been shipping fertiliser to Australian and New Zealand farms since 1907.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: The island it had annexed in 1888, and its share of the phosphate company.

counterparties.name: The Nauruan people and their twelve tribes, the divisions on their own flag
counterparties.lost: One coloniser for three. Their land was already being dug away under German rule; under the mandate it was dug away faster.
counterparties.note: Nauruans were never asked. Their chiefs had signed nothing with Germany either: Germany simply annexed the island in 1888 and disarmed the twelve districts after a ten-year civil war fought with traders' guns.

people.name: Albert Ellis
people.role: prospector who identified Nauruan and Banaban rock as high-grade phosphate in 1900 and spent his career mining both

acquisitions.resistance: None in 1914. Nauruan resistance was later and constitutional: from the 1950s the Nauru Local Government Council refused to accept resettlement in Australia and demanded either fair royalties or independence.

acquisitions.how: The League of Nations granted the mandate not to a country but to 'His Britannic Majesty', to be exercised jointly by Britain, Australia and New Zealand - the three governments that had already bought the phosphate company between them.

counterparties.name: The Nauruan people
counterparties.lost: Their island, at the rate of about a million tonnes of rock a year. Royalties were set by the mining company's owners, who were the same three governments that were supposed to be holding the island in trust.
counterparties.note: This is the clearest conflict of interest in the mandate system: the trustee, the regulator and the mining company were the same three states.

instrument.name: Nauru Island Agreement 1919 and the League of Nations Mandate for Nauru
instrument.note: The 1919 agreement between Britain, Australia and New Zealand created the British Phosphate Commissioners and divided the phosphate 42:42:16. The League mandate was confirmed on 17 December 1920.

evidence.author: Nancy Viviani
evidence.work: Nauru: Phosphate and Political Progress
evidence.supports: The mandate, the British Phosphate Commissioners and the road to independence.

acquisitions.how: The United Nations replaced the mandate with a trusteeship on the same joint terms, adding visiting missions that Nauruan leaders used, from 1963, to argue their case for independence in New York.

counterparties.name: The Nauruan people
counterparties.lost: Nothing further, and gained a forum. Australia proposed moving the entire population to Curtis Island off Queensland in 1963; the Nauruans refused, and the UN Trusteeship Council was where they said so.

instrument.name: United Nations Trusteeship Agreement for Nauru

people.name: Hammer DeRoburt
people.role: head chief who led the campaign for independence and control of the phosphate, and became the first president

statusPeriods.label: Australian military occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An Australian administrator governed by military order and the phosphate kept moving; the German company's assets were bought out by the three governments in 1919.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

statusPeriods.label: League mandate held by the King, run by Australia
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An Australian administrator governed under a mandate held by the British Crown, while the British Phosphate Commissioners - the British, Australian and New Zealand governments - mined the island and set the royalty.
statusPeriods.franchise: A Council of Chiefs advised the administrator from 1927. Nauruans had no vote.
statusPeriods.note: Royalties in the 1920s and 1930s were a fraction of a penny a tonne. Nauruan landowners received a fraction of that.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation and deportation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan occupied the island, built an airstrip with forced labour, and in 1943 deported 1,200 Nauruans - two thirds of the population - to Chuuk in the Caroline Islands, where 464 of them died of starvation and disease.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: 'Occupied' defaults to 5 where Britain is the occupier. Here Nauru was occupied by Japan; British and Australian authority was nil.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere; the Australian administration was removed
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.
statusPeriods.note: 737 Nauruans returned from Chuuk on 31 January 1946. Independence day was later fixed on 31 January in memory of that return.

statusPeriods.label: Mandate restored while the UN takes over
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Australia resumed administration under the old mandate for two years while the United Nations built the trusteeship system to replace it.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

statusPeriods.label: UN trusteeship; Nauruans argue their case in New York
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Australia administered on behalf of the three governments, but the UN Trusteeship Council sent visiting missions and Nauruan leaders addressed them directly - which is how the plan to move the whole population to Queensland was defeated.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nauru, under the Australian Department of Territories
statusPeriods.franchise: The Nauru Local Government Council was elected from 1951 and became the vehicle of the independence campaign; a Legislative Council followed in 1966.

departures.how: Nauru became independent on the twenty-second anniversary of its people's return from wartime deportation, having refused Australia's offer to resettle them all in Queensland and bought the phosphate industry outright two years later.

led.name: Hammer DeRoburt

led.name: Paul Hasluck

departures.borders: Nauru is one island with no neighbours within 300 kilometres. What was taken from it was not territory but the ground itself: about four fifths of the surface was dug away and never replaced.

instrument.note: The constitutional convention adopted the constitution on 29 January 1968; independence took effect on 31 January 1968.

evidence.author: Christopher Weeramantry
evidence.work: Nauru: Environmental Damage under International Trusteeship
evidence.supports: The mining, the trusteeship's failure and the legal claim against Australia.

toll.note: 464 of the 1,200 Nauruans deported to Chuuk died there of starvation and disease; 737 returned in January 1946. The figures come from the post-war Australian administration's count and are among the best-documented in the wartime Pacific.

warrant.author: The Australian administration of Nauru, in its post-war count
warrant.work: Australian administration returns on the Nauruans deported to Chuuk, 1943–46

populationTransfer.note: Chinese indentured labourers did most of the digging: several thousand were brought in from 1906 onwards to mine phosphate, housed separately and paid a fraction of European wages.

commonwealth.note: Nauru joined as a special member in 1968 and became a full member in 1999. It is the third-smallest state in the world by population.

consequences.economicLegacy: For a few years in the 1970s Nauru had among the highest incomes per head on earth. The phosphate ran out, the trust fund was mismanaged and lost, and since 2001 the largest single source of government revenue has been housing Australia's offshore asylum detention centre.
consequences.borderLegacy: Nauru sued Australia at the International Court of Justice in 1989 over the damage. Australia settled in 1993 for 107 million Australian dollars; Britain and New Zealand contributed 12 million between them, without admitting liability.

evidence.supports: The mandate, the phosphate industry and the independence campaign.

evidence.work: Nauru: Environmental Damage under International Trusteeship

evidence.work: Consuming Ocean Island: Stories of People and Phosphate from Banaba
evidence.supports: The British Phosphate Commissioners and the wider phosphate system that linked Nauru and Banaba.

pedagogy.hook: Britain, Australia and New Zealand were Nauru's legal trustees. They also owned the company digging the island away, and sold its phosphate to their own farmers below the world price.

misconception.belief: The League of Nations mandate system existed to protect small territories from exploitation.
misconception.correction: The Nauru mandate was granted to the British Crown and exercised by the same three governments that owned the phosphate mine. They set the royalty they paid themselves. Nauruans received a small fraction of the value of their island, and in 1963 were offered resettlement in Queensland instead of compensation. They refused, and won independence in 1968.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Nauru is the sharpest case in the empire of extraction with a legal fig leaf. It also shows what independence cannot fix: sovereignty came in 1968, and the island's surface was still gone.
