territories.name: Pitcairn Islands
territories.formalName: Pitcairn, Henderson, Ducie and Oeno Islands

namesOverTime.name: Pitcairn's Island
namesOverTime.note: Named for Robert Pitcairn, the fifteen-year-old midshipman who sighted it from HMS Swallow. The island was charted 300 kilometres out of position, which is exactly why the mutineers chose it.

namesOverTime.name: The Pitcairn Islands
namesOverTime.note: Henderson, Oeno and Ducie were annexed in 1902 and brought into the Pitcairn settlement in 1938, at which point one island's name no longer covered the territory.

to.note: Henderson, Ducie and Oeno were annexed during 1902; the proclamations were made on separate days by a visiting warship.

geoCoverage.label: One island, five kilometres square
geoCoverage.change: Nine Bounty mutineers, six Polynesian men and twelve Polynesian women landed and burned the ship so it could not be seen from the sea.

from.note: The three outer islands were annexed during 1902.

geoCoverage.label: With Henderson, Ducie and Oeno
geoCoverage.change: Britain annexed the three uninhabited neighbours, mainly to keep other powers away from the group.

acquisitions.how: Nine mutineers from HMS Bounty, hiding from the Royal Navy, landed with six Polynesian men and twelve Polynesian women taken from Tahiti and Tubuai, and burned the ship in the bay eight days later.

counterparties.name: No resident population in 1790
counterparties.note: Polynesians had lived on Pitcairn and Henderson between roughly 1000 and 1600 and had gone before the Bounty came: their stone tools, burials and petroglyphs are still there. The island was empty in 1790 but it was not untouched.

counterparties.name: The Polynesian men and women brought from Tahiti and Tubuai
counterparties.lost: Their homes and, for the women, any choice in the matter. Several were taken aboard by force. Within four years every Polynesian man on the island had been killed, along with five of the nine mutineers.

people.name: Fletcher Christian
people.role: led the mutiny on 28 April 1789 and chose Pitcairn because it was charted in the wrong place; killed on the island in 1793

people.name: John Adams, born Alexander Smith
people.role: last surviving mutineer, who taught the children to read from the Bible and was pardoned when the island was rediscovered in 1808

people.name: Mauatua (Isabella)
people.role: Tahitian woman, partner of Fletcher Christian, who outlived every mutineer and died on Pitcairn in 1841

acquisitions.resistance: The Polynesian men rebelled in 1793 after the mutineers took their land and their wives. In the killing that followed all six died and five mutineers were killed with them, leaving four Englishmen, ten women and their children.

cost.note: Between 1793 and 1800 all six Polynesian men and eight of the nine mutineers died violently or by drink. The accounts come from the survivors decades later and do not entirely agree.

evidence.author: Greg Dening
evidence.work: Mr Bligh's Bad Language: Passion, Power and Theatre on the Bounty
evidence.supports: The mutiny, the settlement and the sources' unreliability.

acquisitions.how: Captain Russell Elliott of HMS Fly, asked by the islanders for protection against whaling crews, declared Pitcairn a British settlement and gave it a written constitution - which included votes for every adult, women included.

counterparties.name: The Pitcairn community
counterparties.lost: Nothing they minded losing: they had asked for the flag. What they gained was the earliest universal suffrage, including women, anywhere under the British Crown.
counterparties.note: Pitcairn women voted in 1838, fifty-five years before New Zealand and ninety before all British women.

instrument.name: Elliott's Constitution and Laws for Pitcairn Island
instrument.note: Drawn up on board HMS Fly. It made school attendance compulsory and gave the vote to every islander aged eighteen and over, of either sex.

people.name: Russell Elliott
people.role: naval captain who wrote the constitution

statusPeriods.label: A hiding place, outside British law
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: There was no British authority at all. The settlers were fugitives from a capital charge, and for eighteen years the Admiralty did not know where they were.
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1838.
statusPeriods.note: An American sealer, Mayhew Folger of the Topaz, found the colony by accident in February 1808. Britain was at war and did nothing about it for six years.

to.note: Administration passed from the Western Pacific High Commission to the British High Commissioner in New Zealand as governor when the High Commission was wound up; the change took effect during 1970.

statusPeriods.label: British settlement, governing itself
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The islanders elected their own magistrate and ran their own courts; from 1898 the Western Pacific High Commission in Fiji held formal jurisdiction and sent a visiting officer every few years.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default for a crown colony is 5. Pitcairn had no resident British official at all until 1940, and its elected magistrate governed it; a degree of 5 would describe a government that was not there.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Pitcairn itself; formally from Suva after 1898
statusPeriods.franchise: Every adult islander, women included, from 1838.
statusPeriods.note: In 1856 the entire population of 194 was moved to Norfolk Island; 16 people returned in 1859 and 27 more in 1864, and the island's families descend from them.

from.note: The Western Pacific High Commission was wound up and the governorship passed to the British High Commissioner in New Zealand during 1970.

statusPeriods.label: British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The British High Commissioner in Wellington serves as governor and almost never visits; an elected Island Council runs Pitcairn, and Britain pays most of the bills.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Adamstown, with a governor resident in Wellington
statusPeriods.franchise: All adult islanders. The electorate is about thirty people.

departures.how: Pitcairn never left. It is the last British territory in the Pacific, with about 35 residents, and Britain has kept it partly because nobody has proposed a better idea.

cost.note: No independence process, no deaths. The island's crisis was different: in 2004 six men, a third of the adult male population, were convicted of sexual offences against girls, after a British investigation and trials held under English law with judges flown in from New Zealand.

departures.borders: Pitcairn's four islands are spread over 500 kilometres of empty ocean and give Britain an exclusive economic zone of over 800,000 square kilometres, most of it now a marine reserve.

stillBritish.note: Pitcairn is the smallest jurisdiction in the world by population - about 35 people, nearly all descended from the Bounty mutineers and the Polynesian women who were brought with them.

populationTransfer.note: Twice the island was emptied: in 1856 the whole community of 194 sailed to Norfolk Island, and since the 1950s steady emigration to New Zealand has cut the population from 233 to about 35.

violence.note: The settlement began with killing - all six Polynesian men and most of the mutineers died in the 1793 uprising - and in 2004 a British prosecution convicted six men of sexual offences against girls, exposing decades of abuse on an island of fifty people.

consequences.economicLegacy: Postage stamps, honey and carved curios sold to passing cruise ships. Britain funds most of the island's budget, and a supply ship calls a few times a year.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Pitkern, a creole of eighteenth-century English and Tahitian, is still spoken. English law applies, which is what made the 2004 trials possible - and which the defendants argued had never properly been extended to the island at all.

peak.populationNote: The 1937 peak of 233 people. Pitcairn itself is 4.6 square kilometres; the other 42 are Henderson, Ducie and Oeno, all uninhabited.

evidence.author: Greg Dening
evidence.work: Mr Bligh's Bad Language: Passion, Power and Theatre on the Bounty
evidence.supports: The mutiny and the settlement, and how much of the story rests on unreliable testimony.

evidence.author: Kathy Marks
evidence.work: Lost Paradise: From Mutiny on the Bounty to a Modern-Day Legacy of Sexual Mayhem
evidence.supports: The 2004 trials and the island's contemporary society. Reported at first hand by one of six journalists allowed on the island.

evidence.author: Robert W. Kirk
evidence.work: Pitcairn Island, the Bounty Mutineers and Their Descendants: A History
evidence.supports: The island's continuous history from 1790 to the present.

contested.note: Almost everything about the first four years on Pitcairn comes from survivors interviewed decades later, chiefly John Adams, who had reason to shape the story. The number and order of the 1793 killings differ between accounts and cannot be settled.

pedagogy.hook: In 1838 Pitcairn Island gave every adult the vote, women included - fifty-five years before New Zealand, and eighty-nine before all women in Britain.

misconception.belief: The Bounty mutineers founded a free community on an empty island - a romantic escape from tyranny.
misconception.correction: They took six Polynesian men and twelve Polynesian women with them, several by force, then divided the land among the nine Englishmen and gave the Polynesian men none. The Polynesians rebelled in 1793 and all six were killed. The island's population today descends from four Englishmen and the Polynesian women who survived them.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Pitcairn is the empire's smallest surviving fragment and its strangest: founded by criminals, given a democratic constitution by a passing naval captain, emptied and refilled, and still British because nobody has decided what else to do with it.

territories.name: Papua (British New Guinea)
territories.formalName: British New Guinea, from 1906 the Territory of Papua

namesOverTime.name: Territory of Papua
namesOverTime.note: 'Papua' comes through Portuguese and Malay, probably from a Malay word for frizzy hair; the people it names had hundreds of names of their own.

namesOverTime.name: Papua New Guinea
namesOverTime.language: Tok Pisin, Hiri Motu and English

modernSuccessors.name: Independent State of Papua New Guinea

geoCoverage.label: The south-eastern quarter of New Guinea
geoCoverage.change: Britain proclaimed a protectorate over the south coast three days after Germany took the north, and only because Queensland had already tried to annex the whole island and been overruled. Most of the interior was unvisited by any official for another fifty years.

acquisitions.how: Commodore James Erskine declared a protectorate over the southern coast at Port Moresby, three days after Germany claimed the north - Britain had refused Queensland's attempt to annex the island in 1883 and changed its mind only when a rival arrived.

counterparties.name: The Motu, Koitabu, Mekeo, Orokolo, Koiari and hundreds of other peoples of southern New Guinea
counterparties.lost: Sovereignty over a coast, on paper. The interior - where most people lived - was not reached by any administration until the 1930s, and some highland valleys not until the 1950s.
counterparties.note: New Guinea has over 800 languages, more than a tenth of all the languages on earth. No European in 1884 had any idea how many people lived there; the answer turned out to be about a million more than anyone had guessed.

people.name: James Erskine
people.role: commodore who read the proclamation at Port Moresby

people.name: Thomas McIlwraith
people.role: Queensland premier who tried to annex the whole of eastern New Guinea in 1883 and was overruled by London

people.name: William MacGregor
people.role: administrator 1888-98 who walked much of the territory, banned land sales to settlers and built the Armed Native Constabulary

acquisitions.resistance: Frequent and local. Punitive expeditions against villages that killed traders or missionaries were routine into the 1930s, and the colonial 'pacification' of the Papuan Gulf and the Highlands involved shooting that was recorded in patrol reports and rarely elsewhere.

evidence.author: Donald Denoon
evidence.work: A Trial Separation: Australia and the Decolonisation of Papua New Guinea
evidence.supports: The annexation, Australian administration and decolonisation.

acquisitions.how: Britain turned the protectorate into the outright colony of British New Guinea, on condition that the Australian colonies of Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria paid for running it.

counterparties.name: The peoples of British New Guinea
counterparties.lost: Their land in law: all land became Crown land unless a village could show it was in use, though MacGregor's rule that only the government could buy land did protect Papuans from settler purchase.

instrument.name: Letters Patent annexing British New Guinea

statusPeriods.label: Protectorate on the coast, paid for by Australia
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Special Commissioner with a small staff held a coastline; the Australian colonies paid the bills and expected influence in return.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Moresby, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

statusPeriods.label: British New Guinea
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An administrator, an Armed Native Constabulary of Papuan police under white officers, and a rule that only the government could buy land - which made Papua unusual among settler-adjacent colonies.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

to.note: Civil administration was suspended and replaced by the Australian New Guinea Administrative Unit during the first months of 1942 as Japanese forces advanced.

statusPeriods.label: A British possession administered by Australia
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Papua remained legally British territory, but was 'placed under the authority of the Commonwealth of Australia': Australians governed, Papuans were British subjects, and Hubert Murray ran it as Lieutenant-Governor for 32 years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Moresby, under the Australian Department of Territories
statusPeriods.franchise: Papuans had no vote and were subject to separate laws - curfews in Port Moresby, a ban on drinking alcohol, and the White Women's Protection Ordinance of 1926, which made the death penalty available for rape or attempted rape of a European woman by a Papuan man.
statusPeriods.note: Murray's paternalism was mild by the standards of the mandated territory next door, and it still rested on indentured labour recruited under contracts most workers could not read.

from.note: The Japanese advance and the collapse of civil government happened over several weeks in early 1942.

statusPeriods.label: War: Kokoda, Milne Bay and military government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Civil administration was abolished and the Australian New Guinea Administrative Unit ran Papua under military law. Japanese forces held the north coast; the Kokoda campaign was fought across the mountains between July and November 1942.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: 'Occupied' here means occupied by Australia's own military government, not by an enemy: most of Papua stayed in Allied hands throughout, so the degree stays at 5 rather than dropping to 0 as it does for Nauru or the Solomons.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Moresby, under Australian military command
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Around 50,000 Papuans and New Guineans were conscripted as carriers and labourers under the Australian administration, many of them by force.
statusPeriods.note: Australian troops depended completely on Papuan carriers over the Kokoda Track. Australia called them 'fuzzy wuzzy angels', a nickname that was affectionate, racial, and no substitute for pay - compensation for wartime service was still being argued about fifty years later.

statusPeriods.label: Joined administratively to the Trust Territory of New Guinea
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: From 1949 Papua and the trust territory of New Guinea were administered as one unit from Port Moresby, though they kept different legal statuses to the very end: Papua was British soil, New Guinea was a UN trust.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Papua itself was never a trusteeship - it was an Australian-administered British possession. The status here describes the joint administration it was governed through from 1949, and the degree follows the trusteeship default.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Moresby, under the Australian Department of Territories
statusPeriods.franchise: A Legislative Council with three elected Papua New Guinean members came in 1961; the first House of Assembly elected on a common roll with universal adult suffrage met in 1964.
statusPeriods.note: The union was administrative, not legal. Papuans were Australian citizens by virtue of Papua being a British possession under Australian authority; New Guineans, in the trust territory, were not.

departures.how: Papua and the trust territory of New Guinea became one independent country, after Australia decided in the late 1960s that the United Nations and the cost of holding on had made departure cheaper than staying.

becomes.name: Independent State of Papua New Guinea

led.name: Michael Somare
led.role: leader of the Pangu Pati, chief minister from 1972 and first prime minister

led.name: Albert Maori Kiki
led.role: Pangu Pati founder and first foreign minister; his autobiography Ten Thousand Years in a Lifetime named what colonisation felt like from inside

led.name: Gough Whitlam
led.role: Australian prime minister who accelerated the timetable, over the objections of many Papua New Guineans who wanted longer

departures.movement: Pangu Pati

cost.note: Independence itself was peaceful. Bougainville declared its own independence fifteen days before Papua New Guinea's and was talked back in; the same grievance produced a civil war in 1988 that killed thousands.

departures.borders: The border with Indonesian Papua is the 141st meridian, drawn by the Netherlands and Britain in 1895 straight through the middle of one island and dozens of peoples. It is still there, and so is the war on the other side of it.

instrument.name: Papua New Guinea Independence Act 1975 (Cth) and the Constitution of Papua New Guinea
instrument.note: The constitution was adopted by the House of Assembly on 15 August 1975 and came into force at independence on 16 September.

evidence.author: Donald Denoon
evidence.work: A Trial Separation: Australia and the Decolonisation of Papua New Guinea
evidence.supports: The speed and politics of the Australian withdrawal.

violence.note: Colonial control was extended by patrol: officers with police walked into valleys, and where they were resisted they shot. The Highlands 'pacification' of the 1930s to 1950s is documented mostly in the patrol officers' own reports.

populationTransfer.note: Indentured labour moved Papuans to plantations and goldfields under contracts of three years; around 50,000 were conscripted as wartime carriers, thousands of whom died.

commonwealth.note: Papua New Guinea is a Commonwealth realm; the British monarch is head of state, represented by a Papua New Guinean governor-general.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copra and gold, then copper from Bougainville and Ok Tedi, then liquefied natural gas. Mining has financed the state and wrecked rivers, and the Bougainville mine started a war.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Over 800 languages, three official ones - Tok Pisin, Hiri Motu and English - and a constitution that recognises customary law and customary land title over 97 per cent of the country.

peak.populationNote: Approximate: the 1966 census of the Territory of Papua and New Guinea counted about 2.18 million people in total, of whom roughly 700,000 lived in Papua. Papua's own population had never been properly counted before the 1950s because much of the interior was unadministered.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1966 census of Papua (British New Guinea)
populationWarrant.supports: Papua (British New Guinea)’s largest recorded population: 700,000 people, counted in 1966.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Donald Denoon
evidence.work: A Trial Separation: Australia and the Decolonisation of Papua New Guinea
evidence.supports: Australian administration and the path to independence.

evidence.author: Hank Nelson
evidence.work: Taim Bilong Masta: The Australian Involvement with Papua New Guinea
evidence.supports: Everyday colonial rule, the kiap system and the war years.

evidence.author: Bill Gammage
evidence.work: The Sky Travellers: Journeys in New Guinea 1938-1939
evidence.supports: The first contact patrols into the Highlands and what they did.

pedagogy.hook: In the 1930s gold prospectors walked into the New Guinea Highlands and found about a million people no government had suspected existed - in a territory coloured British on maps for fifty years.

misconception.belief: By 1900 the world had been mapped and every population was known to the empires that claimed them.
misconception.correction: Not in New Guinea. Michael Leahy's patrols of 1930-35 walked into densely farmed highland valleys holding around a million people whom the administration on the coast had never heard of. Some communities did not meet a government officer until the 1950s, seventy years after Britain claimed their country.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Papua is the clearest case of a claim that stayed on paper for decades, and one of the few colonies where the rule that only the government could buy land actually protected local ownership - which is why 97 per cent of Papua New Guinea is still under customary title.

date.note: The Leahy brothers' first Highlands prospecting trip began in May 1930; the major discoveries came in 1933.

territories.name: Territory of New Guinea
territories.formalName: Territory of New Guinea, a League of Nations mandate and then a United Nations trust territory

namesOverTime.name: Papua New Guinea
namesOverTime.language: Tok Pisin, Hiri Motu and English

modernSuccessors.name: Independent State of Papua New Guinea

geoCoverage.label: North-eastern New Guinea, the Bismarcks and Bougainville
geoCoverage.change: An Australian expeditionary force took the German colony in September 1914. Its Highlands interior stayed outside any administration until the 1930s.

acquisitions.how: The Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force landed near Rabaul on 11 September 1914, fought a small action at Bita Paka in which six Australians and about thirty Melanesian police died, and took the German surrender at Toma on 17 September.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Its main Pacific colony, its wireless station and its plantations, all inside a fortnight.

counterparties.name: The Tolai, Sepik, Madang, Bougainvillean and Highlands peoples
counterparties.lost: One imperial power for another, with the labour system intact: German-era indenture, head tax and plantation contracts were carried over almost unchanged by the Australians.

people.name: William Holmes
people.role: commanded the Australian expeditionary force

people.name: Eduard Haber
people.role: acting German governor who signed the surrender at Toma

acquisitions.resistance: The fighting at Bita Paka was done largely by Melanesian police fighting for Germany against Australians; most of the dead were New Guineans on the German side.

cost.note: Bita Paka, 11 September 1914: six Australians and one German killed, and about 30 Melanesian police in German service. It was Australia's first action of the First World War.

acquisitions.how: The League of Nations gave Australia a Class C mandate over the territory, which meant it could be governed as if it were Australian soil, with a yearly report to Geneva and nothing more.

counterparties.name: The peoples of the mandated territory
counterparties.lost: Any chance of the German plantations being returned to the villages they had been taken from: the mandate confirmed the alienated land in Australian hands and expropriated German owners in favour of Australian ex-servicemen.

instrument.name: League of Nations Class C Mandate for New Guinea

evidence.author: Hank Nelson
evidence.work: Taim Bilong Masta: The Australian Involvement with Papua New Guinea
evidence.supports: Australian administration of the mandated territory.

acquisitions.how: The United Nations replaced the mandate with a trusteeship carrying a duty to prepare the territory for self-government, and sent visiting missions every three years that pushed Australia into moving faster than it wanted to.

counterparties.name: The peoples of the trust territory
counterparties.lost: Nothing further. The trusteeship is why Papua New Guinea became independent in 1975 rather than in the 1990s: UN pressure set the timetable, and Australia followed it.

instrument.name: United Nations Trusteeship Agreement for New Guinea

statusPeriods.label: Australian military administration
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Australian officers ran the German system with German records, German plantation contracts and the same head tax, because it worked and nobody had a better idea.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

statusPeriods.label: Australian Class C mandate
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A civil administrator at Rabaul governed through district officers - the kiaps - who walked in with police, appointed village officials, collected head tax and recruited indentured labour for the plantations and goldfields.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Rabaul, then Lae from 1937, under the Australian Department of Territories
statusPeriods.franchise: New Guineans had no vote and were not Australian citizens - unlike Papuans next door, who were British subjects.
statusPeriods.note: In January 1929 about 3,000 indentured workers in Rabaul walked out in the largest strike in the colonial Pacific. The organisers were jailed and the wage stayed where it was.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan took Rabaul in January 1942 and held New Britain, New Ireland, Bougainville and the north coast for over three years. Australian and Allied forces fought their way back island by island.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: 'Occupied' defaults to 5 for a British or Australian occupation. Here Australia was the party removed: the mandate was under Japanese military government and Australian authority was nil.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere; the civil administration was evacuated or captured
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.
statusPeriods.note: On 1 July 1942 the Montevideo Maru, carrying about 1,050 Australian prisoners and civilians from Rabaul, was torpedoed by an American submarine with almost no survivors - Australia's worst maritime disaster, and it happened because Australia had not evacuated Rabaul.

statusPeriods.label: UN trust territory, administered with Papua
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Australia administered New Guinea jointly with Papua from Port Moresby from 1949, under a UN trusteeship whose visiting missions kept asking when self-government was coming.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Moresby, under the Australian Department of Territories
statusPeriods.franchise: The first House of Assembly elected on a common roll with universal adult suffrage met in 1964; self-government came on 1 December 1973.
statusPeriods.note: The trusteeship began formally on 13 December 1946; Australian civil administration resumed from the surrender in September 1945.

departures.how: The trust territory and Papua became one independent state, with Australia setting a fast timetable that many Papua New Guinean leaders thought too fast and the United Nations thought overdue.

becomes.name: Independent State of Papua New Guinea

led.name: Michael Somare
led.role: chief minister and first prime minister; a Sepik man who built the first national party

led.name: John Guise
led.role: first governor-general; had led the elected members of the House of Assembly through the 1960s

led.name: Leo Hannett
led.role: Bougainvillean leader who declared the Republic of the North Solomons fifteen days before Papua New Guinea's independence

departures.movement: Pangu Pati and the elected members of the House of Assembly

cost.note: Independence was peaceful. What followed on Bougainville was not: the civil war of 1988-98 killed between about 10,000 and 20,000 people, most of them from disease and hunger under a blockade.

departures.borders: New Guinea kept the line Germany and Britain drew in 1885 and the 141st meridian the Dutch and British agreed in 1895. It also kept Bougainville, which Germany had held and which belongs geographically to the Solomons chain - the single most consequential colonial border in the Pacific.

instrument.name: Papua New Guinea Independence Act 1975 (Cth)

populationTransfer.note: Indenture was the engine of the territory: tens of thousands of men were recruited on three-year contracts for plantations and the Wau and Bulolo goldfields, and villages lost their young men for years at a time.

violence.note: Patrol officers extended control by walking into unadministered country with armed police; where villages resisted, they shot. The Japanese occupation and the Allied reconquest then killed New Guineans on a scale nobody has ever counted.

toll.note: No count exists of New Guinean civilian deaths in 1942-45 from fighting, forced labour, bombing and famine. Estimates run into the tens of thousands. The Australian and Japanese military dead were counted; the people whose islands they fought over were not.

commonwealth.note: Papua New Guinea joined the Commonwealth at independence as a realm with the British monarch as head of state.

consequences.economicLegacy: German and then Australian plantations, gold at Wau and Bulolo in the 1930s, and copper at Panguna on Bougainville from 1972 - which at its peak provided nearly half of Papua New Guinea's export earnings and then started a war.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Tok Pisin, which grew out of the plantation labour trade across Melanesia, became the language that made a nation of 800 language groups possible to govern.

peak.populationNote: Approximate: the 1966 census of the Territory of Papua and New Guinea counted about 2.18 million people, of whom roughly 1.48 million were in the trust territory of New Guinea.

populationWarrant.work: The 1966 census of Territory of New Guinea
populationWarrant.supports: Territory of New Guinea’s largest recorded population: 1,480,000 people, counted in 1966.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.

evidence.supports: Australian rule, the kiaps, indenture and the war.

evidence.author: Stewart Firth
evidence.work: New Guinea under the Germans
evidence.supports: The German colony Australia inherited and the labour system it kept.

evidence.author: Donald Denoon
evidence.work: A Trial Separation: Australia and the Decolonisation of Papua New Guinea
evidence.supports: The trusteeship, UN pressure and the independence timetable.

pedagogy.hook: Australia took New Guinea from Germany in a fortnight in 1914 and then kept running it with German records, German plantation contracts and the same head tax, because the system worked.

misconception.belief: A League of Nations mandate meant international supervision that protected the people living there.
misconception.correction: A Class C mandate let Australia govern New Guinea as if it were Australian soil. New Guineans had no vote, no citizenship and no appeal; when 3,000 workers struck in Rabaul in 1929 the organisers went to prison. Real supervision only came with the UN trusteeship after 1946, and then it did work: its visiting missions set the clock that ran out in 1975.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: New Guinea is where you can see the twentieth-century international system doing its job badly and then well: a mandate that changed nothing, and a trusteeship that produced an independent country inside thirty years.

territories.formalName: Bougainville and Buka, in German New Guinea and then the Territory of New Guinea

namesOverTime.name: Bougainville
namesOverTime.note: Named for the French navigator Louis-Antoine de Bougainville, who sailed past. Bougainvilleans call themselves by their own peoples' names - Nasioi, Nagovisi, Halia, Buin and others - and increasingly Me'ekamui.

modernSuccessors.name: Papua New Guinea (Autonomous Region of Bougainville)
modernSuccessors.note: In a referendum held between 23 November and 7 December 2019, 97.7 per cent of Bougainvilleans voted for independence. The result is not binding; negotiations with Papua New Guinea continue.

geoCoverage.label: Bougainville and Buka: Solomon Islands geography, New Guinea politics
geoCoverage.change: Australian forces occupied the German district headquarters at Kieta in December 1914, three months after taking Rabaul.

acquisitions.how: Australian forces occupied the German station at Kieta, taking possession of two islands that Germany had kept in 1899 when it handed the rest of the Solomons chain to Britain.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: The southern outpost of its New Guinea colony, and the plantations at Kieta and Buka Passage.

counterparties.name: The Nasioi, Nagovisi, Buin, Halia and other peoples of Bougainville and Buka
counterparties.lost: Nothing they could see at the time - and, in the long run, the right to be part of the Solomon Islands, whose people are their kin and whose colonial border stopped one island short of them.

acquisitions.resistance: None recorded in 1914. Bougainvillean resistance came sixty years later, against a copper mine and a national government neither of which its people had chosen.

statusPeriods.label: Australian military administration
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Part of the Australian military government of the former German colony, run from Rabaul 700 kilometres away.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

to.note: Japanese forces occupied Buka and Bougainville during March 1942; the landings were made on different days.

statusPeriods.label: Part of Australia's mandated territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: District officers, head tax and copra plantations, administered as the southernmost district of the mandate - even though Bougainville is geologically, culturally and linguistically part of the Solomon Islands.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

from.note: Japanese landings on Buka and Bougainville took place over several days in March 1942.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation and a three-year campaign
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan built airfields and based over 60,000 troops on the island; American and then Australian forces fought there from November 1943 to the surrender. Bougainvilleans were caught between two armies that both took their food and their labour.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: 'Occupied' defaults to 5 where Britain or Australia is the occupier. Here the island was occupied by Japan and Australian authority was nil.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere; the Australian administration was evacuated
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.
statusPeriods.note: Bougainvilleans died in large numbers in the campaign and afterwards from famine. No reliable count was ever made.

statusPeriods.label: Trust territory district, then a copper mine
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Australia administered Bougainville as a district of the trust territory. In 1967-72 it forced through the Panguna copper mine over landowner objections, moving villages and paying royalties to Port Moresby rather than to the people whose land it was.
statusPeriods.franchise: Bougainvilleans voted in House of Assembly elections from 1964 and used them to demand separation from the start.
statusPeriods.note: Panguna opened in 1972 and at its peak produced nearly half of Papua New Guinea's export earnings, from land whose owners received about 0.5 to 1.25 per cent of the profits.

departures.how: Bougainville left Australian trusteeship inside Papua New Guinea, against the wishes of many of its people: its leaders had declared the Republic of the North Solomons independent fifteen days earlier, on 1 September 1975, and were talked back in with a promise of provincial government.

becomes.name: North Solomons Province, Papua New Guinea

led.name: Leo Hannett
led.role: declared the Republic of the North Solomons on 1 September 1975 and later became provincial premier

led.name: Francis Ona
led.role: Panguna landowner and surveyor who led the mine closure in 1988 and the Bougainville Revolutionary Army

led.name: Joseph Kabui
led.role: provincial premier and later the first president of the Autonomous Bougainville Government

departures.movement: The North Solomons separatist movement; later the Bougainville Revolutionary Army

cost.note: The civil war of 1988-98 followed directly from the mine and the merger. Estimates of the dead range from about 10,000 to 20,000 out of a population of around 160,000, most from disease and hunger during a Papua New Guinea blockade rather than from fighting. No census was possible and the range is wide for that reason.

departures.borders: Bougainville is 8 kilometres from the Solomon Islands and 800 from Port Moresby. The border that put it in Papua New Guinea was drawn by Germany and Britain in 1899, when Germany kept Bougainville and gave Britain the rest of the chain.

evidence.author: Anthony J. Regan
evidence.work: Light Intervention: Lessons from Bougainville
evidence.publisher: United States Institute of Peace Press
evidence.supports: The origins of the conflict, the peace process and the referendum provisions.

violence.note: The Bougainville civil war of 1988-98 began when landowners shut the Panguna mine and Papua New Guinea sent in its army; a blockade cut off medicine and fuel for years.

toll.note: The commonly cited range is 10,000 to 20,000 dead, mostly indirect deaths under the blockade. Some researchers regard the upper figure as too high. Nobody counted at the time and the range reflects that honestly.

consequences.economicLegacy: Panguna produced about three million tonnes of copper concentrate and left a tailings-filled valley. It has been closed since 1989, and reopening it is the central question of Bougainville's economic future.
consequences.borderLegacy: An Anglo-German bargain over Samoa in 1899 put Bougainville on the wrong side of a line, and 120 years later 97.7 per cent of its people voted to cross back.

peak.populationNote: 1971 census of the Bougainville District, approximately 96,000. The population today is around 300,000.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Bougainville’s largest recorded population: 96,000 people, counted in 1971.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Anthony J. Regan
evidence.work: Light Intervention: Lessons from Bougainville
evidence.publisher: United States Institute of Peace Press
evidence.supports: The conflict, the peace agreement and the referendum.

evidence.author: Donald Denoon
evidence.work: Getting Under the Skin: The Bougainville Copper Agreement and the Creation of the Panguna Mine
evidence.supports: How the mine was imposed on landowners under Australian administration.

pedagogy.hook: Bougainville is eight kilometres from the Solomon Islands and 800 from its own capital. It ended up in Papua New Guinea because in 1899 Germany kept it and gave Britain the rest of the chain.

misconception.belief: Colonial borders were arbitrary but harmless - what mattered was what happened inside them.
misconception.correction: Bougainville is the counter-example. An 1899 line separating it from its kin in the Solomons put it inside Papua New Guinea in 1975, over its own declaration of independence. A copper mine on that land started a war in 1988 that killed perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people, and in 2019 its people voted 97.7 per cent to leave. One line, drawn over Samoa, is still killing people ninety years later.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Bougainville shows how a border and a mine compound each other, and it is the live case: the referendum has been held, the result is not binding, and the negotiation is happening now.

keyDates.what: Germany keeps Bougainville and hands Britain the rest of the Solomons
Australian forces occupy Kieta

date.note: Commercial production at Panguna began during the first half of 1972.

keyDates.what: The Panguna copper mine opens
The Republic of the North Solomons declared, 15 days before PNG independence

date.note: Sabotage of the mine escalated through November and December 1988; the mine closed in May 1989.

keyDates.what: Landowners shut Panguna; the civil war begins
97.7 per cent vote for independence

events.title: Cook claims the east coast on Possession Island
events.summary: On a small island off Cape York, James Cook raised the flag, fired three volleys and claimed the entire eastern coast of the Australian continent for George III, having landed on it in only a handful of places and spoken to almost no one who lived there.
events.significance: It is the legal origin of British Australia. Because Cook did not obtain consent and did not report the country as conquered, the land was treated as legally empty - which meant no treaty, no purchase and no compensation were owed to anyone. That doctrine governed Australian land law for 222 years.

places.name: Possession Island, Torres Strait
places.note: Where the claim was made.

places.name: Kamay (Botany Bay)
places.note: Where the Endeavour first landed, on 29 April 1770, and where two Gweagal men tried to stop it.

people.name: James Cook
people.role: commander of HMS Endeavour

people.name: Joseph Banks
people.role: naturalist; later told a parliamentary committee the country was thinly populated and suitable for convicts

people.name: Cooman
people.role: one of two Gweagal men who confronted the landing party at Kamay and was shot at; his shield is in the British Museum and his descendants have asked for it back

people.name: Tupaia
people.role: Ra'iatean navigator and priest who sailed with Cook, whose Polynesian navigation and diplomacy made much of the voyage possible; he died at Batavia in 1770

pedagogy.hook: Cook's secret orders told him to take possession only with the consent of the people living there, or if the land was uninhabited. He met people repeatedly, got no consent, and claimed it anyway.

misconception.belief: Cook discovered Australia.
misconception.correction: Aboriginal people had been there for at least 65,000 years, Makassan fleets from Sulawesi had been trading on the north coast for centuries, and Dutch ships had charted the west and south coasts since 1606. Cook charted the east coast and claimed it. 'Discovery' names the moment Europe found out, not the moment the place began.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Everything about Australian land law until 1992 runs back to what Cook did and did not do on 22 August 1770.

evidence.author: Nicholas Thomas
evidence.work: Discoveries: The Voyages of Captain Cook
evidence.supports: The voyage, the instructions and the claim.

evidence.author: Maria Nugent
evidence.work: Captain Cook Was Here
evidence.supports: The Botany Bay landing and how Aboriginal and settler accounts of it differ.

events.title: The First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove
events.summary: Eleven ships under Arthur Phillip, carrying about 1,370 people of whom roughly 750 were convicts, landed at Sydney Cove after eight months at sea. It was the first British settlement in Australia and the start of 80 years of penal transportation.
events.significance: Britain solved a prison overcrowding problem created by losing America by founding a colony on the other side of the world. About 162,000 convicts were transported to Australia between 1788 and 1868, and their descendants are a substantial part of the modern Australian population.

places.name: Sydney Cove (Warrane)
places.note: Where the fleet landed on 26 January 1788.

places.name: Kamay (Botany Bay)
places.note: The intended site, rejected after a week for lack of fresh water.

people.name: Arthur Phillip
people.role: governor; commanded the fleet

people.name: Bennelong
people.role: Wangal man seized on Phillip's orders in November 1789 to act as go-between; later sailed to England and came home

people.name: Barangaroo
people.role: Cammeraygal woman, Bennelong's wife, who refused to wear British clothes or accept British food and argued publicly against the settlement's presence

people.name: Pemulwuy
people.role: Bidjigal leader who began attacking the settlement's farms in 1790

toll.note: 48 people died on the voyage out, a low figure for the period. The far larger toll came in April 1789, when smallpox killed perhaps half the Aboriginal people around Sydney Harbour. Its source has never been established.

pedagogy.hook: Australia's national day marks the morning a prison fleet dropped anchor. Many Aboriginal Australians call it Invasion Day, and the argument about the date is not really about the date.

misconception.belief: Convicts were mostly hardened criminals and political prisoners.
misconception.correction: Most were thieves, and most of what they stole was small: clothing, food, handkerchiefs. Around a fifth were women. About a quarter were Irish, and a minority of those were political. Transportation was a punishment for poverty as much as for crime, and after seven years most convicts were free settlers with land.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the empire using a colony as an instrument of domestic policy: the problem being solved was in London, and the solution was imposed on people 17,000 kilometres away who had no idea it was coming.

evidence.author: Robert Hughes
evidence.work: The Fatal Shore: A History of the Transportation of Convicts to Australia, 1787-1868
evidence.supports: The fleet, the convict system and its scale.

evidence.author: Grace Karskens
evidence.work: The Colony: A History of Early Sydney
evidence.supports: The first years at Sydney Cove and relations with the Eora.

events.title: The Australian frontier wars
events.summary: For nearly 150 years Aboriginal peoples fought the taking of their country, and colonists, police and Native Police units fought back with guns, poison and punitive expeditions. It was not one war but hundreds of local ones, moving with the pastoral frontier from Sydney to the Kimberley.
events.significance: This is how Australia was actually taken. Because the land was legally 'settled' rather than conquered, the fighting had no treaties, no formal declarations and no place in the national war memorial - which is why generations of Australians were taught that the continent was occupied peacefully.

places.name: Bathurst, New South Wales
places.note: Martial law declared against the Wiradjuri, 14 August 1824.

places.name: Coniston, Northern Territory
places.note: The last officially sanctioned massacre, 1928.

people.name: Pemulwuy
people.role: Bidjigal leader around Sydney, 1790-1802

people.name: Windradyne
people.role: Wiradjuri leader in the Bathurst war of 1824, who walked to Parramatta to make peace with the word 'PEACE' on his hat

people.name: Jandamarra
people.role: Bunuba leader who fought a three-year campaign in the Kimberley, 1894-97

people.name: Multuggerah
people.role: Yagara leader who blockaded the Toowoomba range road in 1843

toll.note: Henry Reynolds's long-standing estimate is about 20,000 Aboriginal and 2,000 to 2,500 settler deaths across the continent. Raymond Evans and Robert Orsted-Jensen argue for at least 24,000 in Queensland alone, and possibly far more. The University of Newcastle massacre-mapping project has documented over 400 massacre sites with more than 11,000 named victims. The upper end is contested; the lower end is not.

pedagogy.hook: The last officially sanctioned massacre of Aboriginal people in Australia happened in 1928 - twenty-seven years after Australia became a country, and eleven years after the Battle of Passchendaele.

misconception.belief: Aboriginal people did not resist; they simply died of disease or moved away.
misconception.correction: They resisted for 146 years. Pemulwuy raided farms around Sydney until 1802; martial law was declared at Bathurst in 1824 and in Van Diemen's Land in 1828; Jandamarra fought the Western Australian police until 1897; the Kalkadoon fought pitched battles in Queensland in the 1880s. Disease killed enormous numbers, and so did guns.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Australia is the only major settler nation whose founding wars are not commemorated as wars. Naming them changes what kind of country the map describes.

evidence.author: Henry Reynolds
evidence.work: The Other Side of the Frontier: Aboriginal Resistance to the European Invasion of Australia
evidence.supports: Aboriginal resistance as organised warfare, and the casualty estimates.

evidence.author: Henry Reynolds
evidence.work: Forgotten War
evidence.supports: The argument that the frontier conflicts were wars and should be commemorated as such.

evidence.author: John Connor
evidence.work: The Australian Frontier Wars 1788-1838
evidence.publisher: University of New South Wales Press
evidence.supports: Military analysis of the early frontier conflicts.

contested.note: The death toll is genuinely disputed and the dispute is political as well as scholarly. Keith Windschuttle argued in 2002 that the recorded killings are far fewer than historians claim; Lyndall Ryan, Henry Reynolds, Raymond Evans and the contributors to Robert Manne's Whitewash (2003) replied using the colonial records themselves. What is not disputed is that colonial governments declared martial law, funded the Native Police, and recorded 'dispersals'.

positions.claim: At least 20,000 Aboriginal people and around 2,000 to 2,500 settlers were killed in frontier conflict between 1788 and the 1930s.
positions.heldBy: Henry Reynolds and most Australian historians

positions.claim: Queensland alone accounts for 24,000 to 65,000 Aboriginal deaths, so the continental total is far higher.
The documented killings number in the low thousands and were criminal acts rather than warfare.

events.title: The Black War in Van Diemen's Land
events.summary: The Oyster Bay and Big River nations fought an eight-year campaign against the settlers taking their hunting grounds. Governor Arthur declared martial law, put a bounty on captives, and in 1830 marched 2,200 men across the island in a human chain called the Black Line.
events.significance: It is the most concentrated frontier war in Australian history and the one the colonial government most openly treated as a war. The survivors were removed to Flinders Island, where most died, and the belief that the Tasmanian Aboriginal people were extinguished became a founding myth that the community itself disproved.

places.name: Wybalenna, Flinders Island
places.note: The settlement where the survivors were taken from 1833; most died there.

places.name: Hobart
places.note: Where martial law was proclaimed on 1 November 1828.

people.name: Tongerlongeter
people.role: Oyster Bay leader who commanded the eastern campaign and surrendered on terms at the end of 1831

people.name: Montpelliatta
people.role: Big River leader who fought alongside Tongerlongeter

people.name: George Arthur
people.role: lieutenant-governor who declared martial law and organised the Black Line

people.name: George Augustus Robinson
people.role: builder turned 'conciliator' who persuaded the survivors to give themselves up and take exile on Flinders Island

people.name: Truganini
people.role: Nuenonne woman who travelled with Robinson, survived Wybalenna and Oyster Cove, and died in 1876; her skeleton was displayed in a museum until 1947 and cremated only in 1976

toll.note: Nicholas Clements and Lyndall Ryan, working from settler depositions and newspapers, count roughly 220 colonists and between 600 and 900 Aboriginal Tasmanians killed between 1824 and 1831. Killings of Aboriginal people were systematically under-reported, so the true figure is likely higher than the recorded one.

pedagogy.hook: The Black Line cost 30,000 pounds, involved a tenth of the colony's adult male population, swept the island for seven weeks - and captured one man and one boy.

misconception.belief: Truganini was the last Tasmanian Aboriginal person.
misconception.correction: She was the last survivor of the people removed to Flinders Island. Tasmanian Aboriginal families descended from women taken to the Bass Strait islands by sealers survived independently, kept their identity, and were formally recognised in the twentieth century. Tens of thousands of Tasmanians identify as Aboriginal today.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest case in the empire of a colonial government treating dispossession as a military campaign - and of a survival story that the official record declared impossible.

evidence.author: Lyndall Ryan
evidence.work: Tasmanian Aborigines: A History Since 1803
evidence.supports: The war, the removals and the community's survival.

evidence.author: Nicholas Clements
evidence.work: The Black War: Fear, Sex and Resistance in Tasmania
evidence.supports: The conduct of the war and the counts of palawa and settler dead.

evidence.author: Henry Reynolds
evidence.work: Fate of a Free People
evidence.supports: The 1831-32 surrenders as negotiated terms rather than capitulation.

contested.note: Tasmania is the sharpest front in Australia's history wars. Keith Windschuttle's The Fabrication of Aboriginal History (2002) disputed the scale of the killing; Ryan, Clements, Reynolds and the contributors to Robert Manne's Whitewash (2003) answered with the settler record. The count is disputed; the martial law proclamation, the bounty and the Black Line are documents.

events.title: Batman's treaty and Bourke's proclamation
events.summary: John Batman got eight Wurundjeri elders to mark a document exchanging 600,000 acres around Port Phillip for blankets, knives, scissors and a yearly tribute. Governor Bourke declared it void eleven weeks later, ruling that only the Crown could grant land in Australia.
events.significance: It is the only time British settlers in Australia tried to buy land from its Aboriginal owners, and the Crown destroyed the attempt precisely because recognising a purchase would have recognised an owner. Bourke's proclamation is the clearest official statement of the doctrine the High Court finally rejected in 1992.

places.name: Merri Creek, Melbourne
places.note: The traditional site of the meeting, though the exact place is disputed.

people.name: John Batman
people.role: Van Diemen's Land grazier who staged the purchase; he had previously led parties hunting Aboriginal Tasmanians

people.name: Billibellary
people.role: Wurundjeri ngurungaeta whose mark is on the document

people.name: Richard Bourke
people.role: Governor of New South Wales, whose proclamation of 26 August 1835 voided the deal

people.name: William Barak
people.role: Wurundjeri boy present at the meeting who spent his adult life defending Coranderrk station

pedagogy.hook: The only land purchase agreement ever signed between British settlers and Aboriginal Australians was cancelled by the government in eleven weeks - because admitting they could sell it meant admitting they owned it.

misconception.belief: Batman's treaty was a decent attempt at fair dealing that the Aboriginal signatories understood and agreed to.
misconception.correction: It was a land grab dressed as a treaty by a syndicate that wanted title before other squatters arrived. The ceremony the elders performed, tanderrum, granted temporary safe passage across country, not ownership of it. And Batman's document was written in London-style legal English that nobody present could read.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Bourke's proclamation is the moment terra nullius was stated as policy rather than assumed. It is the document Mabo overturned.

evidence.author: Bain Attwood
evidence.work: Possession: Batman's Treaty and the Matter of History
evidence.supports: The document, the ceremony, the proclamation and their long afterlife.

evidence.author: Henry Reynolds
evidence.work: The Law of the Land
evidence.supports: The legal doctrine of terra nullius and the alternatives that were argued at the time.

events.title: The Myall Creek massacre and the trials
events.summary: Eleven stockmen rounded up about 28 Wirrayaraay people - mostly women, children and old men, camped peacefully at a station on the Gwydir River - tied them together, led them away and killed them with swords. Seven of the killers were hanged in Sydney on 18 December 1838.
events.significance: It is the only time in Australian history that white men were executed for killing Aboriginal people in a frontier massacre. The public reaction was outrage - at the hangings, not at the killings - and the lesson the frontier drew was not to stop, but to leave no witnesses and no bodies.

places.name: Myall Creek station, near Bingara, New South Wales
places.note: The site is now a memorial where descendants of both the victims and the killers meet each June.

people.name: John Plunkett
people.role: Attorney-General of New South Wales, an Irish Catholic, who insisted on a second trial after the first jury acquitted and secured seven convictions

people.name: George Gipps
people.role: governor who refused to commute the death sentences

people.name: William Hobbs
people.role: station superintendent who reported the killings, and was blacklisted for it

people.name: Yintayintin (Davey)
people.role: Aboriginal stockman whose evidence helped identify the killers

toll.note: About 28 Wirrayaraay people were killed; the exact number is unknown because the bodies were burned. Eleven men were charged, all acquitted at the first trial, and seven convicted at the second and hanged on 18 December 1838.

pedagogy.hook: Seven men were hanged for killing 28 Aboriginal people at Myall Creek in 1838. It never happened again anywhere in Australia in the next century.

misconception.belief: Colonial law did not apply to violence against Aboriginal people, so nobody was ever punished.
misconception.correction: The law did apply - Aboriginal people were British subjects and killing them was murder. It was almost never enforced, because juries of settlers acquitted, witnesses were Aboriginal and therefore could not swear an oath in court, and evidence was destroyed. Myall Creek is famous because it is the exception, and the exception took two trials and an attorney-general who would not let it go.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows that colonists knew what they were doing was murder. After 1838 the killing continued, but the reports stopped.

evidence.author: Roger Milliss
evidence.work: Waterloo Creek: The Australia Day Massacre of 1838, George Gipps and the British Conquest of New South Wales
evidence.supports: The context of frontier killing on the Gwydir and the politics of the trials.

evidence.author: Mark Tedeschi
evidence.work: Murder at Myall Creek: The Trial that Defined a Nation
evidence.supports: The trials, the evidence and John Plunkett's prosecution.

events.title: The Eureka Stockade
events.summary: Gold miners at Ballarat, furious at a monthly licence fee, licence hunts and having no vote, burned their licences, swore allegiance to the Southern Cross flag and built a stockade. Soldiers and police stormed it before dawn on 3 December and the fight was over in about fifteen minutes.
events.significance: Thirteen men were tried for high treason and every jury acquitted them. Within two years Victoria had manhood suffrage, the secret ballot and payment of members of parliament, and the licence was replaced by a miner's right that carried a vote with it. It is the rare colonial revolt that lost the battle and won the argument.

places.name: Eureka lead, Ballarat
places.note: Where the stockade stood.

people.name: Peter Lalor
people.role: Irish-born miner who led the stockade, lost an arm and later became Speaker of the Victorian parliament

people.name: Raffaello Carboni
people.role: Italian miner and eyewitness whose book The Eureka Stockade is the main first-hand account

people.name: Charles Hotham
people.role: lieutenant-governor whose licence hunts provoked the revolt

people.name: John Joseph
people.role: African American miner, the first of the thirteen tried for treason; his acquittal was cheered by a crowd of ten thousand in Melbourne

toll.note: About 22 miners and six soldiers died in the fighting or shortly afterwards; some accounts put miner deaths above 30 because men died of wounds away from the site. Nobody made a full count.

pedagogy.hook: Thirteen men were tried for high treason after Eureka. Every single one was acquitted, and one of them, Peter Lalor, was elected to parliament within a year.

misconception.belief: Eureka was the birth of Australian democracy or an attempt to found a republic.
misconception.correction: The miners wanted the licence fee abolished and the vote extended - the demands were closer to Chartism than to revolution. Victoria already had a partly elected parliament, and the reforms that followed had been in the works. Eureka mattered because it made them urgent, and because the juries refused to convict.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the counter-example to the idea that colonial rebellions were always crushed: this one was crushed militarily and then conceded politically within two years, because the rebels were white men whom the colony intended to enfranchise anyway.

evidence.author: John Molony
evidence.work: Eureka
evidence.supports: The stockade, the trials and the political settlement that followed.

evidence.author: Geoffrey Blainey
evidence.work: The Rush That Never Ended: A History of Australian Mining
evidence.supports: The goldfields, the licence system and the economics behind the revolt.

events.title: The Coniston killings
events.summary: After a dingo trapper was killed at a soak in central Australia, police led punitive parties across Warlpiri, Anmatyerre and Kaytetye country for eight weeks. The official count was 31 Aboriginal people killed; Warlpiri accounts and later historians put it far higher.
events.significance: It is the last officially sanctioned massacre of Aboriginal people in Australia, and a board of inquiry in 1929 found the killings justified. It happened twenty-seven years after federation and in the same decade as Australian troops were being commemorated at Villers-Bretonneux.

places.name: Yurrkuru (Brooks Soak), Northern Territory
places.note: Where the trapper Frederick Brooks was killed, starting the reprisals.

people.name: William George Murray
people.role: mounted constable who led the punitive parties and told the inquiry he had shot to kill

people.name: Bullfrog Japanangka
people.role: Warlpiri man who killed Frederick Brooks, in a dispute over Brooks's treatment of his wife

people.name: Annie Lock
people.role: missionary at Harding Soak whose presence and reports the 1929 board of inquiry blamed for unsettling Aboriginal people, rather than blaming the police who did the shooting

toll.note: The 1929 board of inquiry accepted 31 deaths and cleared the police. Warlpiri, Anmatyerre and Kaytetye oral histories and subsequent research put the number between 60 and 200. The lower figure is the killers' own count.

pedagogy.hook: A board of inquiry looked at the Coniston killings in 1929 and found them justified. Warlpiri families were still afraid to camp at some of the waterholes fifty years later.

misconception.belief: Frontier massacres belong to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
misconception.correction: Coniston happened in 1928, when Australia had radio, aeroplanes and a national parliament. There are Warlpiri people alive today whose grandparents survived it, and the Northern Territory government did not formally acknowledge it until the eightieth anniversary in 2008.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It sets the frontier inside living memory, which is the single fact that changes how students read the rest of Australian history.

evidence.author: Tony Roberts
evidence.work: Frontier Justice: A History of the Gulf Country to 1900
evidence.supports: Frontier violence and policing in the Northern Territory.

evidence.author: Peter Read
evidence.work: Long Time, Olden Time: Aboriginal Accounts of Northern Territory History
evidence.supports: Warlpiri, Anmatyerre and Kaytetye accounts of the 1928 killings. Written with Jay Read.

contested.note: The only official count, 31, comes from the men who did the killing and from an inquiry that cleared them. Aboriginal oral history gives higher numbers and names more sites. There is no independent record, which is itself part of the history.

events.title: The Commonwealth of Australia is proclaimed
events.summary: Six self-governing British colonies became one federation under a constitution Australians had written themselves and Westminster had enacted. About 250,000 people watched the proclamation in Centennial Park, Sydney.
events.significance: Australia became a nation without a war, a revolution or a break with Britain, and the constitution it adopted excluded Aboriginal people from the census and from the parliament's ordinary law-making power. The first substantial statutes of the new parliament created the White Australia policy.

places.name: Centennial Park, Sydney
places.note: Where the Commonwealth was proclaimed on 1 January 1901.

places.name: Royal Exhibition Building, Melbourne

people.role: first prime minister

people.role: attorney-general, later prime minister; architect of both federation and the White Australia policy

people.name: Catherine Helen Spence

pedagogy.hook: Australia's constitution mentions Aboriginal people twice, and both times to exclude them. Section 127 said they were not to be counted in the population at all.

misconception.belief: Australia became independent from Britain in 1901.
misconception.correction: It became a single self-governing country under the Crown. Britain still made Australia's foreign policy, declared war on its behalf in 1914 and 1939, and housed its highest court of appeal. Australia adopted the Statute of Westminster only in 1942 and cut the last legal links in 1986.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Federation shows how a settler colony left the empire's control - slowly, legally, and by keeping the Crown - and it shows who was written out at the founding.

events.title: The Immigration Restriction Act: White Australia
events.summary: One of the first acts of the new federal parliament let officials exclude any immigrant who failed a dictation test of fifty words in a European language - which could be any European language, chosen to make failure certain. A companion act deported Pacific Islanders already working in Queensland.
events.significance: White Australia was not a fringe policy but the founding consensus of the new nation, supported by both major parties and by the labour movement. It shaped immigration for seventy years, was dismantled between 1958 and 1973, and was copied and admired across the settler empire.

places.name: Royal Exhibition Building, Melbourne
places.note: Where the first federal parliament sat and passed the Act.

people.name: Edmund Barton
people.role: prime minister who introduced the Act, telling parliament that 'the doctrine of the equality of man was never intended to apply' to racial equality

people.name: Alfred Deakin
people.role: attorney-general who designed the dictation test to avoid naming any race, so as not to offend Japan or embarrass Britain over Indian subjects

people.name: Joseph Chamberlain
people.role: British Colonial Secretary who pressed Australia not to name races in the Act, because millions of British subjects in India would be insulted

toll.note: Under the Pacific Island Labourers Act 1901 about 7,500 Pacific Islanders were deported from Queensland between 1904 and 1908. Around 1,600 to 2,500 were permitted to stay, mostly long-resident people with families. Figures come from Commonwealth deportation records.

pedagogy.hook: The dictation test could be given in any European language. An official who wanted to keep someone out simply chose a language they did not speak - one man was tested in Scottish Gaelic.

misconception.belief: White Australia was a piece of nineteenth-century prejudice that Australia grew out of.
misconception.correction: It was written in 1901 as the founding policy of a brand-new democracy, supported across the political spectrum and especially by the labour movement, which saw non-white labour as a threat to wages. It was not fully dismantled until 1973. And Britain's objection was not to the racism but to naming it, in case it offended India and Japan.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows an empire of many races producing a self-governing nation whose first act was to exclude most of that empire's subjects - and Britain helping to phrase it politely.

evidence.author: Marilyn Lake
evidence.work: Drawing the Global Colour Line: White Men's Countries and the International Challenge of Racial Equality
evidence.supports: The international making of white-settler immigration policy. Written with Henry Reynolds.

events.title: Gallipoli and the ANZACs
events.summary: Australian and New Zealand troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula as part of a British and French plan to force the Dardanelles. After eight months of stalemate the Allies withdrew. About 8,700 Australians and 2,780 New Zealanders died there, alongside far greater Ottoman losses.
events.significance: Gallipoli became the founding national story of both Australia and New Zealand, which is odd for a defeat in a campaign designed in London. It is also where both countries began to draw the conclusion that their soldiers should not be spent on someone else's plan - an argument that shaped their move away from Britain.

places.name: Anzac Cove, Gallipoli
places.note: Where the Australian and New Zealand corps landed on 25 April 1915.

people.name: William Birdwood
people.role: British general commanding the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps

people.name: John Monash
people.role: Australian brigade commander at Gallipoli who went on to command the Australian Corps in France in 1918

people.name: Mustafa Kemal
people.role: Ottoman commander whose defence of the heights above the landing held the line, and who later founded the Turkish Republic

people.name: Charles Bean
people.role: Australian war correspondent whose reporting and official history made Gallipoli into the national legend

toll.note: Total deaths on all sides at Gallipoli are usually given as between 100,000 and 130,000, the great majority Ottoman. Australian deaths were about 8,709 and New Zealand's about 2,779. Ottoman figures are the least reliable.

pedagogy.hook: New Zealand sent about 100,000 people overseas in the First World War from a population of just over a million. Proportionally, no country in the empire sent more.

misconception.belief: Gallipoli was where Australia and New Zealand became independent nations.
misconception.correction: Both were already self-governing, and neither had any say in the campaign: Britain declared war on their behalf and planned the operation. What Gallipoli produced was a national story and an argument. Australia and New Zealand fought under British command again in 1939-41, and it was the fall of Singapore in 1942, not Gallipoli, that broke the habit.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest illustration of what dominion status meant in practice: full self-government at home, and no vote at all on whether your soldiers went to war.

evidence.author: Christopher Pugsley
evidence.work: Gallipoli: The New Zealand Story
evidence.supports: The New Zealand experience of the campaign and its casualties.

evidence.author: Les Carlyon
evidence.work: Gallipoli
evidence.supports: The campaign, the command decisions and the Australian experience.

events.title: The Stolen Generations

date.note: Child removal began earlier in some colonies - New South Wales legislated in 1883 - and the systematic, legally authorised phase runs from about 1910 to 1970. No single start date fits all jurisdictions.

endDate.note: Removal policies were wound back at different dates in different states; the last of the specific protection statutes went in the early 1970s.

events.summary: Australian governments removed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families under laws that made officials their legal guardians. Children were placed in institutions and white foster homes, often forbidden to speak their languages, and frequently told their parents were dead.
events.significance: It was policy, not accident: the Northern Territory's Aboriginals Ordinance 1918 made the Chief Protector the legal guardian of every Aboriginal child, and similar laws operated in every state. The 1997 Bringing Them Home inquiry documented it, and the Australian parliament apologised in 2008.

places.name: The Bungalow, Alice Springs
places.note: One of the institutions where removed children of mixed descent were held.

places.name: Parliament House, Canberra
places.note: Where Kevin Rudd delivered the national apology on 13 February 2008.

people.name: A.O. Neville
people.role: Chief Protector of Aborigines in Western Australia 1915-40, who told a 1937 conference the aim was to 'forget that there were ever any aborigines in Australia'

people.name: Cecil Cook
people.role: Chief Protector in the Northern Territory who pursued a policy of 'breeding out the colour'

people.name: Ronald Wilson
people.role: former High Court judge who chaired the Bringing Them Home inquiry

people.name: Kevin Rudd
people.role: prime minister who delivered the national apology on 13 February 2008

toll.note: There is no agreed total, and none can now be made: no jurisdiction ever kept a single register of removals. Bringing Them Home concluded that between one in ten and one in three Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were removed between 1910 and 1970, and gave a proportion because the state and mission files that survive are patchy and uneven. The figures in the tens of thousands are reconstructions from those files. The report deliberately gave a proportion rather than a total.
toll.source: The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, Bringing Them Home (1997), which gave a proportion because no register was ever kept.

pedagogy.hook: In 1937 a national conference of Aboriginal protection officials agreed that the aim of policy was that Aboriginal Australians should eventually disappear as a distinct people.

misconception.belief: Children were removed for welfare reasons, as they were from poor white families.
misconception.correction: White children could only be removed by a court on evidence of neglect. Aboriginal children could be removed by an official's decision, without a court, because they were Aboriginal - and the stated goal at the 1937 conference was biological and cultural absorption. That is a different law for a different reason.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the point where the frontier war becomes administrative: the same objective - the disappearance of Aboriginal Australia - pursued with a filing cabinet instead of a rifle.

evidence.author: Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission
evidence.work: Bringing Them Home: Report of the National Inquiry into the Separation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children from Their Families
evidence.supports: The policy, its legal basis, its scale and its effects, from 535 testimonies.

contested.note: The number removed is disputed because no register was ever kept and the surviving files are patchy; the Bringing Them Home range of one in ten to one in three has been criticised as too wide and too high. The existence of the laws, the institutions and the 1937 policy statement is documented and not disputed.

events.title: The 1967 referendum
events.summary: Australians voted by 90.77 per cent - the largest yes vote in the country's history - to delete section 127, which excluded Aboriginal people from being counted in the population, and to let the federal parliament make laws for Aboriginal people.
events.significance: It ended the constitutional exclusion written in at federation and gave Canberra the power that produced the 1976 land rights act and the 1993 Native Title Act. It did not give Aboriginal people the vote - that had come federally in 1962 - and it did not grant citizenship, though both beliefs are widespread.

places.name: Parliament House, Canberra
places.note: The old Parliament House, where the referendum bill passed unopposed.

people.name: Faith Bandler
people.role: campaigner of South Sea Islander descent who led the ten-year public campaign for the referendum

people.name: Charles Perkins
people.role: Arrernte and Kalkadoon activist who led the 1965 Freedom Ride through New South Wales country towns that made segregation national news

people.name: Jessie Street
people.role: campaigner who drafted the petition that started the referendum campaign

people.name: Harold Holt
people.role: prime minister whose government put the question

pedagogy.hook: Until 1967 Australia's constitution said Aboriginal people were not to be counted in the population. Removing that sentence took a ten-year campaign and produced the biggest yes vote in Australian history.

misconception.belief: The 1967 referendum gave Aboriginal people the vote and citizenship.
misconception.correction: It did neither. Aboriginal Australians were British subjects and then Australian citizens like everyone else; they won the federal vote in 1962 and the last state bar fell in Queensland in 1965. The referendum changed two clauses: it let them be counted, and it let the federal parliament legislate for them. That second change is what made land rights law possible.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the moment the exclusions written into the constitution in 1901 were undone, and the beginning of federal Aboriginal policy - for better and worse.
