events.title: Mabo: the High Court rejects terra nullius
events.summary: The High Court of Australia ruled six to one that the Meriam people held native title to their land on Mer in the Torres Strait, and that the doctrine that Australia had been legally empty in 1788 was wrong in law and indefensible in fact.
events.significance: It overturned 204 years of Australian property law and produced the Native Title Act 1993. Native title now covers more than half the Australian continent in some form - and it can be extinguished by valid government grants, so the ruling changed the law far more than it changed the map.

places.name: Mer (Murray Island), Torres Strait
places.note: The island whose gardens and boundaries were the evidence in the case.

places.name: High Court of Australia, Canberra
places.note: Where the judgment was delivered on 3 June 1992.

people.name: Eddie Koiki Mabo
people.role: Meriam man who brought the case after being told he did not own the land his family had gardened for generations; he died on 21 January 1992, five months before the judgment

people.name: David Passi
people.role: Meriam plaintiff and Anglican priest who was one of the successful claimants

people.name: Ron Castan
people.role: barrister who argued the case for the plaintiffs over ten years

people.name: Gerard Brennan
people.role: High Court justice whose leading judgment held that the common law should not perpetuate a doctrine that offended contemporary values

pedagogy.hook: Eddie Mabo spent ten years proving in court that his family owned the garden they had farmed for generations. He died five months before he won.

misconception.belief: Mabo gave Aboriginal people their land back.
misconception.correction: It recognised that native title survived British settlement where an unbroken connection to country could be proved and where no valid government grant had extinguished it. Freehold, most leases and public works extinguish it, so the places where native title survives are largely places nobody else wanted. Recognition and restoration are not the same thing.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the point at which the legal fiction created in 1770 and stated as policy in 1835 was finally struck down - by the descendants of people on the last islands Queensland annexed.

events.title: When did Australia and New Zealand become independent?

date.note: There is no agreed date for either country. Candidates: dominion status (Australia 1901, New Zealand 1907); the Statute of Westminster 1931; its adoption (Australia 1942, backdated to 1939; New Zealand 1947); and the final statutes (Australia Act 1986; New Zealand's Constitution Act 1986, in force 1 January 1987).

events.summary: Neither Australia nor New Zealand has an independence day. British authority over them was removed in pieces: the Balfour Declaration of 1926, the Statute of Westminster 1931, its adoption in Canberra in 1942 and Wellington in 1947, and the constitutional acts of 1986.
events.significance: This is what decolonisation looked like where the settlers were the electorate: no war, no negotiation with a liberation movement, no ceremony - just statutes passed when it became convenient. Both countries still have the British monarch as head of state.

places.name: Parliament House, Canberra
places.note: Where the Statute of Westminster Adoption Act passed in October 1942.

places.name: Parliament Buildings, Wellington
places.note: Where New Zealand adopted the Statute of Westminster on 25 November 1947, sixteen years late.

people.name: John Curtin
people.role: Australian prime minister who in December 1941 said Australia looked to America 'free of any pangs' about its traditional links with Britain

people.name: Peter Fraser
people.role: New Zealand prime minister whose government adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1947

people.name: Arthur Balfour
people.role: author of the 1926 formula defining the dominions as autonomous communities equal in status to Britain

people.name: Bob Hawke
people.role: Australian prime minister who negotiated the Australia Acts with the states and Westminster in 1986

pedagogy.hook: Australia and New Zealand are the only substantial countries in the world with no independence day, because nobody can agree which year they became independent.

misconception.belief: Countries become independent on a single identifiable date, with a flag ceremony at midnight.
misconception.correction: That is what happened in India, Ghana, Fiji and Samoa - where independence had to be demanded. Where the people who would inherit the state were already the electorate, Britain simply stopped legislating for them, one statute at a time, over sixty years. Australia's High Court has treated 1901, 1942 and 1986 as the decisive moment in different cases.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows that the shape of decolonisation depended almost entirely on who counted as a citizen. Settler colonies got statutes; everyone else got a struggle.

evidence.supports: The legal steps and the disagreement about the date.

evidence.publisher: New Zealand Institute of International Affairs
evidence.supports: New Zealand's slow acceptance of dominion autonomy.

contested.note: There is no agreed date for either country and the disagreement is legal, not merely rhetorical: which year counts changes which laws were valid when. This atlas gives the range rather than choosing.

events.title: He Whakaputanga: Britain recognises Maori independence
events.summary: Thirty-four northern rangatira signed He Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni, the Declaration of the Independence of the United Tribes of New Zealand, declaring their country a sovereign state. The British Crown formally acknowledged it in 1836.
events.significance: It means the Treaty of Waitangi five years later was a treaty between two parties Britain itself had recognised as sovereign - not a claim over unowned land. That recognition is the legal foundation of every Maori argument since about what 1840 did and did not transfer.

places.name: Waitangi, Bay of Islands
places.note: Where the declaration was signed and, five years later, the treaty.

people.name: James Busby
people.role: British Resident who drafted the declaration, partly to block a Frenchman's claim to be king of New Zealand

people.name: Te Wharerahi
people.role: Ngapuhi rangatira among the first signatories

people.name: Hone Heke Pokai
people.role: Ngapuhi rangatira who signed the declaration, then the treaty, then fought the Crown

people.name: Charles de Thierry
people.role: French adventurer whose claim to sovereignty over Hokianga prompted Busby to act

pedagogy.hook: Five years before the Treaty of Waitangi, Britain formally recognised New Zealand as an independent country governed by Maori chiefs.

misconception.belief: Britain treated New Zealand as unowned land the way it treated Australia.
misconception.correction: It could not. Britain had already acknowledged He Whakaputanga in 1836 and had recognised a Maori flag in 1834 so that New Zealand-built ships could trade. That is why New Zealand got a treaty and Australia did not: Britain had already conceded there was somebody to sign one with.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the document that makes the two-text problem in the treaty a legal question rather than a moral one.

evidence.work: The Treaty of Waitangi
evidence.supports: The declaration, its recognition and its relation to the treaty.

events.title: The Treaty of Waitangi and its two texts
events.summary: About 540 rangatira signed a treaty with the Crown at Waitangi and at more than fifty gatherings around New Zealand during 1840. The English text ceded sovereignty; the Maori text they signed ceded kawanatanga, governorship, and guaranteed tino rangatiratanga, full chieftainship, over their lands and treasures.
events.significance: It is the founding document of New Zealand and the source of its longest argument. Ignored and called a nullity by the courts for a century, it became enforceable again through the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975 and has since produced settlements worth billions and a permanent place in New Zealand law.

places.name: Waitangi, Bay of Islands
places.note: Where the first signing took place on 6 February 1840.

places.name: Kaitaia
places.note: One of the more than fifty places where sheets were taken for signature during 1840.

people.name: William Hobson
people.role: first governor, who presented the treaty and declared sovereignty on 21 May 1840

people.name: Henry Williams
people.role: missionary who translated the English draft into Maori overnight and chose kawanatanga for sovereignty

people.name: Tamati Waka Nene
people.role: Ngapuhi rangatira whose speech turned the meeting towards signing

people.name: Te Wherowhero
people.role: Waikato paramount chief who refused to sign and was later crowned the first Maori King

people.name: Ana Hamu
people.role: one of at least thirteen women who signed, against the wishes of some missionaries who tried to exclude them

pedagogy.hook: The Treaty of Waitangi exists in two versions that do not say the same thing. Almost every rangatira who signed, signed the Maori one.

misconception.belief: The two texts differ because of a translation error.
misconception.correction: Henry Williams had a word for sovereignty available - mana - and did not use it, because no chief would have signed away his mana. He used kawanatanga, a missionary coinage from the English 'governor', and in the same document guaranteed tino rangatiratanga, the fullest word for chiefly authority. Whether that was diplomacy or deception is the argument; it was not a slip.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: New Zealand is the only settler colony where the founding treaty is still live law, and the reason is that the two texts were never reconciled - so the argument had to be reopened.

evidence.work: The Treaty of Waitangi
evidence.supports: The drafting, the translation, the signings and the aftermath.

contested.note: What the treaty transferred is disputed between the Crown's position - that it acquired sovereignty in 1840 - and the Waitangi Tribunal's 2014 finding that the northern signatories did not cede it. This is a live political argument in New Zealand today, not a settled historical question.

events.title: The New Zealand Wars
events.summary: From Hone Heke's attack on the flagstaff at Kororareka in 1845 to Te Kooti's escape into the King Country in 1872, the Crown fought a series of wars against Maori over land and authority. At the peak in 1864 Britain had about 12,000 imperial troops in New Zealand.
events.significance: Britain deployed more soldiers to New Zealand than to any other settler colony, and lost or drew several campaigns against fortified pa. The decisive weapon was not the army but the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, under which the colonial parliament confiscated about 3.2 million acres from iwi it declared rebels.

places.name: Ruapekapeka pa
places.note: The engineered trench-and-bunker pa that absorbed British artillery in January 1846 - an early anticipation of trench warfare.

places.name: Rangiriri, Waikato
places.note: Where the Waikato invasion was checked in November 1863 at heavy British cost.

places.name: Orakau
places.note: Where Rewi Maniapoto's defenders, surrounded and out of water, refused surrender in 1864.

people.name: Hone Heke Pokai
people.role: Ngapuhi rangatira who cut down the British flagstaff four times and fought the Northern War

people.name: Rewi Maniapoto
people.role: Ngati Maniapoto leader at Orakau in 1864, remembered for the reply that he would fight on for ever

people.name: Titokowaru
people.role: Ngati Ruanui leader whose 1868-69 campaign in Taranaki defeated colonial forces repeatedly

people.name: Te Kooti Arikirangi Te Turuki
people.role: wrongly imprisoned without trial, escaped from the Chatham Islands in 1868 and fought a four-year campaign; founded the Ringatu church

people.name: Duncan Cameron
people.role: British general who commanded the Waikato invasion and quarrelled with the colonial government about fighting a war for settler land

people.name: Tawhiao

toll.note: James Belich counts about 2,150 Maori dead, including Maori fighting for the Crown, and about 745 British, colonial and allied dead. Vincent O'Malley argues Maori civilian deaths from displacement and disease were substantially undercounted. No register was kept.

pedagogy.hook: Maori built trench systems with bomb shelters and firing steps in the 1840s that absorbed British artillery. The same ideas reappeared on the Western Front seventy years later.

misconception.belief: The New Zealand Wars were a series of British victories over outmatched Maori.
misconception.correction: James Belich showed that Maori won or drew several major campaigns, and that British accounts rewrote defeats as victories. The Crown prevailed by weight of numbers, by recruiting Maori allies, and above all by confiscating 3.2 million acres by statute - including from iwi that had fought on its own side.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: These wars produced the raupatu confiscations, which produced the Waitangi Tribunal claims, which produced the settlements New Zealand is still negotiating.

events.title: The invasion of Parihaka
events.summary: About 1,600 armed constabulary and volunteers marched on Parihaka, a Taranaki village of some 2,000 people that had resisted land confiscation for a decade by ploughing and fence-building rather than fighting. They were met by children singing and offering food. The leaders were arrested and the village was destroyed.
events.significance: Parihaka is the largest act of state force against a non-violent community in New Zealand history, and it worked: the Taranaki confiscations stood. It also became a model of organised non-violent resistance decades before Gandhi, and the New Zealand government formally apologised for it in 2017.

places.name: Parihaka, Taranaki
places.note: The village founded in 1866 by Te Whiti and Tohu as a centre of peaceful resistance to confiscation.

people.name: Te Whiti o Rongomai
people.role: founder and leader of Parihaka; arrested and imprisoned without trial

people.name: Tohu Kakahi
people.role: co-leader of Parihaka, arrested with Te Whiti

people.name: John Bryce
people.role: Native Minister who ordered and led the invasion

people.name: Titokowaru
people.role: the former war leader, by 1881 living at Parihaka and committed to its non-violence; arrested with the others

toll.note: Nobody was killed on 5 November 1881. About 1,600 residents were dispersed, the village was demolished, crops and stock were destroyed, women were assaulted, and hundreds of Maori ploughmen arrested in the preceding two years were held without trial in South Island prisons under special legislation.

pedagogy.hook: When 1,600 armed men marched into Parihaka in 1881, the village sent out children with bread and singing. Nobody fought back, and the government demolished the place anyway.

misconception.belief: Non-violent resistance always works because states cannot bring themselves to crush it.
misconception.correction: Parihaka was crushed. The leaders were jailed without trial under laws passed for the purpose, the village was flattened and the confiscated land stayed confiscated. What non-violence bought was a record so damning that it could not be explained away - and 136 years later a government apologised and paid reparations for it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest case in the empire of a state using overwhelming force against people who had deliberately given it no excuse - and of the moral cost being paid, very late, in full public view.

evidence.work: Ask That Mountain: The Story of Parihaka
evidence.supports: The community, the ploughing campaign and the invasion.

events.title: The Waitangi Tribunal reopens the treaty
events.summary: New Zealand's parliament created a standing commission of inquiry to hear Maori claims that the Crown had breached the Treaty of Waitangi. In 1985 its jurisdiction was backdated to 1840, opening 145 years of confiscation, purchase and broken promises to formal investigation.
events.significance: It turned a document the courts had called a legal nullity in 1877 into the basis of settlements worth more than 2.5 billion New Zealand dollars, the return of land and fisheries, and formal Crown apologies. No other former British colony has anything comparable.

places.name: Parliament Buildings, Wellington
places.note: Where the Treaty of Waitangi Act passed in 1975, three weeks after the land march arrived.

places.name: Te Hapua, Far North
places.note: Where Whina Cooper began the 1975 land march that walked the length of the North Island.

people.name: Whina Cooper
people.role: led the 1975 land march from Te Hapua to Wellington at the age of 79, with the slogan 'not one more acre'

people.name: Matiu Rata
people.role: Minister of Maori Affairs who drafted and carried the Treaty of Waitangi Act

people.name: Eddie Durie
people.role: chief judge of the Maori Land Court and Tribunal chairman who shaped its jurisprudence of treaty principles

people.name: David Lange
people.role: prime minister whose government backdated the Tribunal's jurisdiction to 1840 in 1985

pedagogy.hook: In 1877 a New Zealand judge ruled the Treaty of Waitangi was 'a simple nullity'. In 1985 the same country gave a tribunal power to investigate every Crown breach of it since 1840.

misconception.belief: Historic injustices cannot be undone, so there is no point revisiting them.
misconception.correction: New Zealand has been doing it since 1985. Ngai Tahu and Waikato-Tainui each received settlements of 170 million dollars plus land, apologies and the return of sites; more than 70 settlements have been signed. Nobody claims this makes it even - the settlements are typically a small percentage of the value of what was taken - but it is not nothing, and it is a policy other countries study.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the only place in the former empire where a colonial treaty is routinely enforced against the state that broke it.

evidence.author: Claudia Orange
evidence.work: The Treaty of Waitangi
evidence.supports: The treaty's legal history from nullity to enforceability.

evidence.author: Michael King
evidence.work: The Penguin History of New Zealand
evidence.supports: The Maori renaissance of the 1970s and the Tribunal's creation.

events.title: Fiji's chiefs cede the islands
events.summary: Ratu Seru Cakobau and twelve other high chiefs signed a Deed of Cession at Levuka handing Fiji to Queen Victoria. It was their third attempt: Britain had refused in 1858 and again in 1862, and accepted only when settler debt and the labour trade had made the islands ungovernable.
events.significance: Fiji is the clearest case in the Pacific of a colony taken by signature rather than conquest. The deed's terms - especially the protection of Fijian land, which is why 83 per cent of Fiji is still under customary title - are argued about in Fijian politics and courtrooms to this day.

places.name: Levuka, Ovalau
places.note: The colonial capital where the deed was signed; it is now a World Heritage site.

people.name: Ratu Seru Epenisa Cakobau
people.role: Vunivalu of Bau, styled King of Fiji, who signed the cession

people.name: Hercules Robinson
people.role: Governor of New South Wales, who accepted the cession for Britain

people.name: Arthur Hamilton Gordon
people.role: first substantive governor, who made Fijian land inalienable and imported Indian indentured labour instead

people.name: Ma'afu
people.role: Tongan prince who had built a rival kingdom in eastern Fiji and signed the cession alongside Cakobau

pedagogy.hook: Fiji asked to become British three times before Britain said yes. The thing that changed London's mind was a 45,000-dollar bill from the United States government.

misconception.belief: Cession means the colonised chose colonisation.
misconception.correction: Cakobau's kingdom was collapsing under settler land claims, an American damages claim backed by a warship, and a labour trade nobody could police. Signing was the least bad option available, taken under pressure his own actions had helped create. Consent under those conditions is a real signature and not a free choice, and both halves of that sentence matter.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The deed is still cited in Fijian politics as a promise about land and chiefly authority, which makes it one of the few colonial instruments in the Pacific that still has bite.

evidence.author: Deryck Scarr
evidence.work: Fiji: A Short History
evidence.supports: The cession, its causes and Gordon's system.

evidence.author: Brij V. Lal
evidence.work: Broken Waves: A History of the Fiji Islands in the Twentieth Century
evidence.supports: The colonial settlement and its consequences for Fijian politics.

events.title: The 1875 measles epidemic in Fiji

date.note: The epidemic began when the Dido landed in mid-January 1875 and ran through the first half of the year; no single date marks its start.

endDate.note: Deaths continued into the second half of 1875 in remoter districts.

events.summary: Four months after Fiji became British, Cakobau and his sons returned from Sydney carrying measles. The new colonial government did not quarantine them, and a chiefly assembly then gathered people from across the islands. Between a quarter and a third of all Fijians died within months.
events.significance: It is the deadliest single event in Fijian history and it happened at the moment of colonisation, under a government that had the knowledge and the ships to prevent it. The population collapse shaped everything after: labour shortage, the ban on Fijians working plantations, and the decision to import 60,000 Indians instead.

places.name: Levuka, Ovalau
places.note: Where HMS Dido landed the returning chiefs without quarantine.

people.name: Ratu Seru Epenisa Cakobau
people.role: returned from Sydney with his sons carrying measles

people.name: Edgar Leopold Layard
people.role: acting colonial secretary who did not impose quarantine and then summoned a meeting of chiefs, spreading the infection

toll.note: The usual figure is about 40,000 dead, roughly a third of a Fijian population estimated at around 140,000. Some demographers argue the pre-epidemic population was lower and the toll nearer 25,000. Either way it is between a quarter and a third of all Fijians.

pedagogy.hook: Fiji had been British for four months when a ship landed without quarantine and about a third of all Fijians died.

misconception.belief: Disease killed indigenous peoples before colonisation could - it was a tragedy nobody could have prevented.
misconception.correction: Quarantine was standard practice in 1875 and the colonial government chose not to use it, then made things worse by summoning chiefs from across the islands to a meeting. Australia had quarantined ships for decades. This was not the unavoidable arrival of a new disease; it was a governable event, badly governed.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains the shape of modern Fiji: the population collapse produced the labour policy that produced the Indo-Fijian community, and therefore the politics of the last hundred years.

evidence.author: Deryck Scarr
evidence.work: Fiji: A Short History
evidence.supports: The epidemic, the failure to quarantine and the demographic collapse.

evidence.author: Brij V. Lal
evidence.work: Broken Waves: A History of the Fiji Islands in the Twentieth Century
evidence.supports: The consequences of the population collapse for labour policy.

contested.note: The death toll depends on an estimate of Fiji's population before 1875, which is itself uncertain. The commonly cited 40,000 rests on a pre-epidemic population of about 140,000; lower estimates of the population give lower tolls. The proportion - a quarter to a third - is more robust than the absolute number.

events.title: Girmit: Indian indenture in Fiji
events.summary: Between 1879 and 1916, 60,965 people were shipped from India to Fiji on five-year indentures to cut sugar cane. They called the system girmit, from the English word 'agreement'. Recruitment stopped in 1916 and all remaining indentures were cancelled on 1 January 1920.
events.significance: Indenture replaced slavery across the empire after 1834, and Fiji is where it most completely remade a country: about 60 per cent of girmitiyas stayed, and by 1946 their descendants outnumbered indigenous Fijians. Fiji's communal politics, its four coups and its land disputes all run back to this decision.

places.name: Levuka, Ovalau
places.note: Where the Leonidas landed the first 463 indentured migrants on 14 May 1879.

places.name: Nausori sugar mill, Viti Levu
places.note: One of the Colonial Sugar Refining Company mills the system was built to feed.

people.name: Arthur Hamilton Gordon
people.role: governor who banned Fijians from plantation labour and imported Indian workers instead

people.name: Totaram Sanadhya
people.role: girmitiya who served his indenture, stayed, and wrote My Twenty-One Years in the Fiji Islands, the system's most important insider account

people.name: C.F. Andrews
people.role: English clergyman whose 1916 report with W.W. Pearson on conditions in Fiji helped end recruitment

people.name: Kunti
people.role: indentured woman whose 1913 account of resisting an overseer's assault, published in India, became a rallying point for the campaign against indenture

toll.note: 60,965 indentured migrants arrived from India on 87 voyages between 1879 and 1916; the figure comes from the colonial emigration registers and is unusually precise. Mortality on the estates in the early years ran above 40 per thousand a year, and suicide rates among indentured Indians in Fiji were among the highest recorded anywhere.

pedagogy.hook: The word girmit is just 'agreement' in an Indian mouth - the paper people signed with a thumbprint, in a language they could not read, for five years of work 11,000 kilometres from home.

misconception.belief: Indenture was ordinary contract labour: people chose it, were paid, and could leave.
misconception.correction: Indentured workers could be jailed for refusing work or leaving the estate, which is not a feature of employment contracts. Women were about a third of recruits, deliberately, and were exposed to violence with almost no protection. Wages were about a shilling a day with deductions. It was not slavery, and it was not free labour, and the empire designed it precisely to sit between the two.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Indenture is how the empire kept plantations running after abolition, and Fiji is where you can see the whole consequence: two peoples, one country, and a century of politics organised around it.

evidence.author: Brij V. Lal
evidence.work: Girmitiyas: The Origins of the Fiji Indians
evidence.supports: Who the indentured migrants were, where they came from and what happened to them.

evidence.author: Totaram Sanadhya

evidence.supports: First-hand testimony of indenture in Fiji.

events.title: Blackbirding: the Pacific labour trade
events.summary: From 1863 to 1904 recruiters carried about 62,000 Pacific Islanders to Queensland and tens of thousands more to Fiji, Samoa and New Caledonia to cut sugar cane. Some signed contracts they understood; many were tricked, and some were seized at gunpoint or lured aboard by men dressed as missionaries.
events.significance: The trade emptied villages across Vanuatu and the Solomons, spread disease, and built the Queensland sugar industry. It also drove the annexations: Britain declared protectorates over the Solomons in 1893 and the Gilberts in 1892 largely to police its own ships.

places.name: Mackay, Queensland
places.note: The centre of the Queensland sugar industry built on Islander labour; a large Australian South Sea Islander community still lives there.

places.name: Nukapu, Solomon Islands
places.note: Where Bishop John Coleridge Patteson was killed in September 1871, in reprisal for a blackbirding raid.

people.name: Ross Lewin
people.role: one of the most notorious recruiters, who advertised Islanders for sale in Brisbane newspapers and was acquitted of kidnapping in 1871

people.name: John Coleridge Patteson
people.role: Anglican bishop killed at Nukapu in 1871 in reprisal for blackbirders; his death forced the Pacific Islanders Protection Act 1872 through parliament

people.name: James Patrick Murray
people.role: doctor and recruiter who in 1871 imprisoned about 80 Islanders below decks on the brig Carl and had them shot when they resisted; he turned Queen's evidence and was never tried

people.name: Faith Bandler
people.role: daughter of a man kidnapped from Ambrym in 1883; she became a leading Australian civil rights campaigner and named this history for a national audience

toll.note: About 62,000 engagements are recorded for Queensland between 1863 and 1904, and roughly 27,000 more Melanesians went to Fiji. Some people were recruited more than once, so the number of individuals is lower; and mortality was very high - in some years more than 5 per cent of Islanders in Queensland died annually. Figures come from Queensland's own immigration registers, which recorded the legal trade and not the illegal one.

pedagogy.hook: In 1871 a recruiter locked about 80 Islanders below the deck of the brig Carl and shot into the hold when they fought back. He gave evidence against his own crew and was never tried.

misconception.belief: Blackbirding was slavery, so calling it a labour trade is a euphemism.
misconception.correction: Both halves are wrong on their own. Much recruitment was outright kidnapping, especially before 1885; much of it, especially later, was contracted labour that men signed up for repeatedly to get steel tools and money. The system mixed the two deliberately, and the mixture is the point: it let Queensland call it employment and let recruiters behave like slavers when nobody was watching.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It links the Australian colonies to the islands as a single system, and it explains why Britain annexed the Solomons and the Gilberts - to police British subjects, not to protect Islanders.

evidence.author: Clive Moore
evidence.work: Kanaka: A History of Melanesian Mackay
evidence.publisher: Institute of Papua New Guinea Studies
evidence.supports: Recruitment, work and community in the Queensland sugar districts.

evidence.author: Tracey Banivanua Mar
evidence.work: Violence and Colonial Dialogue: The Australian-Pacific Indentured Labor Trade
evidence.supports: The violence inside the trade and how it was described at the time.

evidence.author: Doug Munro
evidence.work: The Pacific Islands Labour Trade: Approaches, Methodologies, Debates
evidence.supports: The historiographical debate over how coercive the trade was.

contested.note: Historians disagree about how much of the trade was kidnapping and how much was consensual recruitment, and the balance changed over time and between islands. Peter Corris and Doug Munro emphasised Islander agency and repeat engagement; Tracey Banivanua Mar and others emphasise the violence that made 'consent' possible. Both are working from the same thin records.

events.title: The Western Pacific High Commission
events.summary: An order in council created a High Commissioner for the Western Pacific with jurisdiction over British subjects in islands not under any recognised government. The Governor of Fiji held the post until 1952, then it moved to Honiara. It was wound up in 1976.
events.significance: It is how Britain governed a quarter of the Pacific without annexing it: a court and a commissioner with authority over British people, created because British ships were kidnapping Islanders and nobody had the power to stop them. Fiji, the Solomons, the Gilberts, the New Hebrides, Tonga and Pitcairn all ran through it.

places.name: Suva, Fiji
places.note: Seat of the High Commission from 1877 to 1952.

places.name: Honiara, Solomon Islands
places.note: Seat from 1953 until the Commission was wound up in 1976.

people.name: Arthur Hamilton Gordon
people.role: first High Commissioner, holding the post alongside the governorship of Fiji

people.name: John Coleridge Patteson
people.role: his killing in 1871 produced the Pacific Islanders Protection Acts under which the Commission was created

pedagogy.hook: For 75 years the Governor of Fiji was also, in his spare time, the ruler of British interests across a quarter of the Pacific Ocean.

misconception.belief: The empire was made of colonies with borders you can colour in.
misconception.correction: The Western Pacific High Commission had jurisdiction over people, not territory: any British subject in any island not under a recognised government. That is a shape no map can show, and it was how Britain operated across the Pacific for decades before it annexed anything much.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the administrative machinery behind half this region's dossiers, and a reminder that imperial authority often followed nationality rather than land.

evidence.work: The Imperial Frontier in the Tropics 1865-75
evidence.supports: The reluctant extension of British authority into the Pacific and the origins of the High Commission.

evidence.work: Fragments of Empire: A History of the Western Pacific High Commission 1877-1914
evidence.supports: The Commission's creation, powers and practice.

events.title: Britain and Germany trade islands over Samoa
events.summary: Britain gave up its claims in Samoa in exchange for Germany renouncing its claims to Tonga and Niue and handing over Choiseul, Santa Isabel, the Shortlands and Ontong Java in the Solomons. Germany kept Bougainville. The Samoan settlement was completed by a three-power convention with the United States on 2 December.
events.significance: Four Pacific countries got their modern shape from these two documents, and none of them was consulted. Samoa was split in two, Tonga became a British protected state, and Bougainville was left on the German side of a line that put it inside Papua New Guinea in 1975 - which produced a war in 1988.

places.name: Apia, Samoa
places.note: Capital of the western islands Germany took.

places.name: Buka Passage, Bougainville
places.note: Just north of the line Germany kept, and 8 kilometres from the Solomon Islands.

people.name: Bernhard von Bülow
people.role: German foreign secretary who wanted Samoa and traded everything else for it

people.name: Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, Marquess of Salisbury
people.role: British prime minister and foreign secretary who made the exchange, weighing German goodwill against Pacific islands

people.name: Mata'afa Iosefo
people.role: Samoan leader whose contested claim to the kingship gave the three powers their pretext to intervene and partition

pedagogy.hook: In 1899 Britain swapped its claim to Samoa for four Solomon Islands and a free hand in Tonga. Germany kept Bougainville - and that one line is why Bougainville is fighting to leave Papua New Guinea today.

misconception.belief: Colonial borders were drawn on the ground by people who knew the territory.
misconception.correction: This one was drawn in European foreign ministries, in a bargain about something else entirely. Nobody consulted a Samoan, a Tongan, a Solomon Islander or a Bougainvillean. The line between Bougainville and the Solomons separates people who speak related languages and see themselves as one chain.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the single clearest example in the Pacific of borders made by trade between empires, and of the consequences arriving a century later.

evidence.author: Paul Kennedy
evidence.work: The Samoan Tangle: A Study in Anglo-German-American Relations 1878-1900
evidence.supports: The negotiation and the exchange of claims.

evidence.author: Judith A. Bennett
evidence.work: Wealth of the Solomons: A History of a Pacific Archipelago, 1800-1978
evidence.supports: The transfer of the northern Solomons and what Germany kept.

events.title: Banaba: an island turned into fertiliser
events.summary: After phosphate was identified on Banaba in 1900, a British company obtained mining rights over the whole island for 999 years at 50 pounds a year. About 22 million tonnes of rock were dug out over 79 years, stripping roughly nine tenths of the surface. In 1945 the surviving Banabans were shipped to Fiji.
events.significance: Banaba and Nauru together fertilised Australian and New Zealand farms for most of the twentieth century, at prices set by the three governments that jointly owned the mine and jointly held the trusteeship. It is the empire's most literal case of consuming a country.

places.name: Banaba (Ocean Island)
places.note: The mined island; it was the capital of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony until 1942.

places.name: Rabi Island, Fiji
places.note: Where 703 Banabans were landed in December 1945; their descendants still live there.

people.name: Albert Ellis
people.role: prospector who recognised the phosphate and spent his life mining Banaba and Nauru

people.name: Rotan Tito
people.role: Banaban leader who campaigned for compensation from the 1940s to his death in 1974

people.name: Robert Megarry
people.role: English judge who heard Tito v Waddell in 1975-76 and found the Crown owed the Banabans no enforceable trust duty

toll.note: 703 Banabans, together with some other residents, were landed on Rabi Island in Fiji in December 1945 with tents and four months of rations. Around 6,000 people of Banaban descent now live in Fiji and about 300 on Banaba. The removal was presented as temporary.

pedagogy.hook: Nine tenths of Banaba was dug up and shipped to Australian and New Zealand farms. Its people were moved 2,600 kilometres to an island in Fiji that had been bought for them with their own royalty money.

misconception.belief: Companies exploited colonies; governments regulated them.
misconception.correction: From 1920 the mine was the British Phosphate Commissioners - owned outright by the British, Australian and New Zealand governments. They set the royalty they paid the Banabans, set the price they charged their own farmers, and administered the colony. Regulator, buyer and owner were the same three states.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Banaba is the plainest answer to the question of who the empire was for. The phosphate went to farms in two dominions; the island is gone; the people live somewhere else.

evidence.author: Katerina Martina Teaiwa
evidence.work: Consuming Ocean Island: Stories of People and Phosphate from Banaba
evidence.supports: The mining, the removal and the Banaban campaign for redress.

evidence.author: Barrie Macdonald

evidence.supports: Banaba's place in the colony's finances and administration.

events.title: The Talune and the 1918 influenza in Samoa
events.summary: The steamer Talune arrived at Apia from Auckland with influenza aboard. New Zealand's administrator, Colonel Robert Logan, allowed it to dock without quarantine. About 8,500 Samoans died in the following weeks - more than a fifth of the population. In American Samoa, under quarantine, nobody died at all.
events.significance: It is the cleanest natural experiment in colonial administration anywhere: two halves of one people, 100 kilometres apart, one governed with quarantine and one without. It destroyed New Zealand's authority in Samoa and helped produce the Mau movement eight years later.

places.name: Apia, Samoa
places.note: Where the Talune docked on 7 November 1918.

places.name: Pago Pago, American Samoa
places.note: Where Governor John Poyer imposed a quarantine and no one died of influenza.

people.name: Robert Logan
people.role: New Zealand administrator who let the Talune dock, refused American offers of medical help, and was recalled

people.name: John Martin Poyer
people.role: US naval governor of American Samoa who quarantined the territory and kept the influenza out entirely

people.name: Helen Clark
people.role: New Zealand prime minister who apologised in Apia in 2002 for the epidemic and for Black Saturday

toll.note: The usual figure is about 8,500 deaths out of a population of roughly 38,000, or 20 to 22 per cent - among the highest national death rates from the 1918 pandemic anywhere in the world. Some estimates are slightly lower. American Samoa recorded no influenza deaths.

pedagogy.hook: Twenty-two per cent of Samoans died of influenza in eight weeks. One hundred kilometres away, in American Samoa, the death toll was zero.

misconception.belief: The 1918 pandemic was a natural disaster that no government could have prevented.
misconception.correction: American Samoa prevented it completely, with quarantine and nothing else. New Zealand's administrator did not impose one, let the ship dock, and then refused an American offer of medical assistance. The two Samoas ran the experiment side by side and the answer is unambiguous.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the strongest single piece of evidence in this atlas that colonial administration was a matter of choices, and that the choices had body counts.

evidence.author: Michael Field
evidence.work: Mau: Samoa's Struggle Against New Zealand Oppression
evidence.supports: The Talune, the epidemic and its political consequences.

evidence.author: Malama Meleisea

evidence.publisher: Institute of Pacific Studies, University of the South Pacific
evidence.supports: The epidemic's effect on Samoan authority and on attitudes to New Zealand rule.

events.title: Black Saturday in Apia
events.summary: New Zealand police fired on an unarmed procession of the Mau movement in Apia. Eleven Samoans were killed, including the Mau's leader Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III, who was shot in the back and told his people as he died not to avenge him. One New Zealand policeman also died.
events.significance: It broke New Zealand's moral standing in Samoa permanently and hardened the Mau into a movement that outlasted the administration. Samoa became the first Pacific country to win independence, in 1962, and New Zealand formally apologised for Black Saturday in 2002.

places.name: Apia, Samoa
places.note: Where the shooting took place on the Beach Road.

people.name: Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III
people.role: Mau leader, shot in the back; his dying words were that his blood had been spilt for Samoa and must not be avenged

people.name: Olaf Frederick Nelson
people.role: Samoan-Swedish merchant who funded and organised the Mau, exiled by New Zealand from 1928

people.name: Stephen Allen
people.role: New Zealand administrator whose police opened fire

people.name: Helen Clark
people.role: New Zealand prime minister who apologised in Apia on 4 June 2002

toll.note: Accounts give between nine and eleven Samoans killed, including Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III, who died of his wounds the following day, and one New Zealand policeman. The lower figure counts only those who died at the scene.

pedagogy.hook: Shot in the back at an unarmed march, the leader of Samoa's independence movement told his people with his last breath not to avenge him. They did not, and they won.

misconception.belief: Independence movements succeed by force or not at all.
misconception.correction: The Mau's programme was a boycott, its own courts, its own police and refusal to pay tax - and after Black Saturday it stayed non-violent, despite having every provocation. New Zealand exiled its leaders, banned it, and could not govern without it. Samoa was independent 33 years later, before any other Pacific state.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the Pacific's clearest case of a colonial power destroying its own legitimacy in a single morning.

events.title: Maasina Rule in the Solomon Islands
events.summary: After watching American forces on Guadalcanal, Malaitans built their own system of chiefs, courts, tax and codified custom, and refused to cooperate with the returning British administration. Britain jailed around 2,000 people, then negotiated, and in 1952 accepted a Malaita Council on Maasina Rule's terms.
events.significance: It is the largest civil disobedience movement in the colonial Pacific and the point at which the Solomons' colonial administration lost the initiative for good. The councils it forced into existence became the local government structure of the independent country.

places.name: 'Aoke, Malaita
places.note: The administrative centre of Malaita, where the confrontation was sharpest.

places.name: Honiara, Guadalcanal
places.note: Built on the American wartime base; the new capital from 1952.

people.name: Nori
people.role: Are'are man, one of the founders of the movement, who had worked with the American forces

people.name: Aliki Nono'oohimae
people.role: Are'are leader of Maasina Rule, jailed by the British and later a member of the country's legislature

people.name: Timothy George
people.role: Malaitan leader imprisoned during the suppression

people.name: William Marchant
people.role: Resident Commissioner who met the movement with mass arrests before his successors changed course

toll.note: Around 2,000 people were arrested and imprisoned between 1947 and 1950, in a protectorate of under 100,000 people. Nobody was killed by the administration; the campaign was non-violent on the islanders' side throughout.

pedagogy.hook: Solomon Islanders watched Americans spend more on their islands in six months than Britain had in fifty years. Then they built their own government and told the British to leave them to it.

misconception.belief: Anti-colonial movements in the Pacific were led by Western-educated elites after the Second World War.
misconception.correction: Maasina Rule was built by returned labourers and wartime carriers, in villages, using custom law written down in exercise books. Its leaders were not lawyers or graduates. Britain called it a cult, arrested 2,000 people, and then adopted its structures because it had nothing better.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the Second World War as the hinge of Pacific decolonisation: the war did not liberate the islands, but it destroyed the assumption that the colonial order was the only possible one.

evidence.publisher: Institute of Pacific Studies, University of the South Pacific
evidence.supports: The movement, its ideas and its suppression, with documents.

evidence.supports: The wider context of labour, war and protest.

events.title: The Battle of Tarawa
events.summary: American Marines assaulted Betio islet in Tarawa atoll, a British colony occupied by Japan. In 76 hours about 1,000 Americans and around 4,700 Japanese and Korean personnel were killed on a strip of coral three kilometres long. Of the defenders, seventeen Japanese and 129 Korean labourers were taken alive.
events.significance: It was the first opposed amphibious landing of the Pacific war and the pattern for every one after it. It also destroyed a British colonial capital and much of an atoll's population's homes, and gave Gilbertese people a first-hand view of an American war machine that made British administration look small.

places.name: Betio, Tarawa atoll
places.note: The islet assaulted on 20 November 1943; wrecked guns and bunkers are still there.

people.name: Keiji Shibazaki
people.role: Japanese admiral commanding Betio, who reportedly said a million men could not take it in a hundred years; killed on the second day

people.name: Julian C. Smith
people.role: American general commanding the 2nd Marine Division

people.name: Robert Sherrod
people.role: war correspondent whose despatches from Betio brought the cost of the Pacific war home to American readers

toll.note: About 1,000 American dead and 2,300 wounded; about 4,700 Japanese and Korean dead. Only 17 Japanese soldiers and 129 Korean labourers surrendered. Gilbertese civilian deaths during the occupation and battle were not systematically counted.

pedagogy.hook: Six thousand people died in 76 hours on a coral islet smaller than most airports.

misconception.belief: The Pacific war was fought between America and Japan over empty islands.
misconception.correction: The islands were British, Australian, French and Japanese colonies with people living on them. Tarawa was a British colony; Japan had executed 22 New Zealand and British coastwatchers there in 1942. Gilbertese, Solomon Islanders and New Guineans lived through the fighting, worked for the Japanese garrison and for the Americans who took it, and died in numbers nobody counted.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The war put the empire's Pacific colonies at the centre of a global conflict they had no say in, and it changed what their people expected afterwards.

evidence.work: Utmost Savagery: The Three Days of Tarawa
evidence.supports: The assault, the casualties and the tactical lessons.

events.title: The Santo rebellion
events.summary: Weeks before independence, Jimmy Stevens's Nagriamel movement declared the island of Espiritu Santo the independent state of Vemarana, with backing from French settlers and an American libertarian foundation. Britain and France would not act; after independence, troops from Papua New Guinea put the rebellion down.
events.significance: It is the sharpest illustration of what the condominium had done to Vanuatu: two colonial powers on opposite sides at the moment of independence, and a new state whose first act was to ask another former colony for soldiers. Vanuatu still runs two school systems in two languages.

places.name: Luganville, Espiritu Santo
places.note: Where Nagriamel declared the state of Vemarana.

places.name: Port Vila
places.note: The condominium capital and then the capital of independent Vanuatu.

people.name: Jimmy Stevens

pedagogy.hook: Vanuatu's first act as a country was to borrow soldiers from Papua New Guinea, because it did not trust either of the two empires that had been governing it the week before.

misconception.belief: Departing colonial powers helped their successors hold the country together.
misconception.correction: In Vanuatu, France backed the secessionists it had cultivated and Britain refused to act without France. The condominium's last act was paralysis, and the new government turned to Papua New Guinea - itself independent for only five years - to restore control of its own territory.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the condominium's incoherence surviving to the last day, and the beginnings of Pacific states helping each other instead of calling London or Paris.

events.title: The Bougainville civil war

date.note: Sabotage at the Panguna mine escalated through November and December 1988; there is no single day on which the conflict began.

events.summary: Panguna landowners, cut out of the profits of a copper mine on their land, sabotaged and closed it. Papua New Guinea sent in its army, then imposed a blockade that lasted years. Estimates of the dead range from 10,000 to 20,000, most from disease and hunger rather than fighting.
events.significance: It is the deadliest conflict in the Pacific since the Second World War, and its causes are colonial: a border drawn by Germany and Britain in 1899, a mine imposed by an Australian administration in 1967-72, and royalties paid to a capital 800 kilometres away. In 2019 Bougainvilleans voted 97.7 per cent for independence.

toll.note: The commonly cited range is 10,000 to 20,000 dead out of a population of about 160,000 - roughly 6 to 12 per cent. Most deaths were indirect, from lack of medicine and food under the Papua New Guinea blockade. No count was possible during the war and researchers regard the upper figure as uncertain.

pedagogy.hook: At its peak the Panguna mine earned nearly half of Papua New Guinea's export income. The people whose land it was received under two per cent of the profits.

misconception.belief: Post-colonial conflicts are internal problems that have nothing to do with the empire that left.
misconception.correction: Bougainville's war has three colonial causes you can date. Germany and Britain put it on the wrong side of a line in 1899. An Australian administration signed the mining agreement in 1967 and pushed it through over landowner objections. And the royalty structure sent the money to Port Moresby. The war started twenty-three years after the mine agreement and thirteen after independence.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest demonstration in this atlas that colonial borders and colonial contracts keep working long after the flag comes down.
